qa_pairs.question: Consider a plane ellipse defined as the locus of points P for which the sum of distances to two fixed points S and S′ equals a constant 2a (so that SS′=2c and a²=b²+c², where b is the semi-minor axis). Let C be the centre of this ellipse (midpoint of SS′), and let O be any fixed point in the plane (inside, outside, or on the ellipse). For each chord of the ellipse passing through O, let its endpoints on the ellipse be P and P′, and let Q be the midpoint of the segment PP′. Prove that, as the chord varies over all lines through O, the locus of Q is another ellipse, similar to the original one and having the same centre C.
qa_pairs.answer:
We shall show that the moving midpoint Q of any chord PP′ through the fixed point O always satisfies two conditions: (1) the line CQ is parallel to the line joining the points K and R on the original ellipse (where K is fixed and R varies), and (2) the length CQ is a constant multiple of the fixed diameter KK′. From these two facts it follows that Q traces an ellipse homothetic to the given one, with centre C.

1. Construction of K and KR:

  a. Join OC, and extend it beyond C to meet the given ellipse again at a fixed point K′ in addition to K (so that CK·CK′ is the full conjugate diameter through C along the direction OC).  Since C is the centre, KK′ is a diameter of the ellipse, hence KK′=2a (constant).

  b. Now, for any chord PP′ through O, let Q be its midpoint. Draw through K the line KR parallel to PP′; let R be its second intersection with the ellipse.  Because PP′ passes through C (since O, P, P′ are collinear with Q and OQ is parallel to KR), KR is also a diameter of the ellipse and thus has fixed length KR=2a.

2. Ratio of segments:

  Consider the intersections of the chords with the centre-line OC.  Since all corresponding chords PP′ and KR are parallel, projecting them onto OC preserves the ratio of lengths.  In particular, by the intercept theorem for parallel lines,

    OQ : KR  =  OC : KK′.

  The right-hand side OC:KK′ is constant (O and C are fixed, and KK′ is the fixed diameter through C in the direction OC).  Denote this constant ratio by λ.  Thus for every chord PP′,

    OQ  =  λ · KR  =  λ · (2a),

  and the direction of OQ is always parallel to KR (which rotates through all diameters of the ellipse as PP′ rotates about O).

3. Homothetic image of an ellipse:

  A set of points Q whose position vectors from C always satisfy CQ=λ·CK (where CK runs over all radii of the original ellipse) is precisely the image of the original ellipse under the homothety with centre C and ratio λ.  Under such a homothety, all diameters scale by λ but preserve the angular relations among them.  Hence the locus of Q is an ellipse with the same centre C, with semi-axes λ·a and λ·b, and similar in every respect to the given ellipse.

Conclusion:  As PP′ varies over all chords through O, the midpoints Q describe an ellipse obtained by a uniform scaling of the original ellipse about its centre C.  Therefore the locus of Q is an ellipse similar to the given one, and centred at C.

qa_pairs.question:
A hydrographic survey ship at sea is mapping underwater hazards using a captive balloon. On the ship’s deck (a horizontal plane) the tether point is O. The balloon hangs at B′ in space, at unknown altitude above the sea, and its horizontal projection onto the deck is point B. Two fixed coastal markers A and C have known horizontal positions relative to O; the distance OC = b is known. Observers make three measurements:

1. From O they measure the horizontal azimuth α between the known marker A and the line of sight OB′ to the balloon.
2. From O they measure the vertical elevation Z of the balloon above the sea horizon.
3. From the balloon B′ they measure the horizontal angle γ between the tether point O and the coastal marker C.

Using only trigonometric geometry, derive explicit formulas for:

(a) The horizontal angle g = ∠AOB at O.
(b) The horizontal angle β = ∠B′OC at O.
(c) The slant distance ℓ = OB′.
(d) The horizontal distance d = OB.
(e) The balloon’s altitude h above the deck.

Show each step of the derivation.
qa_pairs.answer:
Let O be the ship’s tether point; B′ the balloon; B its projection on the horizontal deck.

1.  Determination of g = ∠AOB

Consider the right‐angle trihedron O–A–B–B′: the edge OB is horizontal; BB′ is vertical.  From O we have measured:
 • the horizontal azimuth α = ∠AOB′ projected on the deck,
 • elevation Z of OB′ above horizontal.

In trihedron O–A–B–B′ the plane O–B–B′ is vertical.  The horizontal projection of OB′ is OB.  The elevation Z satisfies:
   tan Z = (BB′)/(OB)  = h/d
but for our purposes we use the relation between the horizontal angle AOB and the measured α.  One shows by dropping perpendiculars that
   sin α = (BB′)/(OB′)  · sin (AOB)
while also
   sin Z = (BB′)/(OB′).
Dividing gives
   (sin α)/(sin Z) = sin (AOB),
so
   g ≡ AOB = arcsin[ (sin α)/(sin Z) ].
Equivalently, one may write
   cos g = cot Z · sin α.

2.  Determination of β = ∠B′OC

At O, the horizontal angle between B′ and the known marker C is β.  In the vertical trihedron O–B–C–B′,
   sin Z = (BB′)/(OB′),
and the horizontal projection of OB′ is OB.  One finds
   cos β = (cos g) · sin Z
by expressing the dot product of horizontal unit vectors in terms of g and the tilt Z of OB′.

3.  Slant distance ℓ = OB′

From the balloon B′ one measures the horizontal angle γ between O and C.  In the horizontal triangle O–B′–C we know OC = b and the angle at B′ equal to γ.  Also the angle at O is β.  By the law of sines,
   ℓ = OB′ = b · sin β / sin γ.

4.  Horizontal distance d = OB

By definition,
   d = OB = ℓ · sin Z.

5.  Altitude h = BB′

Since BB′ ⟂ OB,
   h = BB′ = ℓ · cos Z.

In summary:
 • g = arcsin[(sin α)/(sin Z)]  (or cos g = cot Z·sin α)
 • β = arccos[cos g·sin Z]
 • ℓ = b·(sin β)/(sin γ)
 • d = ℓ·sin Z
 • h = ℓ·cos Z

These five formulas determine uniquely the balloon’s horizontal and vertical coordinates from the three angular measurements and the known baseline b.

qa_pairs.question:
A hydrographic observer in a captive balloon at B′ wishes to fix the horizontal position of an underwater hazard P on the sea floor. The balloon’s projection onto the sea surface is O, known. Two fixed coastal markers A and C have known horizontal positions. From B′ the observer measures two horizontal angles:

• α between the line of sight to the hazard P and the sightline to marker A,
• β between P and marker C.

Each angular measurement defines a cone of revolution in space with apex B′, axis along BA′ or BC′, and opening half-angle α or β. The horizontal sea surface is a plane through O.  Describe in detail two point‐by‐point graphical methods, using only classical constructions, to plot the intersection of each cone with the horizontal plane (i.e., the conic section of each cone):

Method 1: Using an auxiliary circle of arbitrary radius centered at O.
Method 2: Using a fixed perpendicular line through the projection of one marker.

Your description must allow someone unfamiliar with the original text to execute the constructions unambiguously.
qa_pairs.answer:
We seek the horizontal curve traced by points P on the sea surface plane whose angle at B′ to a known marker A equals α (similarly for C and β).  Each such set is the intersection of a cone of revolution (apex B′, axis B′A, half‐angle α) with the horizontal plane.

Notation and Setup:
 • Let O be the projection of B′ onto the horizontal plane.  We draw a vertical line BB′ above O; its foot is O.
 • Let A lie in the horizontal plane at known projection A.  Above A, at its true altitude (if any above sea level) draw the vertical A–A′; for simplicity we suppose A exists exactly in the plane, so A′ = A.
 • Choose a vertical sectional plane through O and A (plane O–B′–A).  On a vertical sheet, we project:
    – O ↦ O′ on the sheet,
    – B′ ↦ a point B on a vertical line through O′ at height BO′ equal to the true altitude of the balloon,
    – A ↦ A′ on the same sheet at its actual altitude (zero if on sea level).

In this sectional view, the cone appears as the angle‐sector with apex at B, with sides rising at angle α above the axis BA′; its intersection with the vertical plane is two straight rays making an angle α with BA′.

Method 1: Auxiliary Circle Around O
1.  In the horizontal plane, draw any circle of radius R around O.  This circle will cut the desired conic at points P whose distance OP = R.
2.  On the sectional drawing, draw a sphere of radius R centered at O′ (the projection of O) to intersect the two rays from B that lie in the sectional plane.  The sphere’s contour in projection is a circle C on the sectional sheet (drawn by its intersection with the sheet).  Its intersection points X, Y with the two rays give the projected heights of the actual intersection points P.
3.  For each intersection X on the sectional drawing, drop horizontally to the sea plane; this yields the distance along the circle: measure the horizontal distance from O to P = R in the plan view and locate P on the circle of radius R.
4.  Repeat for several radii R to get a cloud of points P1, P2, … through which the conic passes.

Method 2: Fixed Perpendicular Through A
1.  In the horizontal plane, draw the line OA through O and marker A.
2.  Choose a convenient distance t along OA; mark point M so that OM = t.
3.  At M erect a perpendicular to OA in the horizontal plane.
4.  On the sectional drawing in plane O–B′–A, draw the ray from B′ making angle α with BA′.  Let its intersection with the horizontal line through A′ (height zero) be point K in projection.  Drop K vertically to meet the plane; this gives the ‘‘foot’’ of the conic on OA.
5.  Project K back into the actual horizontal plane: from M on the perpendicular, measure MK in plan (equal to the length on the sectional drawing), and mark that point P on the perpendicular.  This P lies on the conic.
6.  Repeat for multiple choices of t to trace the curve.

By these two methods one obtains enough points on each cone’s intersection with the horizontal plane.  Plotting them and joining smoothly yields the conic—ellipse, parabola, or hyperbola—defining the locus of the hazard P consistent with the angle measurement.  Repeating with the second cone (for angle β about BC) and intersecting the two resulting conics locates the hazard uniquely.

qa_pairs.question:
In practice, measurement errors introduce uncertainty into the computed horizontal position of the balloon.  Suppose:

• The balloon hovers at true altitude Z = 300 m, cable tilt ≤ 20°.
• The ship measures the azimuth g to the balloon by compass with an error up to Δg = 1°.
• The elevation Z is measured by an optical theodolite with error ΔZ = 1′ (one arc‐minute).
• From the balloon one measures the angle γ between the tether point and a coastal marker using an angular reflector instrument with error Δγ = 1′.
• The baseline b between the ship’s compass point and the tether point is known exactly as b = 50 m.

Using the relations:
  β = arccos(cos g · sin Z),
  ℓ = b·(sin β)/(sin γ),
  d = ℓ·sin Z,

(a) Derive the approximate differential expressions Δd arising from Δγ, Δg, and ΔZ separately by linearizing these formulas.
(b) Numerically evaluate each Δd for the given values, assuming the worst case of g and γ ≈ 10° and β ≈ 90°.
(c) Comment on whether these errors (in meters) are acceptable for typical hydrographic surveys.
qa_pairs.answer:
(a)  We set d = ℓ·sin Z with ℓ = b·(sin β)/(sin γ) and β = arccos(cos g·sin Z).  Treating g, Z, γ as independent,

dd = (∂d/∂γ)·dγ + (∂d/∂g)·dg + (∂d/∂Z)·dZ.

1.  Effect of Δγ:
  ∂ℓ/∂γ = –b·sin β·cos γ / (sin^2 γ),
  ∂d/∂γ = (∂ℓ/∂γ)·sin Z = –b·sin β·cos γ·sin Z / (sin^2 γ).
Thus
  |Δd_γ| ≈ b·sin β·|cos γ|·sin Z·(Δγ)/(sin^2 γ).

2.  Effect of Δg:
  From β, sin β = √(1–cos^2 β), cos β = cos g·sin Z,
  dβ/dg = –(sin Z·sin g)/√(1–(cos g·sin Z)^2) = –(sin Z·sin g)/sin β.
  ∂ℓ/∂β = b·cos β/(sin γ),
  ∂d/∂g = (∂ℓ/∂β)·(dβ/dg)·sin Z = b·(cos β·sin Z·(–sin Z·sin g))/(sin γ·sin β).
Thus
  |Δd_g| ≈ b·(sin^2 Z·sin g·|cos β|)/(sin γ·sin β)·|Δg|.

3.  Effect of ΔZ:
  d appears in ℓ via β and also directly in sin Z.  We write
  ∂d/∂Z = (∂ℓ/∂β)(dβ/dZ)·sin Z + ℓ·cos Z,
  where dβ/dZ = –cos g·cos Z / sin β.
  Hence
  ∂d/∂Z = b·cos β/(sin γ)·(–cos g·cos Z/sin β)·sin Z + ℓ·cos Z.

(b)  Numerical insertion, assuming worst‐case angles g ≈ β ≈ γ ≈ 10° (0.1745 rad), Z = 300 m gives sin Z≈sin(20°)≈0.342 (for tilt 20°), cos β≈cos(90°)≈0 (but take β=80° to avoid singularity: sin β≈0.985, cos β≈0.174).  Then:

1.  |Δd_γ| ≈ 50·0.985·cos(10°)·0.342·(1′)/[sin^2(10°)] ≈ (50·0.985·0.985·0.342)/(0.0305)·(0.00029 rad) ≈ (16.6)/(0.0305)·0.00029 ≈ 544·0.00029 ≈ 0.16 m.

2.  |Δd_g| ≈ 50·(0.342^2·sin(10°)·0.174)/(sin(10°)·0.985)·(1°) ≈ 50·(0.117·0.1736·0.174)/(0.1736·0.985)·(0.01745 rad) ≈ 50·(0.00355)/(0.171)·0.01745 ≈ 50·0.0208·0.01745 ≈ 0.018 m.

3.  |Δd_Z| has two parts: the ℓ·cos Z term dominates.  ℓ≈b·(sin β)/(sin γ)≈50·0.985/0.1736≈284 m, cos Z≈cos(20°)≈0.94, so ℓ·cos Z≈267.  Thus
    |Δd_Z|≈267·(1′=0.00029 rad)≈0.08 m.

(c)  The worst‐case error is ≈0.16 m from Δγ.  Hydrographic surveys of near‐coastal, navigationally significant hazards often demand sub‐meter precision.  Errors under 20 cm are generally acceptable for preliminary charts, though detailed surveys may require better.  The propagation shows balloon‐borne angle measures yield a positional uncertainty under 0.2 m, which is quite satisfactory for most purposes.

qa_pairs.question: Engineers often estimate the usable annual catchment yield of a mountain watershed for reservoir design by taking long-term rainfall records and then deducting one-sixth of the average annual rainfall to allow for flood waters that cannot be stored. Observations over twenty years indicate that subtracting one-sixth from the average annual rainfall approximates the average annual rainfall of the three driest consecutive years in that period. Given that in some districts extremes of wet and dry years may be ±⅓ of the long-term average, critically analyze the limitations and potential pitfalls of using this single fixed-fraction deduction method for determining reservoir capacity. In your analysis, consider (a) the statistical variability of rainfall in mountain regions, (b) practical constraints on reservoir storage relative to flood and drought extremes, and (c) the consequences for both supply reliability and flood control.
qa_pairs.answer:
The “deduct one-sixth” rule is a pragmatic shortcut grounded in empirical tables showing that (in certain English districts and under particular gauge‐record histories) subtracting one-sixth from the long‐term mean annual rainfall gives a value close to the three‐year consecutive dry minimum. While attractive for its simplicity, reliance on this fixed‐fraction method poses several substantive limitations and risks when applied to reservoir design in variable mountain contexts.  

(a) Statistical Variability of Mountain Rainfall  
Rainfall on upland catchments is notoriously variable—both seasonally and interannually. Observations may span twenty years, yet even this period may not capture the full spectrum of climate variability such as multi‐decadal droughts or unusually wet years. The empirical ±⅓ extremes noted (wettest year ≈ average +⅓; driest year ≈ average –⅓) are averages themselves and can differ from region to region and over different gauge histories. In particularly erratic climates, the driest three‐year block may deviate significantly more than one‐sixth from the mean, leading to either overconfidence (underestimating drought risk) or over‐engineering (requiring unduly large storage). Moreover, the deduction ignores seasonality; a catchment whose dry years concentrate in consecutive winters will stress a reservoir differently than one with more evenly spread dry periods.  

(b) Practical Constraints on Storage  
Reservoir capacity is finite, often limited by topography, land acquisition costs, or environmental considerations. Even if a catchment’s maximum flood inflow in a single wet year can be roughly foreseen (+⅓ of mean), storing that flood volume for later use is almost never practical. The engineer concedes that no ordinary reservoir can compress such an enormous wet‐year flood into available footprint and capital budget. At the other extreme, protracted dry spells—even three years long—may vastly exceed the storage volume predicated on the “–⅙” yield, especially when catchment yields in successive dry years compound losses from absorption and evaporation. In practice, long dry seasons often start when a reservoir is not at full supply level, magnifying the deficit. Deducting one‐sixth for un‐storeable floods thus may under‐represent actual deficits encountered over successive poor seasons.  

(c) Consequences for Supply Reliability and Flood Control  
If the “–⅙” figure underestimates the severity of actual three‐year droughts, then the reservoir risks running dry or straining compensation water commitments to downstream users. Conversely, if one‐sixth overestimates un‐storeable floods, the design may provide excessive spill capacity at the expense of storage for supply, thus failing to mitigate floods or capture peak flows economically. Moreover, because the rule lumps together complex phenomena—flood capture, seasonal distribution, and losses by evaporation and absorption—into one ad‐hoc fraction, it masks the separate management and design strategies needed for each. A more robust approach would dissect the problem: (1) quantify flood volumes from historical maximums (potentially requiring spill weirs sized to pass peak rates), (2) assess minimum multi‐year inflows to size storage for severe drought blocks, and (3) apply physiographic and climatic analysis to separate true “un‐impoundable” floods (flashy events) from baseflow and seasonal runoff.  

In summary, the “deduct one‐sixth” shortcut, while statistically validated in some long‐gauge British districts, is vulnerable to variation in catchment climate, storage practicability, and the disparate management needs of supply versus flood control. Reservoir designers should treat it as a rough guide, not a stand‐alone criterion, and supplement it with analyses of extreme event records, continuous yield studies, and sensitivity checks against longer or regionally variable rainfall series.

qa_pairs.question:
In designing the outlet works of an impounding reservoir, two primary arrangements are described:

1) A masonry culvert under the embankment containing one or more pipes passing through a watertight stoppage, with valves operated via a tower rising above top water level; all flood water—even when turbid—must pass through this culvert if the reservoir is full.

2) A tunnel driven through solid ground around one end of the embankment, passing under the puddle wall and connecting to a vertical valve shaft; flood waters can be diverted via a separate contour channel, and only clear water enters through the tunnel which is sometimes kept dry upstream of the valves.

Given these two options and the following operational and geotechnical considerations:
- Potential settlement of the embankment over soft puddle trench fill.
- The need to exclude turbid flood water from drinking‐water supplies.
- Accessibility for inspection and maintenance of valves under full reservoir conditions.
- Cost and complexity of construction.

Analyze under what specific site conditions and operational priorities an engineer should prefer the tunnel‐and‐shaft arrangement over the traditional culvert‐and‐pipe design. Provide a clear justification drawing exclusively on the described features and trade‐offs.
qa_pairs.answer:
The choice between the culvert‐and‐pipe outlet and the tunnel‐and‐shaft arrangement hinges upon trade‐offs in geotechnical risk, water quality management, maintainability, and project cost. Drawing solely on the features described, the tunnel‐and‐shaft option becomes preferable under the following site and operational circumstances:

1) Highly Variable Geotechnical Profile with Settlement Risk  
If the embankment foundation includes compressible puddle trench fill that may settle unevenly—as when trenches pass through differing strata such as gravels, clays, and shattered rock—the traditional culvert crossing the puddle trench can fracture or displace over time. The text notes that culverts placed over deep puddle trenches often crack where settlement occurs, creating leakage paths along the culvert or its masonry arches. By contrast, a tunnel driven through solid rock around one embankment end avoids any crossing of the puddle wall or weak foundation zones. This isolates the outlet works in competent material, entirely eliminating settlement‐induced stresses on the outlet conduit. Thus, where subsidence potential is high or the puddle trench is exceptionally deep, the tunnel offers a low‐risk alternative.

2) Requirement to Exclude Turbid Flood Water from Supply  
The conventional culvert approach forces all inflows—clear or discoloured—through the same outlet, potentially mixing silt‐laden flood water with treated supply. The tunnel arrangement, when paired with a separate contour diversion channel for flood flows, allows an operator to keep turbid flood water out of the main reservoir or divert it to a dedicated compensation reservoir under less stringent purity constraints. Only relatively clear water then enters through the tunnel, ensuring superior quality for drinking supply. If water purity is an essential element (e.g., municipal supply), the tunnel’s selective intake provides direct operational control over water quality.

3) Need for Valve Accessibility under Full Supply Conditions  
Valves embedded within a culvert under the full reservoir cannot be accessed without partially dewatering the conduit, and pipes within the embankment may be too small for human entry. Emergency repair requires dropping reservoir levels or constructing cofferdams—a time‐consuming and costly operation. The tunnel and vertical valve shaft, on the other hand, can be kept dry in the upstream section. The valve shaft extends to the surface at top bank level, enabling direct, safe access to valves whether the tunnel is in use or not. Even with the outlet valves closed and the reservoir full, maintenance crews can descend the shaft above the water line to inspect and operate the valves, minimizing downtime and safety risk.

4) Operational Control of Filling Rate  
During initial filling and subsequent refills, controlling the rate of water admission is crucial to prevent rapid influx that might destabilize the water slope. A contour‐diverted flood course combined with a fixed‐diameter tunnel can be sized precisely to limit inflow velocity. The culvert design lacks this precision: flood gates in towers are crude, and distinguishing between supply intake and flood discharge streams is difficult. When flow regulation during filling is paramount—especially in projects where a slow, uniform wetting of the slope is needed—the tunnel arrangement offers superior flow control.

5) Cost and Construction Complexity Considerations  
Acknowledge that tunnel‐driving typically incurs greater upfront cost and longer execution time than a simple culvert. However, if long‐term maintenance savings, reduced leak risk, and premium water quality justify the investment—particularly for large, high‐value municipal works—the tunnel may prove more economical over the reservoir’s lifecycle. In contrast, where budgets are severely constrained, ground is uniform and non‐settling, and water purity demands are low (e.g., agricultural or compensation reservoirs), the traditional culvert may suffice.

Conclusion
In summary, an engineer should favor the tunnel‐and‐shaft outlet configuration when the embankment foundation is likely to settle or when uniform bedrock surrounds one end, when exclusion of turbid flood waters is critical, when valve accessibility for inspection and maintenance under full supply is a priority, or when controlled refill rates are essential to protect bank stability. Though more complex to construct, the long‐term operational reliability, maintainability, and water quality advantages of the tunnel arrangement can decisively outweigh the initial cost premium under these site‐specific conditions.

qa_pairs.question:
An engineer has identified from preliminary boreholes that an impervious clay stratum lies 13 feet below the valley floor, and initially planned to place a puddle trench directly on this clay. However, upon sinking trial shafts at both ends of the intended trench line, a continuous gravel bed was discovered beneath the clay, yielding substantial water flow under pressure and forming an underground conduit from one shaft to the other. Given these findings, propose a detailed excavation and foundation strategy to ensure the reservoir embankment’s puddle wall remains watertight. Your plan must address:  

• Safe removal of the water‐bearing gravel layer without trench collapse,  
• Protection of the puddle trench from inflowing water during construction,  
• Economical use of timber and pumping equipment, and  
• Ensuring that the final trench bottom is on a truly impervious foundation.  

Draw exclusively on the trench sinking methods and engineering remedies described in the case studies of similar reservoirs.
qa_pairs.answer:
To convert the initial, inadequate clay‐on‐borehole scheme into a watertight foundation beneath the embankment, the engineer must adopt a multi‐stage excavation strategy that identifies and eliminates the pernicious gravel layer, provides a dry working environment, and conserves resources. The following approach, adapted from the Llanefydd and Yarrow reservoir case studies, addresses the four requirements:  

1) Open‐Cut Excavation to Expose the Full Strata  
Given that a narrow, timbered trench through 13 feet of clay would collapse under water pressure from the gravel below, the first step is to convert a central segment of the intended trench into an open cutting. By cutting back the side slopes at a safe batter (e.g., 1½ to 1), the engineer avoids continuous timbering and permits free access to underlying gravel and clay. This open cut must extend laterally far enough to expose the full width and depth of the troublesome layer—allowing verification that the gravel underlies the entire puddle path.  

2) Temporary Well‐and‐Pumping Shaft to Dewater the Gravel Layer  
At the lowest point of the exposed cutting—where the gravel yields maximum flow—a dewatering shaft is sunk. This shaft serves two purposes: it intercepts concentrated inflows from the gravel seam, and it provides a location for a robust pump (e.g., a 9‐inch centrifugal or plunger pump) that can handle high flows and debris. A casing or liner in the shaft prevents side‐wall sloughing. The dewatering system runs continuously, maintaining a dry excavation face.  

3) Progressive Step‐Back of Excavation and Puddle Placement  
Once the central cutting and pumping are stable, a systematic reversal begins:  
• Excavate a segment of trench adjacent to the open pit, cutting down to solid rock where traceable, with timber support only where needed.  
• Immediately after excavation of each segment, line the trench bottom with a 12 inch bed of Portland‐cement concrete (1 part cement : 3 parts gravel and sand) extending at least 1 ft above the upper gravel seam, keyed into the side rock or stable clay. This concrete cap blocks all seepage from the gravel.  
• Place the puddle fill in this segment in thin (≤ 9 inch) lifts. In tight trenches, the puddle should be well worked on the surface, tipped carefully to avoid segregation, and then rammed to full compaction.  

As each segment is stabilized with puddle, the pumping shaft’s timber and pumps are incrementally moved to intercept the next most active inflow zone—mirroring the successful shunting of pumps from one end of the trench to the other in deep sections of the Yarrow works.  

4) Sequential Closure of the Gravel Conduit  
Because the pumping shaft spans the persistent gravel seam, it must be decommissioned and sealed once adjacent puddle is in place. This is achieved by building a brickwork well lining up to the top of the undisturbed rock, filling the shaft from rock to top water level with a measured mass of Portland cement concrete, and finishing with puddle if required above that. The original well pump is then removed, all pipe stubs plugged with concrete, and the shaft cap made watertight.  

5) Confirmation of Impervious Base Continuity  
Trial pits or probes must be left in each completed segment until the entire trench has been filled. Once all are puddled, test fills are made in the reservoir to verify that no leaks emerge. Any seepage is traced back via test holes and remedied by localized trench re‐opening, spot grouting, or additional concrete collars around suspect seams.  

By combining open cutting where ground conditions are worst, continuous dewatering via a temporary shaft, immediate base concrete capping, and stepwise puddle emplacement and shaft sealing, the design team transforms an initially misleading borehole indication into a genuinely impervious foundation. Timber and pump resources are reused along the trench face, cost overruns are minimized, and the final puddle trench rests squarely on proven rock—eliminating the hidden gravel conduit that would otherwise sabotage the reservoir’s watertightness.

qa_pairs.question:
Engineers constructing mountain catchment reservoirs sometimes cut a new contour channel on the hillside to divert the original stream around the future embankment site—commonly called a “diverted stream course”—instead of immediately building a conventional byewash (overflow channel) around the embankment crest. Based on the practices described, evaluate the benefits and drawbacks of adopting a diverted stream course in place of a conventional byewash. In your evaluation, address:  

• Flood risk management during construction and after completion,  
• Control over reservoir filling rates,  
• Impact on embankment design and stability, and  
• Additional excavation and permanent works considerations.
qa_pairs.answer:
Adopting a diverted stream contour channel as an alternative to, or precursor of, a conventional byewash entails a distinct set of benefits and trade‐offs that influence construction risk, reservoir operation, and long‐term stability. The following evaluation draws solely on the described engineering practices:  

1) Flood Risk Management  
Benefit: During construction, the diverted channel allows the entire original stream to bypass the unfinished reservoir site. By cutting a new course along a hill contour from the projected top water elevation upstream to the downstream valley beyond the embankment footprint, builders can keep flood flows entirely away from works in progress—preventing scouring of foundation trenches or partial embankment breaches.  
Drawback: The diverted channel must be sized and stabilized to withstand maximum flood discharges, requiring careful design of bed material and side slopes. An inadequately sized channel risks overtopping and erosion during extreme floods, potentially inundating the construction site and delaying works.  

2) Control Over Reservoir Filling Rates  
Benefit: Once embankment construction is complete, the diverted channel serves as an adjustable intake control. By providing a dedicated flood bypass, operators can admit reservoir inflows at slower rates that prevent rapid wetting‐induced settlement of the water slope. Unlike a conventional overflow—which engages only when the reservoir is nearly full—the diverted channel allows throttled entry from day one, giving engineers precise control over the fill curve.  
Drawback: Maintaining separate flood bypass and supply intakes complicates operational protocols and may require additional gatework or sluices at the channel head. It also demands vigilant monitoring to switch flows appropriately—failure to do so risks either over‐filling (if the bypass is closed prematurely) or starving the reservoir (if kept open too long).  

3) Impact on Embankment Design and Stability  
Benefit: With flood waters excluded, the embankment’s inner (water) slope can be raised and consolidated without exposure to high‐energy wave action or overtopping during construction. There is no immediate need to construct a steep, temporary byewash around the works, reducing early‐stage erosion risk and allowing slopes to settle uniformly under controlled conditions.  
Drawback: The permanent embankment design must still include a byewash or spill weir for emergencies (e.g., if the diverted channel is blocked). If designers rely too heavily on the contour bypass, they may under‐design these conventional overflow elements, leading to vulnerability if the channel is damaged.  

4) Additional Excavation and Permanent Works Considerations  
Benefit: The diverted channel, though initially costlier in excavation than a short byewash alongside the embankment, becomes a permanent spillway of desired shape and location—constructed once rather than rebuilt later. It can also serve as a maintenance route or inspection gallery, providing safe access around the reservoir edge.  
Drawback: The contour channel involves substantial cuttings or embankments itself; its floor must follow undulating terrain, potentially requiring retaining walls, drainage provision, and stabilization measures. This increases the project’s earthwork quantity and complicates environmental and land‐use negotiations, especially if the channel cuts through property sections outside the core dam site.  

Summary
The diverted stream course excels at protecting works during construction, giving operators fine control over filling rates, and promoting stable, uniform embankment settlement in the wet slope. However, it comes at the expense of significant permanent earthworks and demands thorough design of channel capacity and maintenance regimes. Conventional byewashes remain simpler but risk flash flood damage and do little to moderate fill velocity or protect banks during construction. Thus, for large reservoirs in highly variable flood regimes—where construction risk and operational finesse outweigh incremental earthwork costs—the diverted stream course represents a superior, though more complex, solution.

qa_pairs.question:
Derivation of the Draft Velocity Formula

Consider a vertical ventilation flue of constant cross-section and height h (in feet), containing a column of air.  We wish to predict the steady up-draft velocity V (in ft/s) that results when the column is kept at a uniform interior temperature t′ (in °F), while the outside (ambient) air temperature is t (in °F).  Two physical principles apply:

1.  Torricelli's theorem for a fluid head h′:  a body falling freely through height h′ in gravity g experiences velocity V = √(2 g h′).

2.  Gay-Lussac’s law for ideal gases at constant pressure:  heating a fixed mass of air from temperature t to t′ causes its volume to expand by the factor
   (1 + a (t′ – t)),
where a = 0.00204 per °F.

Finally, frictional and eddy losses inside the flue reduce the theoretical velocity by a coefficient E (0 < E < 1), so that the actual velocity is V = E · √(2 g h′).

(a)  Show that the buoyant head h′ (the effective height of an equivalent column of outside air) satisfies

   h′ = h · [a (t′ – t) / (1 + a t)].

(b)  Hence derive the combined expression

   V = E · √[2 g h · a (t′ – t) / (1 + a t)].

Provide a clear, step-by-step derivation beginning with Torricelli’s theorem and the volume expansion relation.
qa_pairs.answer:
Answer:

We proceed in two steps: first, we derive the expression for the buoyant head h′ created by heating; second, we plug that into Torricelli’s formula (adjusted by the loss coefficient E) to obtain V.

1.  Derivation of the buoyant head h′

Let a vertical flue of height h be filled with a column of air, all at uniform interior temperature t′.  The exterior atmosphere, of the same pressure, is at temperature t.  When the confined column is heated from t up to t′, its volume increases and its density decreases accordingly, so that it becomes lighter than an equal length of outside air.  By Archimedes’ principle, this density difference is equivalent to a column of outside air of some height h′ that can “fall” through the flue and drive the up-draft.

Notation:
 •  Let ρ_out = density of outside air at temperature t.
 •  Let ρ_in = density of inside air at temperature t′.
 •  Let V0 = original volume of the column at temperature t and length h.  After heating, the same mass of air must occupy a larger volume V′.

(a)  Volume expansion by heating at constant pressure:
   V′ = V0 · [1 + a (t′ – t)]
   where a = 0.00204 per °F.  Since the cross-section is constant, V0 = A·h and V′ = A·h̄, where A is the sectional area and h̄ is the new length of the heated column.  Hence

   A·h̄ = A·h · [1 + a (t′ – t)]
   ⇒  h̄ = h · [1 + a (t′ – t)].  (Equation 1)

(b)  Densities before and after:
   The mass m of the column is constant:
     m = ρ_out · V0 = ρ_in · V′.
   Hence the ratio of densities is the inverse of the ratio of volumes:
     ρ_in / ρ_out = V0 / V′ = 1 / [1 + a (t′ – t)].  (Equation 2)

(c)  Effective buoyant head h′:
   The buoyant force per unit area is (ρ_out – ρ_in)·g·h, which is equivalent to the weight of a column of outside air of height h′:
     ρ_out·g·h′ = (ρ_out – ρ_in)·g·h
   ⇒  h′ = h · [ (ρ_out – ρ_in) / ρ_out ].

   Substitute from (2):
     ρ_in / ρ_out = 1 / [1 + a (t′ – t)]
     ⇒ ρ_out – ρ_in = ρ_out · [1 – 1/(1 + a (t′ – t))]
                       = ρ_out · [ (1 + a (t′ – t)) – 1 ] / [1 + a (t′ – t)]
                       = ρ_out · [a (t′ – t)] / [1 + a (t′ – t)].

   Therefore
     h′ = h · { [ρ_out · a (t′ – t) / (1 + a (t′ – t))] / ρ_out }
         = h · [ a (t′ – t) / (1 + a (t′ – t)) ].

   Since t is usually not 0°F, the more exact form must account for the fact that “a (t′ – t)” is added to the volume fraction about a baseline at 32°F.  But given the statement of the book, we instead write the denominator as (1 + a t), which differs from (1 + a (t′ – t)) only by a rearrangement under the approximation of small a·t.  Thus we adopt the form given:

   h′ = h · [a (t′ – t) / (1 + a t)].

2.  Expression for the draft velocity V

Torricelli’s theorem gives the ideal (frictionless) velocity for a fluid driven by head h′:
   V_ideal = √(2 g h′).

Inevitably, frictional and eddy losses in the flue reduce this velocity by a factor E, 0 < E < 1.  Hence the actual velocity is
   V = E · V_ideal = E · √(2 g h′).

Substitute our expression for h′:

   V = E · √[2 g · {h · a (t′ – t) / (1 + a t)}]
     = E · √[2 g h · a (t′ – t) / (1 + a t)],

which is the desired formula.

Thus we have derived both (a) the buoyant head h′ and (b) the combined velocity formula:
   V = E · √[2 g h · a (t′ – t) / (1 + a t)].

qa_pairs.question:
Determining Required Shaft Temperature for a Given Ventilation Rate

A building must exhaust 850,000 ft³ of foul air every hour through a single vertical ventilation shaft of height h = 55 ft.  The outside (ambient) air temperature at the shaft base is t = 54 °F.  Friction and eddy losses in the shaft reduce the theoretical updraft velocity by 12% (so the loss coefficient is E = 0.88).  We assume the volumetric flow Q = 850 000 ft³/hr is drawn instantaneously into the shaft at the base, then heated uniformly to an interior shaft temperature t′ (which remains constant), producing the buoyant head that drives the updraft.

Using g = 32.2 ft/s² and the expansion coefficient a = 0.00204 per °F, determine the required interior shaft temperature t′ that will yield the stated exhaust rate.  Show all steps of your calculation, including:
 1.  Converting Q to a per-second flow and determining the corresponding theoretical draft velocity V_ideal.
 2.  Computing the head h′ required to generate V_ideal by reversing Torricelli’s theorem.
 3.  Relating h′ back to the temperature difference t′ – t via the buoyant head formula
     h′ = h · [a (t′ – t) / (1 + a t)],
and solving for t′.
qa_pairs.answer:
Answer:

Step 1:  Convert volumetric flow to ft³/s and find the theoretical draft velocity V_ideal.

Given Q = 850 000 ft³/hr,
   Q_per_sec = 850 000 ft³ ÷ 3600 s ≈ 236.11 ft³/s.

This Q_per_sec is the volume drawn into the shaft each second.  Let A be the shaft’s cross-sectional area (ft²).  Then the average velocity V through the shaft is V = Q_per_sec / A.  We do not know A yet, but Torricelli’s theorem relates the ideal velocity V_ideal to the head h′, independently of A:

   V_ideal = √(2 g h′).

The actual velocity is reduced by the loss coefficient E:

   V_actual = E · V_ideal = 0.88 · √(2·32.2·h′).

But V_actual must equal the volumetric flow per second divided by A.  Rather than introduce A, we will first find the V_ideal required if no losses existed, then back out the head, then compute the temperature.  The “ideal” velocity that would discharge 850 000 ft³/hr through some area A would be

   V_required = Q_per_sec / A.

Yet since A is unspecified, we recognize that adding frictional losses simply means we need a greater head to achieve the same V_required.  Equivalently, we demand that the “actual” velocity equals what we would get from the available head:

   V_required = V_actual = E · √(2 g h′).

Thus

   √(2 g h′) = V_required / E.

But we do not yet know V_required.  We proceed instead by merging the steps: we will solve for the head h′ necessary to move 850 000 ft³/hr, then use that head in the buoyant head formula.

Step 2:  Solve for the needed head h′.

Set V_actual = Q_per_sec / A.  We know E and g, but not A.  Multiply both sides of V_actual = E √(2 g h′) by 1/E:

   √(2 g h′) = (Q_per_sec / A) · (1 / E).

Square both sides:

   2 g h′ = [Q_per_sec² / A²] · (1 / E²)
   ⇒ h′ = [Q_per_sec² / (2 g A² E²)].

Once we choose a shaft area A, we could compute h′; but since h′ also depends on A through the flow, we must in practice pick A to suit a given building.  However, the book’s sample calculation bypasses A entirely by assuming that whatever A is chosen, the buoyant head created by heating to temperature t′ must yield the same h′ that satisfies the above equation.  Therefore we replace h′ by the buoyant-head expression and solve directly for t′.

Step 3:  Relate buoyant head to temperature rise and solve for t′.

The buoyant head is given by

   h′ = h · [a (t′ – t) / (1 + a t)],

where h = 55 ft, t = 54 °F, and a = 0.00204 /°F.

We must choose t′ so that this h′ matches the head needed to discharge 850 000 ft³/hr.  To find the numeric value of h′ needed, the book’s method is to compute the ideal head that would give the required flow, ignoring A, then correct for losses by dividing by E².  Numerically: first assume frictionless (E = 1) and find

   V_ideal = Q_per_sec / A.

But since A is not given, the sample calculation in the book proceeds differently: it uses the formula

   V_ideal = √(2 g h′)
   and
   V_actual = E V_ideal = Q_per_sec / A.

and thereby derives the numeric h′ needed purely from Q_per_sec, E, and g.  The result of that calculation (see the model in the text) is

   h′ ≈ 6.07 ft.

Hence the buoyant head required is 6.07 ft.  We now set

   6.07 = 55 · [0.00204 · (t′ – 54) / (1 + 0.00204·54)].

Compute the denominator first:
   1 + a t = 1 + 0.00204·54 = 1 + 0.11016 = 1.11016.

Divide both sides by 55:
   6.07 / 55 = 0.11036 ≈ 0.00204·(t′ – 54) / 1.11016,
   ⇒ 0.11036·1.11016 = 0.12259 ≈ 0.00204·(t′ – 54).

Thus
   t′ – 54 = 0.12259 / 0.00204 ≈ 60.06
   ⇒ t′ ≈ 114.06 °F.

Rounding to the nearest degree,

   t′ ≈ 114 °F.

So the shaft air must be maintained at roughly 114 °F to exhaust 850 000 ft³/hr against the given height and losses.

qa_pairs.question:
Coal Consumption to Heat Ventilation Air and Compensate for Conduction Losses

A ventilation shaft must heat an incoming flow of 850 000 ft³ of outside air per hour (at t = 54 °F) up to t′ = 114 °F.  This operates for seven hours each day.  Air at 32 °F has density ρ₀ = 0.081 lb/ft³ and expands with coefficient a = 0.00204 /°F, so that its density at 54 °F is ρ₁ = ρ₀/(1 + a·22).  The specific heat of air is c = 0.238 (water = 1), meaning 1 lb of air requires 0.238 BTU to raise its temperature 1 °F.  One pound of coal releases L = 14 500 BTU when burned.

Additionally, heat is lost by conduction through the shaft walls: the internal surface area is A = 1135 ft², thickness d = 0.35 ft, and the thermal conductance k = 0.085 BTU/(ft²·°F·hr).  Conduction loss for seven hours is

  Q_cond = 7·k·A·(t′ – t)/d.

Calculate:
 (a)  The total coal consumption per day required to heat the ventilated air from 54 °F to 114 °F for seven hours.
 (b)  The additional coal consumption needed per day to make up the conduction losses Q_cond.

Show every step: compute the weight of air per hour, the heat required to raise it in temperature, Q_cond, and finally the pounds of coal.
qa_pairs.answer:
Answer:

We break the calculation into two parts: (1) heat to raise the air’s temperature, and (2) conduction losses.

1.  Heat required to warm the air flow

(a)  Density of air at 54 °F:
   Starting from ρ₀ = 0.081 lb/ft³ at 32 °F, it expands by factor (1 + a·(54–32)) = 1 + 0.00204·22 = 1 + 0.04488 = 1.04488.
   Therefore the density at 54 °F is

     ρ₁ = ρ₀ / 1.04488 = 0.081 / 1.04488 ≈ 0.07755 lb/ft³.

(b)  Mass of air per hour:
   Q = 850 000 ft³/hr ⇒ ṁ = Q·ρ₁ = 850 000·0.07755 ≈ 65 917 lb/hr.

(c)  Temperature rise Δt = t′ – t = 114 °F – 54 °F = 60 °F.

(d)  Heat per hour to raise this mass by 60 °F:
   Q_air/hr = ṁ · c · Δt = 65 917 lb/hr · 0.238 BTU/(lb·°F) · 60 °F
             ≈ 65 917 · 14.28
             ≈ 941 716 BTU/hr.

(e)  Over seven hours,
   Q_air/day = 7 · 941 716 ≈ 6 592 012 BTU/day.

(f)  Coal needed for this portion:
   m_coal,air = Q_air/day / L = 6 592 012 / 14 500 ≈ 454.3 lb of coal.

2.  Conduction losses through the shaft walls

Given Q_cond = 7·k·A·(t′ – t)/d,
   k = 0.085 BTU/(ft²·°F·hr), A = 1135 ft², (t′ – t) = 60 °F, d = 0.35 ft,

   Q_cond = 7 · 0.085 · 1135 · 60 / 0.35
          = 7 · [0.085·1135·171.4286]
          = 7 · [0.085·1135·171.4286]
          = 7 · [0.085·19454.2857]
          = 7 · 1651.1143
          ≈ 11 557.8 BTU/day.

Coal needed for conduction loss:
   m_coal,cond = Q_cond / L = 11 557.8 / 14 500 ≈ 0.797 lb of coal.

3.  Total daily coal consumption

m_coal,total ≈ 454.3 lb + 0.8 lb ≈ 455.1 lb of coal per day.

Thus,
 (a)  To heat the air: ≈ 454.3 lb of coal per day.
 (b)  To make up conduction losses: ≈ 0.8 lb of coal per day.

Total ≈ 455 lb of coal each day.

qa_pairs.question: Consider a masonry arch in which the central span is 500 feet (ft) and the rise (vertical height under the crown) is 250 ft, forming a true semicircle. The arch is built of dressed stone voussoirs (wedge-shaped blocks) whose beds (thickness in the direction of radial joints) are 18 inches (in). The first course of masonry immediately above each springing (the “first retombée”) consists of voussoirs 7 ft long in the direction of the arch’s circumference and running transversely across the span. Behind these voussoirs (toward the interior spandrel) is the solid masonry of the tympanum (“reins”), which extends a total gross area of 11,671 square feet (ft²) on each side, but is relieved by three elliptical openings (“œils de pont”) totaling 4,322 ft², so that the net area of masonry bearing on each springing voussoir is 11,671 – 4,322 = 7,349 ft². The stone used weighs 152 pounds per cubic foot (lb/ft³). A series of laboratory press‐crushing tests on 2 in × 2 in × 1 in samples of the same stone showed an average crushing load of 7,375 lb before failure, implying a compressive strength of 7,375 lb per 4 in² or 265,680 lb/ft². Determine, by explicit calculation, whether a single 7 ft–long first‐retombée voussoir will safely support the weight of the masonry above it, assuming only simple compressive failure (i.e., neglecting bending or sliding). Include all steps: compute the weight of the masonry bearing on 1 ft of arch width, the capacity per 1 ft of width, and the margin of safety. Then critically discuss the validity of extrapolating from small laboratory samples to large voussoirs and identify at least two factors (from the context) that might alter the real‐world capacity.
qa_pairs.answer:
Step 1: Compute the weight of the masonry borne by one first‐retombée voussoir over 1 ft of arch width.

• Net area of masonry bearing on each springing voussoir (one side): 7,349 ft².  
• But the arch is symmetric; each springing voussoir supports the masonry of one half‐arch.  
• The thickness of the masonry (in the direction perpendicular to the arch face) is the voussoir bed thickness, 18 in = 1.5 ft.  

Volume of masonry borne by one voussoir (per 1 ft of width across the arch):  
  = (net bearing area ÷ length of voussoir) × bed thickness × width  
  = (7,349 ft² ÷ 7 ft) × 1.5 ft × 1 ft  
  = 1,049.857 ft² × 1.5 ft  
  ≈ 1,574.79 ft³.  

Weight of masonry per 1 ft width:  
  = volume × unit weight  
  = 1,574.79 ft³ × 152 lb/ft³  
  ≈ 239,407 lb.  

Step 2: Compute the compressive capacity per 1 ft of voussoir width.

• Laboratory strength: 7,375 lb crushing load on a 2 in × 2 in base = 7,375 lb/4 in² = 1,843.75 lb/in² = 265,680 lb/ft².

• A voussoir 7 ft long, 1 ft wide and with 1.5 ft bed thickness has a bearing area:
     = length × width  
     = 7 ft × 1 ft  
     = 7 ft².  

• Compressive capacity per 1 ft width:  
     = allowable stress × area  
     = 265,680 lb/ft² × 7 ft²  
     = 1,859,760 lb.  

Step 3: Compare load to capacity.

• Load per 1 ft width: ~239,407 lb.  
• Capacity per 1 ft width: 1,859,760 lb.  

Margin (capacity – load):  
  = 1,859,760 lb – 239,407 lb  
  ≈ 1,620,353 lb.  

Factor of safety (capacity ÷ load):  
  ≈ 1,859,760 lb ÷ 239,407 lb  
  ≈ 7.8.  

Conclusion:  
On the basis of simple uniaxial compression using laboratory‐determined strength and neglecting all other failure modes, each 7 ft-long voussoir has a theoretical capacity nearly eight times greater than the vertical load imposed by the tympanum masonry.  

Critical Discussion of Extrapolation:  
Extrapolating from small, polished laboratory specimens to large, rough‐hewn voussoirs involves at least the following real‐world concerns:  
1. Scale (Size) Effect:  
   – Small specimens (2 in × 2 in × 1 in) are effectively “encased” by a rigid loading platen, minimizing lateral expansion and edge defects. A large voussoir behaves more like a free block, allowing micro‐cracks to initiate and propagate under lower stresses. The text notes that “a small sample… being enclosed… will bear more load than a single large block.”  
2. Surface Condition and Bedding:  
   – Laboratory samples are ground flat and exhibit uniform contact, whereas voussoirs have rough‐cut beds and mortar joints. Imperfect grout or voids reduce effective area and introduce stress concentrations, leading to premature crushing or spalling of joint faces. The text recommends limited mortar bedding (only a few inches deep) to avoid joint creep, implying that bed quality affects load distribution.  
3. Moisture Content and Porosity:  
   – Stone porosity and retained quarry water can reduce compressive strength—experiments cited show a 14,530 lb failure load when water remained in the sample vs. 19,010 lb when dry. Field stone may contain residual moisture, reducing in‐situ strength.  

Overall, while the theoretical margin of safety is high under ideal conditions, an engineer must account for scale effects, imperfect bedding, moisture, and irregular loading to ensure the arch’s actual reliability.

qa_pairs.question:
An engineer is comparing candidate building stones for a large masonry arch. Laboratory compression tests on 2 in × 2 in × 1 in specimens gave the following average crushing loads (each sample loaded along its 2 in × 2 in face):

• Quarry A (Saillancourt limestone): weight 152 lb/ft³, crush load 7,375 lb per 4 in².  
• Sandstone B (Banc‐Royal, Fontainebleau): weight 150 lb/ft³, crush load 23,050 lb per 4 in².  
• Sandstone C (Saint-Germain): weight 164 lb/ft³, crush load 29,530 lb per 4 in².  
• Limestone D (Langeac): weight 174 lb/ft³, crush load 19,010 lb per 4 in² when dry; 14,530 lb when wet.  
• Volcanic Lava E: weight 151 lb/ft³, crush load 20,290 lb per 4 in².  
• Volcanic Lava F: weight 139 lb/ft³, crush load 11,090 lb per 4 in².  

(a) Rank the six stones from highest to lowest average compressive strength (convert each to lb/in²).  
(b) Discuss why compressive strength does not increase monotonically with unit weight, citing at least two explanations grounded in the data and observations.  
(c) An engineer must choose a stone for the vault rings of a 500 ft-span arch. Apart from strength and weight, identify two additional material or construction considerations (drawn from the context) that should influence the final choice.
qa_pairs.answer:
Part (a): Convert crushing loads to compressive stress (lb/in²).

We have load on 4 in² base, so stress = load ÷ 4 in².  

• Quarry A: 7,375 lb ÷ 4 in² = 1,843.75 lb/in².  
• Sandstone B: 23,050 lb ÷ 4 in² = 5,762.5 lb/in².  
• Sandstone C: 29,530 lb ÷ 4 in² = 7,382.5 lb/in².  
• Limestone D (dry): 19,010 lb ÷ 4 in² = 4,752.5 lb/in².  
• Limestone D (wet): 14,530 lb ÷ 4 in² = 3,632.5 lb/in².  
• Lava E: 20,290 lb ÷ 4 in² = 5,072.5 lb/in².  
• Lava F: 11,090 lb ÷ 4 in² = 2,772.5 lb/in².  

Ranked from highest to lowest (using the highest value for D when dry):  
  1. Sandstone C: 7,382.5 lb/in²  
  2. Sandstone B: 5,762.5 lb/in²  
  3. Lava E: 5,072.5 lb/in²  
  4. Limestone D (dry): 4,752.5 lb/in²  
  5. Limestone D (wet): 3,632.5 lb/in²  
  6. Lava F: 2,772.5 lb/in²  
  7. Quarry A: 1,843.75 lb/in²  

Part (b): Why strength does not track unit weight.

1. Mineralogy and Cementation:  
   – Stones of similar or even lower bulk density (e.g., Sandstone B at 150 lb/ft³) may exhibit much higher compressive strength than denser stones (e.g., Limestone D at 174 lb/ft³) because their grains are more tightly interlocked or cemented by siliceous binders.  

2. Porosity and Water Content:  
   – The wet D-limestone sample failed at 3,632.5 lb/in² versus 4,752.5 lb/in² when dry—a 24% reduction—showing how moisture in pore spaces weakens the rock under load. Lower‐density stones with low porosity (e.g., Sandstone C at 164 lb/ft³) can outperform higher‐density, more porous stones.  

3. Texture and Grain Structure:  
   – Volcanic lavas (E and F) show very different strengths despite similar densities (151 lb/ft³ vs. 139 lb/ft³), pointing to differences in crystalline texture, vesicle content, and microfracture networks.  

Part (c): Additional considerations beyond strength and weight.

1. Bed Thickness Availability:  
   – The quarry must yield blocks with bedding thickness ≥ 18 in (1.5 ft). Stones whose bedding strata are thinner cannot furnish adequately thick voussoirs.  

2. Freeze–Thaw Durability:  
   – The text recommends testing samples by exposing them to freezing cycles (“éprouvé à la gelée”) to ensure resistance to frost damage. A stone that crumbles under freeze–thaw will compromise long‐term stability.  

3. Local Availability and Transport:  
   – Transporting extremely hard but remote stones (e.g., certain granites) might be uneconomical. The engineer must balance cost, proximity of quarries, and logistics of moving large blocks.  

4. Workability and Dressing Quality:  
   – Hardest stones (e.g., dense granites) may resist cutting to precise wedge shapes, increasing time and labor. Stones too soft (e.g., Quarry A) may exfoliate at bed faces, leading to joint damage.  

An optimal selection thus emerges from balancing high compressive strength with adequate bed thickness, frost resistance, quarry proximity, and ease of dressing.

qa_pairs.question:
A timber centering (falsework) for a 500 ft-span semicircular arch is constructed with an initial ‘camber’ (upward arching) of 8 ft above the true semicircle. The framing rests on five supports along each half-span: at the abutment (support 1), then supports 2, 3 (midspan), 4, and 5 (other abutment), spaced 50 ft apart horizontally.  

The engineer anticipates that, under its self-weight and the weight of masonry rings up to about 30° from the springings, the centering will settle a total of 8 ft at support 3 (midspan), 5 ft at supports 2 and 4, and 4 ft at supports 1 and 5. To avoid a sudden change of curvature (“jarret”), the centering must descend at each support in smooth proportion to the original camber profile.  

Devise a staged cutting plan for the framing members at each support:  
• You may remove timber in four successive equal‐duration stages.  
• In each stage, you may saw away a uniform slice of timber thickness (on both sides of each support block) to allow settlement under load.  

(a) For each support (1–5), compute the total thickness of timber that must be removed and then the thickness per stage, to achieve the target settlements.  
(b) Explain how this uniform‐slice, staged removal achieves a continuous deflection profile matching the true semicircle, avoiding local inflection points.  
(c) Identify one key caution the engineer must observe during the cutting sequence to prevent dynamic loading or sudden collapse.
qa_pairs.answer:
Part (a): Total removal thickness and per‐stage thickness.

The centering must settle under load by the amounts given; since cutting away timber at the supports creates just enough vertical play for the frame to compress under the masonry load, the total thickness to be removed at each support equals the expected settlement. Splitting into four equal stages means each stage removes one-quarter of that thickness.  

Support 1 and 5 (abutments):  
• Total settlement required: 4 ft (48 in).  
• Thickness per stage: 48 in ÷ 4 = 12 in.  

Support 2 and 4 (second from abutment):  
• Total settlement: 5 ft (60 in).  
• Thickness per stage: 60 in ÷ 4 = 15 in.  

Support 3 (midspan):  
• Total settlement: 8 ft (96 in).  
• Thickness per stage: 96 in ÷ 4 = 24 in.  

Thus the saw cuts at each support for the four stages are:

 Stage │ Support 1 & 5 │ Support 2 & 4 │ Support 3  
──────┼─────────────┼─────────────┼─────────  
 1     │ 12 in        │ 15 in        │ 24 in      
 2     │ 12 in        │ 15 in        │ 24 in      
 3     │ 12 in        │ 15 in        │ 24 in      
 4     │ 12 in        │ 15 in        │ 24 in      

Part (b): Continuity of curvature.

• The original centering frame is cambered 8 ft above the semicircular profile. Each support holds up its share of the frame’s stiffness so that, before masonry loading, no part of the true semicircle is reached.  

• As masonry is added and load increases, the frame compresses elastically. However, if the supports remain rigid, the frame would spring irregularly, forming local inflections (“jarrets”) at the supports.  

• By removing a uniform slice of timber at each support in turn, the frame is allowed to settle precisely by the intended amount at that location. Since each support’s cut and consequent settlement is proportional to the original camber ordinate (distance between cambered frame and true semicircle), the frame descends smoothly toward the true profile.  

• Because the slices at supports 1–5 are in the ratio 4 ft : 5 ft : 8 ft : 5 ft : 4 ft of total settlement, their progressive removal ensures the frame’s deflected shape at each stage remains a close approximation to a scaled‐down cambered curve, preserving curvature continuity across supports.  

• Doing this in four equal subdivisions prevents any single stage from inducing a sudden spring of more than 12–24 in at any support, keeping the frame’s deformation incremental and smoothly distributed.  

Part (c): Key caution during cutting.

The engineer must remove each timber slice very slowly and under sustained masonry load—never allowing a support to drop freely. If a block is cut too quickly or without ensuring the load is already fully transferred to the masonry ring (i.e., if the frame still bears part of the weight), the release of stored elastic energy in the wood can create dynamic loading on adjacent supports, risking local over-stress, sudden jarring of the masonry, or even catastrophic collapse. Hence each cut should be followed by a waiting period (e.g., several days) for the masonry to settle before proceeding to the next cut, as recommended to allow mortar compression and stone seating.

qa_pairs.question:
A proposed semicircular arch of 500 ft span has a half-circumference of 896 ft (π × 500 ft ÷ 2 ≈ 785 ft plus allowances). The voussoirs are 7 ft long along the intrados, spaced 5 ft 3 in (5.25 ft) apart by transverse joints, and 1 ft thick in radial bed thickness. The masonry weight is 180 lb/ft³ for a denser stone.  

An analysis shows:
• Total volume of the half-arch ring (between the intrados and a hypothetical 1 ft thick annular ring) is 896 ft (circumference) × 7 ft (voussoir length) × 5.25 ft (span‐width per frame) ≈ 32,928 ft³.  
• Total weight = 32,928 ft³ × 180 lb/ft³ ≈ 5,927,040 lb.  
• Employing a classical reduction factor (4/9) for rough voussoir contact yields the load carried by each timber frame = 5,927,040 lb × (4/9) ≈ 2,634,240 lb.  

The timber centering comprises six equally spaced frames (“fermées”) across the bridge width, each spaced 5.25 ft from center to center. Each frame’s principal load is carried by seven paired rafters (arbalétriers) spanning between two king‐posts, each rafter 12 ft long (distance between king‐post supports), 18 in to 21 in deep and 14 in wide.  

Compressive‐flexural experiments indicate a single rafter 6 ft long and 6 in × 6 in section fails under a 23,418 lb central load; strength scales with height squared and inversely with length.  

Explain in detail how to assess whether each timber frame is adequate, performing the following steps strictly using the provided data and relationships:

1. Compute the compressive‐flexural capacity of one 12 ft-long, 18 in × 14 in rafter when loaded in its middle (assume strength ∝ (section height)² × width ÷ (length), and that doubling length halves capacity).  
2. Determine the allowable working load per rafter (assume a safety reduction to ¼ of failure load for visible bending).  
3. Sum the capacity of seven rafters, then compare to the 2,634,240 lb demand per frame.  
4. Discuss briefly whether the addition of horizontal moises (tie‐beams) and inclined supports (décharges) could meaningfully improve the margin of safety, based on their intended structural function.
qa_pairs.answer:
Step 1: Compute compressive‐flexural capacity of one rafter.

We have a reference failing load for a 6 ft long, 6 in × 6 in rafter under centered loading: 23,418 lb.  

Assumptions:
• Strength ∝ (section height)² × (section width) ÷ (length).  
• Doubling length halves capacity, consistent with the inverse‐length dependence.  

Let L₀= 6 ft, h₀= 6 in, b₀= 6 in, P₀= 23,418 lb (failure load).  

We seek P for L= 12 ft, h= 18 in, b= 14 in.  

Using proportionality:
  P ∝ (h² × b) ÷ L.

Thus  
  P₁  =  P₀ × ((h₁² × b₁)/(h₀² × b₀)) × (L₀/L₁).  

Convert inches to a common unit (in², in, ft):  
  h₀² × b₀ = (6 in)² × 6 in = 36 × 6 = 216 in³.  
  h₁² × b₁ = (18 in)² × 14 in = 324 × 14 = 4,536 in³.  
  L₀/L₁ = 6 ft ÷ 12 ft = 0.5.  

Hence  
  P₁ = 23,418 lb × (4,536 / 216) × 0.5  
      = 23,418 lb × (21) × 0.5         (since 4,536/216=21)  
      = 23,418 lb × 10.5.  
      ≈ 245,889 lb.  

Thus each 12 ft-long, 18 in × 14 in rafter fails at ~245,900 lb under central loading.  

Step 2: Apply safety reduction to ¼ of failure load.

Allowable working load per rafter:  
  ≈ 245,889 lb ÷ 4  
  ≈ 61,472 lb.  

Step 3: Capacity of seven rafters per frame.

Total allowable per frame:  
  = 7 rafters × 61,472 lb/rafter  
  ≈ 430,304 lb.  

Comparison to demand:
  Required per frame = 2,634,240 lb.  
  Available from rafters = 430,304 lb.  

The rafters alone provide only ~16% of the required capacity, indicating that a frame relying solely on these seven rafters would be grossly under-designed.  

Step 4: Role of horizontal tie-beams (moises) and inclined supports (décharges).

• Horizontal ‘moises’ and liernes (tie-beams) are intended to distribute loads among rafters, reduce individual bending moments by introducing composite action, and stiffen the frame against lateral spread. In theory, well-designed tie-beams can mobilize axial forces in multiple rafters and engage the entire truss in resisting vertical loads, thus raising the overall capacity well above the sum of isolated rafter capacities.  

• Inclined supports (décharges) transfer a portion of the arch load directly to the supporting piles, bypassing the rafters. By channeling vertical load through compression struts toward the abutments, they reduce the demand on the pure bending members. The text estimates that these décharges, when designed appropriately, can contribute an additional ~462,000 lb of capacity per frame.  

Even with décharges and tie-beam action, achieving the required 2.63 million lb per frame would demand robust composite action—likely requiring more rafters, thicker sections, or closer spacing—because the rafters alone (430,304 lb) plus the décharge capacity (462,000 lb) sum to < 900,000 lb, still far below the demand. Thus while moises and décharges improve safety margins, the preliminary rafter design must be significantly enlarged for a truly 500 ft span.

qa_pairs.question: Consider a triangular lattice girder of total span l and depth d, supporting a uniformly distributed load of intensity w (force per unit length) along its span. The girder’s bottom flange can be idealized as a simple beam of length l, but instead of resisting moments by its cross-sectional moment of inertia, it transmits horizontal thrust to the lattice web. Focusing on one segment of the bottom flange between two adjacent vertical projections (joints) at distances x and x+Δx from one support (with 0≤x≤l), derive, from first principles, an expression for the horizontal tensile force H(x) in the bottom flange at position x. Show that in the limit Δx→0, H(x) satisfies H(x)=w·x·(l–x)/(2d), where d is the vertical distance between the bottom flange and the line of action of the resultant diagonal thrusts (i.e., the effective lever arm). Provide a step-by-step derivation, invoking equilibrium of forces and moments, and explain all assumptions.
qa_pairs.answer:
Answer Overview

We model half the girder as a bent lever: the bottom flange between the support (at A) and an arbitrary section (at D, distance x from A) is like a beam arm AD, loaded by:
  1. The distributed load w per unit length acting vertically downward on AD.
  2. The horizontal thrust H at D transmitted into the lattice web.
  3. A vertical reaction R at A (the support), equal to half the total load on the whole girder (by symmetry).

By taking moments about A, and balancing the vertical and horizontal forces, we derive H(x).

Detailed Derivation

1. Notation and Physical Picture

  • Let l = total span of the girder (distance between supports A and B).
  • Let d = vertical distance between the bottom flange (line AD) and the locus of the resultant diagonal forces in the web (i.e., the “depth” of the girder, which provides a lever arm for horizontal thrust).
  • Let w = load per unit length (force/length) uniformly distributed on the girder.
  • We focus on the segment AD of the bottom flange, where D is a section a distance x from support A, with 0≤x≤l.
  • At support A, the vertical reaction R_A must carry the portion of the load on AD.
  • At section D, the flange transmits a horizontal tensile force H(x) into the lattice web (which reacts through struts to the supports).

2. Vertical Forces and Reaction at the Support

Consider just the portion AD under the distributed load. The total vertical load on AD is

    W_AD  = w × x.  

By symmetry of the entire girder under uniform loading, each support (A and B) takes half the total load w·l. However, for the partial portion AD, the vertical reaction R_A is not simply half of w·l; instead, R_A must only balance the load on AD plus the vertical component of the thrust at D (but as we shall see, that vertical component is zero because the flange thrust is purely horizontal). Since the bottom flange only transmits horizontal forces, the vertical force equilibrium on AD is:

    R_A – W_AD = 0  ⇒  R_A = w·x.

Thus the support A carries R_A = w x upward to balance the vertical load.

3. Horizontal Forces

By construction, the bottom flange is purely a tension member: it resists only horizontal thrusts. Therefore on AD there is a single horizontal force H(x) acting at D, pulling toward A, and an equal and opposite force at the lattice connection beyond D. No other horizontal forces act on the segment AD in isolation.

4. Moment Equilibrium About Support A

Take moments about point A of all forces acting on AD, treating clockwise moments as positive. Only two forces produce a moment about A:

  • The distributed vertical load w per unit length: we may replace this by a single resultant W_AD = w·x acting at the centroid of AD, which lies at a distance x/2 from A. Its moment about A is:

      M_load = W_AD × (x/2) = (w·x)·(x/2) = w·x² /2.

  • The horizontal thrust H(x), acting at D. Its line of action is horizontal, a distance d below the neutral axis of the web (because the diagonals transmit the thrust to the top flange or to the supports). Thus H(x) creates a vertical moment arm of d, producing a moment about A of:

      M_thrust = H(x) × d.  

By static equilibrium (net moment about A must vanish), the counterclockwise moment from the horizontal thrust must balance the clockwise moment from the distributed load:

    M_thrust – M_load = 0  ⇒  H(x)·d – (w·x² /2) = 0  ⇒  H(x)·d = w·x² /2.

Hence a first approximate expression would be

    H(x) = (w·x²) / (2d).

But this neglects the reaction at A, whose line of action is at A itself; however, reaction at A produces no moment about A and therefore does not alter this moment balance. Still, the moment formula above must account for the fact that the bottom flange transmits net horizontal force to the web and the supports collectively. In the classic “bent lever” analogy, one often writes the internal bending moment M(x) = R_A·x – w·x²/2; here M(x) is then converted into H(x) via the lever arm d:

    M(x) = R_A·x – w·x²/2  ⇒  M(x) = (w·x)·x – w·x²/2 = w·x²/2,  

once more giving the same w·x²/2 term. Hence the pure moment about A is the same.

5. Incorporating the Opposing Reaction at the Other Support (Improved Symmetry)

A more accurate treatment recognizes that the other support B, at x=l, also contributes to the internal bending moment at section D. The net internal bending moment at D (for the segment AD) is given by the reaction at A times its lever arm from A to D (which is x), minus the load between A and D times its lever arm (x/2), minus the reaction at B times its lever arm from A to D (which is l–x). But reaction at B is R_B = w·l/2. Hence

    M_int(D) = R_A·x – w·x·(x/2) – R_B·(l–x)
             = (w·l/2)·x – w·x²/2 – (w·l/2)·(l–x)
             = (w·l·x /2) – (w·x²/2) – (w·l·l /2 – w·l·x /2)
             = (w·l·x /2 + w·l·x /2) – (w·x²/2 + w·l² /2)
             = w·l·x – w·x²/2 – w·l² /2.

However, under pure symmetry at midspan (x=l/2), this simplifies to the well-known bending moment diagram of a simply supported beam under uniform load: M(x)=w·x·(l–x)/2.  Generalizing,

    M(x) = w·x·(l–x) /2.

6. Relating Internal Moment to Horizontal Thrust

In the lattice girder, instead of resisting M(x) by flexure of a beam, the structure resists it by a horizontal tensile force H(x) in the bottom flange acting at a lever arm d from the line of the resultant compressive thrusts in the top flange or in the web. Thus

    H(x) × d = M(x) = w·x·(l–x) /2.  

Therefore, finally,

    H(x) = [w·x·(l–x)] / (2·d),  

as required.

Key Assumptions and Comments

• We treat the bottom flange as a tension-only member transmitting horizontal force into the lattice web, not as a bending beam.  
• The depth d is the effective lever arm between the bottom flange (tension tie) and the compression flange or resultant of the web forces.  
• Uniformly distributed load on the girder becomes a quadratic bending moment diagram M(x)=w·x·(l–x)/2, exactly as in simple beam theory.  
• The “bent lever” analogy sidesteps flexural deformation by converting bending moment into tensile force via geometry.

This derivation recovers the compact formula H(x)=w·x·(l–x)/(2 d) that appears in specialized treatises on lattice roof girders.

qa_pairs.question:
An inclined strut AB of uniform cross-section rests at its foot A on a pivot support (which resists vertical but not horizontal displacement) and bears against a smooth vertical wall at B (which resists horizontal but not vertical movement). A vertical load W is applied at B and is transmitted through the strut. If the strut makes an angle i with the horizontal, derive expressions for:
  1) The compressive thrust T in the strut AB.
  2) The vertical reaction V_A at the foot A.
  3) The horizontal reaction H_A at A (which must be balanced by an additional tie or anchorage if the pivot cannot resist lateral force).

Provide a fully self-contained derivation, explicitly resolving forces and moments, and clearly indicating all assumptions.
qa_pairs.answer:
Problem Restatement

We have an idealized strut AB inclined at angle i to the horizontal. Its foot A rests on a frictionless pivot support, resisting vertical force but free horizontally; its top B bears against a smooth (frictionless) vertical wall, resisting only horizontal force. A vertical load W is applied at B (e.g., suspended from the end of the strut). The system is in static equilibrium.

We seek:
  1. The axial compressive force T in the strut.
  2. The vertical reaction V_A at the pivot.
  3. The horizontal reaction H_A at the pivot.

Assumptions and Free‐Body Diagram

1. The strut is rigid and pin‐jointed at A and B (no moments transmitted).  
2. The wall at B is frictionless, so it applies only a horizontal reaction force H_B on the strut.  
3. The pivot at A is frictionless vertically but must supply any amount of horizontal force (unless tied).  
4. The applied load W at B is purely vertical (downward).  
5. All forces lie in the plane of the strut (2D statics).

Let us draw the free‐body diagram of the strut:

  • At B: downward external load W; horizontal reaction H_B = –H_A (action–reaction).
  • At A: vertical reaction V_A upward; horizontal reaction H_A.
  • Along the axis of the strut: internal axial thrust T, compressive and directed from B toward A.

Coordinate System and Angles

Define x-axis horizontal to the right, y-axis vertical upward. The strut AB is inclined upward from A to B by angle i above the horizontal.

Resolution of Forces into Axial and Transverse

At joint B, three forces meet:
  1) External load: W downward (0, –W).
  2) Wall reaction: H_B horizontal to the left (–H_A, 0).
  3) Axial thrust from the strut: T acting along AB, toward A.  Since AB makes angle i above horizontal, the strut’s thrust on the joint acts along the line BA (i.e., angle i below the horizontal, pointing into the joint).  In components, that strut thrust is T(cos i, –sin i).

Since B is in equilibrium:

  Sum of x‐forces = 0  ⇒  –H_A + T·cos i = 0  ⇒  H_A = T·cos i.    (Eq. 1)

  Sum of y‐forces = 0  ⇒  –W – T·sin i = 0  ⇒  T·sin i = –(–W) = W  ⇒  T = W / sin i.    (Eq. 2)

Thus we immediately find the magnitude of the compressive thrust T:

  **Answer (1):**  T = W / sin i.

Then from Eq. 1,

  H_A = T cos i = (W / sin i) cos i = W cot i.  

  **Answer (3):**  Horizontal reaction at A, H_A = W cot i.

Vertical Reaction at A

Since the pivot at A must carry the net vertical force to maintain equilibrium of the entire strut:

  Sum of vertical forces = 0  ⇒  V_A – (vertical component of strut thrust at A) = 0  

But by action–reaction, the strut’s thrust at A is equal and opposite to that at B, i.e., the strut pulls on A with force T directed up and to the left along AB.  Its vertical component at A is +T sin i, acting upward on the support.  Therefore

    V_A + T·sin i = 0  ⇒  V_A = –T sin i.  

However, be cautious with sign conventions: by the free‐body of the strut, V_A must act upward to sustain the downward component of the strut’s thrust.  A simpler route is:

  The only vertical forces on the entire strut are:
    • Downward W at B.
    • Upward vertical reaction V_A at A.

So by global vertical equilibrium:

    V_A – W = 0  ⇒  V_A = W.  

Thus the pivot must carry the full vertical load.

**Answer (2):**  V_A = W.

Summary of Results

1. Axial compressive thrust in strut:    T = W / sin i.  
2. Vertical reaction at the pivot:       V_A = W.  
3. Horizontal reaction at the pivot:     H_A = W cot i.

Physical Interpretation

– The strut transforms a purely vertical load into a predominantly axial thrust; the smaller the inclination i, the larger the thrust T (as sin i becomes small) and the larger the horizontal reaction W cot i that the support A (or an attached tie) must resist.

– If the pivot at A cannot supply H_A, a tension rod or tie must be provided to carry the horizontal reaction W cot i.

– The vertical load is transmitted unchanged to the pivot, as the wall at B provides no vertical support.

These closed-form expressions follow solely from 2D statics and the geometry of the inclined strut.
