qa_pairs.question:
A circular dome is subject to a uniform load distributed over its surface. Consider a horizontal ‘‘ring’’ or joint of the dome having diameter d′, and examine the portion of the dome above that ring. The total load carried by the dome above this ring is W. At the ring, the meridional (radial) lines of the dome make an angle i with the horizontal tangent.  

a) Derive the magnitude of the resultant horizontal radiating thrust H_rad at the ring.  
b) Given that the dome wants to spread horizontally, show how to compute the tension T_hoop that must be carried by a circumferential hoop (ring) at that joint to resist the spreading.  

Provide a self-contained derivation, beginning with force equilibrium of the free-body (the dome above the ring), and express answers in terms of W, i, and d′.
qa_pairs.answer:
Problem Setup

We ‘‘cut’’ the dome by a horizontal plane at a ring of diameter d′.  Consider the portion of the dome above this ring as a free body.  It carries:
  • Gravity load W acting vertically downward (the total weight of all shell material above the cut).
  • Internal membrane forces along the cut:  
      1) A resultant of meridional tensions/compressions (acting along the ‘‘latitude’’ directions), which resolve into vertical and horizontal components.  
      2) A circumferential (hoop) tension T_hoop acting tangentially around the ring, resisting tensile opening of the ring due to meridional thrusts.

We assume:
  – The dome shell carries only in‐plane stresses (no bending).  
  – Each meridian (great‐circle) acts like a two‐force member, so all meridional forces at the cut are directed along the tangent to the shell, at angle i above the horizontal.  
  – Hoop stresses are uniform around the ring.

Our task:
  a) Find the resultant horizontal radiating force H_rad at the ring due to meridional tensions.
  b) Find the hoop tension T_hoop required to keep the ring from expanding.

Free-Body Force Equilibrium

Let N be the total resultant of all meridional (radial) tensions/compressions acting along the ring toward the cut section.  By symmetry, N must be in pure tension (since the dome above pushes outward on the ring).

Resolve N into vertical and horizontal components:

  • Vertical component: N·sin i (upward on the cut),  
  • Horizontal component: N·cos i (horizontal, radially outward on the cut).

Since the only vertical loads on the portion of dome above the ring are the gravity load W (downward) and the vertical component of N (upward), vertical equilibrium demands:

    N·sin i – W = 0   ⇒   N = W / sin i.  

Hence the total meridional tension resultant along all meridians (summed around the ring) is N = W csc i.

a) Radiating Horizontal Thrust H_rad

This is simply the horizontal component of N:

    H_rad = N·cos i = (W / sin i)·cos i = W·cot i.  

Thus all the meridians collectively push the ring outward with force W cot i.

b) Circumferential Hoop Tension T_hoop

To resist this outward ‘‘spreading,’’ a circumferential ring or hoop must carry tension.  By symmetry, we distribute H_rad uniformly around the circle of circumference π·d′.  Hence hoop tension per unit length (force/length) is

    H_unit = H_rad / (π·d′) = (W·cot i) / (π·d′).  

If one prefers the total hoop tension force (integrated around the circumference), note that the ring in tension acts like a closed string carrying a uniform tension T_hoop.  The net outward pressure it exerts on each infinitesimal segment balances the meridional thrust.  However, engineers often speak of hoop tension as force per unit width; the above H_unit is precisely that.  If instead you define T_hoop as the total tension in one half of the ring (for instance, between two diametrically opposite points), then the total hoop force is

    T_hoop_half = (H_rad / 2) = (W·cot i) /2,  

but more conventionally, one writes the required hoop tension per unit circumference as:

    **T_hoop = (W·cot i) / (π·d′).**

Summary of Final Formulas

1. Total horizontal radiating thrust:  H_rad = W·cot i.  
2. Hoop tension per unit length (around circumference):  T_hoop = H_rad / (π·d′) = (W·cot i) / (π·d′).

Interpretation

– As the dome becomes steeper (i→90°), cot i→0, so both horizontal thrust and hoop tension vanish: a tall, steep shell transmits mostly vertical loads.  
– As the dome becomes flatter (i small), cot i grows large, and the hoop must carry large tension to prevent the shell from bursting outward.  
– The required hoop tension inversely scales with d′: larger diameter rings spread less for the same W and inclination.

These results follow solely from force equilibrium of a symmetric shell segment, without invoking bending.

qa_pairs.question: In the philosophical analysis of axioms for geometry, one views axioms not as innate necessities of pure intuition but as idealizations of empirical observations.  Empirical measurements of spatial relations always carry finite precision and depend on particular conditions.  When formulating axioms, one replaces these approximate, context-bound empirical statements by claims of absolute generality and precision, subject only to fitting the data and avoiding logical contradiction.  Moreover, one invokes Mach’s principle of the “economy of thought,” so that among all axiom systems fitting the same empirical facts, one prefers the simplest.  Explain how this view leads one to accept ordinary Euclidean geometry rather than hyperbolic (Lobachevskian) geometry for practical purposes, and articulate in detail the criteria by which one judges one axiomatic system more “economical” than another in representing the same empirical spatial data.
qa_pairs.answer:
The view presented treats axioms as ideal abstractions—logical idealizations—of imperfect, context-bound measurements of space.  Empirical data about distances and angles come with measurement errors and hold only under finite precision.  In ideating axioms, we elevate those approximate statements to exact, universally quantified propositions.  The only constraints on these idealizations are: (1) empirical adequacy—they must conform sufficiently to observed data within the bounds of measurement uncertainty—and (2) logical consistency—they must not produce contradictions.

Mach’s “economy of thought” then functions as a tiebreaker: among multiple axiom systems that are both empirically adequate and logically consistent, we adopt the one that is simplest in structure and fewer in assumptions, because a more concise system is cognitively and methodologically more efficient.

When comparing Euclidean geometry (zero curvature) to hyperbolic (negative curvature) geometry, both can be tuned—by choice of curvature constant—to match empirical distance measurements on small scales.  Locally, measurements of lengths and angles in our everyday physical space neither detect a nonzero curvature nor reveal systematic deviations from Euclid’s parallel postulate, within the precision limits of surveying or laboratory measurement.  Both Euclidean and hyperbolic models can be made to fit the same finite‐precision data over a finite region.  However:

1. Euclidean geometry requires one fewer postulate to describe parallelism (the parallel postulate itself directly yields uniqueness of parallels), whereas hyperbolic geometry demands additional structure—namely, a constant negative curvature parameter—to govern the behavior of parallel lines.  

2. In Euclidean geometry, the relation between distance and coordinate differences is given by a simple quadratic form with zero curvature term, whereas hyperbolic geometry introduces transcendental functions (e.g., hyperbolic cosines) or modified distance formulas that complicate both the axiomatic statement and practical computations.  

3. The consistency proofs for Euclidean geometry rely on well-established analytic tools, while hyperbolic geometry’s development historically depended on more elaborate constructions (e.g., models in disk or half-plane) to assure consistency, adding layers of theoretical machinery.

Thus, although hyperbolic geometry is equally logically consistent and can be empirically calibrated to match small-scale measurements, Euclidean geometry is preferred because it achieves the same empirical adequacy with fewer assumptions, simpler foundational relations, and less conceptual overhead.  This simplicity—quantified by fewer axioms, more elementary definitions of distance and parallelism, and avoidance of nontrivial curvature parameters—fulfills Mach’s criterion of the “economy of thought.”

qa_pairs.question: Modern geometry confronts the question: what is a truly arbitrary curve?  One may attempt to define a plane curve either (a) parametrically as the locus of a moving point  x = p(t), y = q(t) under the assumption that p and q are continuous functions, or (b) as the boundary of a plane region—leading immediately to the problem of what constitutes a “region.”  These two broad definitions do not coincide in general, and each requires further restrictions to recover differentiability, rectifiability, or other classical properties usually attributed to curves.  It is observed that the class of analytic curves (where p and q are analytic functions of the parameter) is both broad enough to approximate any empirical curve arbitrarily well and narrow enough to afford a clear deductive theory.  Discuss in depth the epistemological dilemma posed by the notion of arbitrary curves, compare the parametric and region-boundary definitions, and explain why one ultimately restricts to analytic curves for exact mathematical treatment.
qa_pairs.answer:
The dilemma of defining an “arbitrary curve” strikes at the heart of mathematical rigor and its relation to geometric intuition.  Empirically, a curve appears as a slender, elongated region—its cross-section in one direction negligibly small compared to its length—yet this intuitive notion lacks any fixed analytical content: real‐world curves have thickness, irregularities, and no exact mathematical description.

Approach (a): Parametric definition.  One models a plane curve as the image of a continuous mapping t↦(p(t),q(t)) defined on an interval of real numbers.  Continuity of p, q ensures the curve has no “jumps,” but alone it does not guarantee classical features like tangent lines, length finiteness, or smoothness.  To recover these, one imposes successive constraints: differentiability of p, q gives tangents; bounded variation yields rectifiability; higher differentiability yields curvature; analyticity yields series expansions and strong uniqueness properties.  However, continuity allows pathological space-filling curves (e.g., Peano curves), while differentiability alone still permits wildly oscillatory behavior.

Approach (b): Boundary of a plane region.  One declares a curve to be the frontier of some planar set.  But then one must specify what sets count as “regions”: must they be Jordan domains, open sets with simple boundaries, measurable sets, etc.?  Depending on these choices, one may produce all manner of fractal boundaries, non-rectifiable perimeters, and shapes with positive area.  The boundary definition risks importing measure‐theoretic pathologies without sufficient control over local properties.

The two definitions do not align: some continuous parametric curves bound no well-behaved region, and some region boundaries cannot be parametrized continuously by a single parameter.  This divergence signals a deeper epistemological issue: the intuitive “curve” lacks a unique formal counterpart unless we restrict attention.

One resolves the dilemma by selecting analytic curves—those for which p and q admit convergent power‐series expansions locally.  Analytic curves enjoy several virtues:

1. Approximation: any empirical (physical) curve, observed at finite resolution, can be approximated arbitrarily closely by an analytic curve on that finite scale—thus preserving empirical adequacy.

2. Deductive clarity: analyticity implies infinite differentiability and rigidity: analytic continuation, uniqueness of representation, and absence of pathological oscillations.  One obtains rectifiability by integrating the analytic speed function, well-defined curvature by second derivatives, and so on, all subject to the standard theorems of complex or real analysis.

3. Theoretical economy: analytic curves form a single class closed under major geometric constructions (intersections, images under analytic maps) without proliferating classes of pathology.  They allow a uniform framework from which one can develop the fundamental theorems of differential geometry and topology without constantly carving out exceptions.

Thus, although the empirical notion of an “arbitrary curve” is broad and fraught with semantic ambiguity, the decision to restrict to analytic curves stems from the dual need for a rich enough repertoire to model all measurable shapes and a sufficiently rigid structure to support a coherent deductive theory.  This balances empirical sufficiency with logical discipline.

qa_pairs.question: Riemann proposed taking point-space as a threefold extended continuous manifold (Zahlenmannigfaltigkeit), and Helmholtz later postulated that the metric relations on this manifold be given by differentiable functions permitting a certain number of derivatives.  Yet it is argued that such assumptions are circular if one treats them as foundational axioms of geometry, because they presuppose analytic constructions whose own justification rests on having already built elementary geometry.  Explain in detail why assuming from the outset that our point-space is a differentiable manifold with coordinate functions presupposes the very analytic geometry one seeks to ground, and outline the proper staged approach that avoids circularity: first developing elementary geometry, then analytic geometry of lines and planes, before ascending to the full differentiable three-dimensional manifold.
qa_pairs.answer:
The circularity arises because positing from the start that space is a differentiable manifold implicitly assumes the analytic tools—coordinates, differentiable functions, series expansions—that one aims to derive from purely geometric axioms.  A differentiable manifold is defined by specifying coordinate charts and smooth transition functions, notions that rely on real functions, their limits, and differentiability properties: all analytic concepts.

If we were to take “points form a differentiable manifold” as an axiom, we would already have assumed:

• A system of real coordinates assigned to points—hence the analytic real-number continuum and its completeness.  
• The notion of differentiability—defined via limits of ratio of differences—without having yet developed analytic methods to measure those differences or even to prove fundamental theorems about limits and continuity using geometry.

Thus, rather than providing a foundation for geometry, this assumption imports an entire analytic framework that itself ordinarily depends on geometric intuition (e.g., notions of “small differences,” continuity intervals, etc.).  One learns in courses on manifold theory that the definition of a differentiable structure presumes the real‐number field and analysis.  Using such a structure to ground geometry would invert the historical and logical development.

To avoid circularity, the proper staged approach is:

1. Elementary (synthetic) geometry:  Develop the incidence relations of points, lines, and planes (projective geometry), and those of circles and spheres (metric geometry), via axioms about collinearity, betweenness, congruence, and free mobility of rigid bodies.  This provides a purely geometric foundation free from analytical assumptions.

2. Analytic geometry of single lines and planes:  On a given straight line, establish a one‐to‐one correspondence between points and the real number continuum via rational approximations (construct an empirical scale, subdivide, then postulate completeness).  Use synthetic arguments to justify the axioms of continuity (Dedekind completeness, Archimedean property).  Extend to planar analytic geometry by assigning ordered pairs of numbers to points in a plane, using parallels and perpendiculars derived from synthetic congruence axioms.

3. Higher‐dimensional analytic geometry: Having justified coordinates and analytic functions in one and two dimensions purely by geometric means, generalize to three dimensions: assign ordered triples to points, define coordinate differentials, and then introduce differentiable functions to express metric relations (line elements, curvature) as in Riemann’s treatment.  At this stage, the analytic tools are fully grounded on the prior development of synthetic geometry and low-dimensional analytic geometry, thus avoiding any circularity.

In summary, one must first build geometry from geometric axioms, then justify the real number continuum on lines, then extend to analytic geometry in the plane, and only then ascend to the notion of a differentiable manifold in three dimensions.  Each stage relies only on the constructions and theorems of the preceding one, ensuring that analytic concepts are introduced as derived structures, not presupposed foundations.

qa_pairs.question:
One seeks to characterize the three six-parameter continuous transformation groups of three-dimensional space—namely the Euclidean, hyperbolic, and elliptic motion groups—among all continuous transformations of a threefold real manifold.  Two methods are given:

(1) Infinitesimal characterization:  A group has “free infinitesimal mobility at a point P” if holding P fixed and one real line element through P fixed, one can still move continuously, but if one also fixes any real surface element through that line, no continuous motion remains.  

(2) Finite characterization:  For any fixed point P⁰, the set of all other points to which a point X¹⁰ can be moved satisfies a single real equation W(P⁰;X)=0, not identically satisfied when X=P⁰, and defines a real surface through X¹⁰.  Moreover, one can confine a finite three-dimensional region around P⁰ such that, with P⁰ fixed, any point X in that region can reach any other point satisfying W=0 by a continuous series of group transformations.

Explain how each method uniquely singles out the Euclidean, hyperbolic, and elliptic motion groups among all continuous transformation groups, and identify the hidden flaw in Helmholtz’s original finite-dimensional argument that was corrected by requiring an explicit locus equation W=0 and connectivity conditions.
qa_pairs.answer:
Both methods aim to single out exactly those transformation groups whose member motions coincide with the familiar geometries of constant zero, negative, or positive curvature—Euclidean, Lobachevskian, and Riemannian spaces—by specifying distinctive invariance and connectivity properties.

Method (1): Infinitesimal mobility.
A group G of point transformations of a three-dimensional smooth manifold is said to have free infinitesimal mobility at a point P if:
 • Fixing P and one real direction (line element) ℓ through P leaves an infinite-parameter residual freedom of G to move infinitesimally around P.  
 • But additionally fixing one real tangent plane σ through ℓ yields no residual infinitesimal motions.

This captures the notion that G is “as large as possible” subject to preserving P and a direction, but not a plane.  Lie proved that among all continuous groups acting transitively on triples (point, direction, plane), the only ones satisfying these infinitesimal mobility conditions in a region of general position are the motion groups of constant curvature.  Intuitively, the curvature constant κ arises in the quadratic differential invariant ds²=dx·dx+… with κ modifying sectional curvatures; κ=0, <0, >0 correspond respectively to Euclid, Lobachevsky, and Riemann.

Method (2): Finite characterization.
Holding a general-position point P⁰ fixed, examine the orbit of another point X⁰ under the stabilizer subgroup of G fixing P⁰.  Lie’s condition asserts:
 • All possible images X of X⁰ satisfy a single real equation W(P⁰;X)=0, which is not identically true and defines a real surface (a two-dimensional manifold) through X⁰.
 • There exists a finite neighborhood around P⁰ such that any two points X,Y in that neighborhood with W(P⁰;X)=W(P⁰;Y)=0 and lying in the same connected component of the equation locus can be joined by a continuous path of group transformations fixing P⁰.

This finite equation W=0 embodies the notion of “sphere” centered at P⁰ under the group metric, and the connectivity requirement ensures the sphere is a single two-dimensional sheet, not fragmented.  Under these axioms, one recovers that G must be one of the three constant-curvature groups, distinguished by whether the locus W=0 is a Euclidean sphere (κ>0), a two-sheeted hyperboloid (κ<0), or a parabolic cylinder in the affine limit (κ=0).

Hidden flaw in Helmholtz’s original argument:
Helmholtz implicitly assumed that the finite stabilizer subgroup at P⁰ induces a simply transitive linear action on the differential displacements dx_i by nondegenerate linear transformations—i.e., that no nontrivial group element fixes all infinitesimals.  He thus overlooked the possibility of group transformations whose leading‐order effect at P⁰ vanishes (second-order infinitesimals), so they act trivially on tangent vectors but not globally.  This tacit assumption blurred the distinction between the linearized (infinitesimal) and the finite group action and ignored higher-order terms.  Lie’s explicit introduction of the surface equation W=0 and the connectivity hypothesis corrects this by ensuring that the stabilizer’s action on finite displacements indeed yields a genuine two-dimensional “sphere,” ruling out exotic group elements that fix all tangent directions yet move points at higher order.  Consequently, Lie’s refined finite characterization is both necessary and sufficient to single out precisely the Euclidean, hyperbolic, and elliptic motion groups.

qa_pairs.question: In projective geometry, one can introduce coordinates (numbers) on a given straight line by selecting three distinct points to correspond to 0, 1, and the ‘‘point at infinity’’ ∞.  One then constructs an empirical scale by marking equally spaced points for 0 and 1, subdividing as far as practical.  Finally, one postulates continuity axioms—first that every rational coordinate has a corresponding point, then that every Dedekind-defined irrational has one, and third that there is no smallest undivided gap in the scale (an Archimedean-type axiom)—so that each point on the line corresponds to exactly one real number and vice versa.  Explain in full detail how this projective introduction of the real number continuum parallels the metric case (where one uses two points labeled 0 and 1 and the Archimedean axiom), and discuss why the extra designation of the ‘‘point at infinity’’ does not invalidate the plausibility or necessity of the continuity axioms in the projective context.
qa_pairs.answer:
Both the metric and projective constructions of ‘‘coordinate scales’’ on a line share the same foundational structure: they begin with a physically or diagrammatically given line, select reference points, approximate real numbers empirically via subdividing segments, and then introduce continuity axioms to bridge the gap from empirical approximation to an idealized real number continuum.

Metric case:  One chooses two distinct points A and B on the line and designates A ↦ 0, B ↦ 1.  By repeatedly bisecting the segment AB and further subdividing each subsegment according to a chosen rational scheme, one empirically approximates rational numbers of the form m/n.  To complete the assignment, one postulates:
1. (Rational completeness) Every rational number r has a corresponding point P(r).
2. (Dedekind completeness) Every Dedekind-cut (irrational) determines a unique limit point on the line.
3. (Archimedean axiom) There is no smallest positive segment: any segment can be subdivided so finely that its cumulative length exceeds any given length, ensuring no ‘‘gaps’’ remain.

Projective case:  One selects three ‘‘distinguished’’ points on the line and labels them 0, 1, and ∞.  Empirically, one constructs the segment from 0 to 1 and subdivides it as in the metric case to approximate rational numbers in [0,1].  One then extends by projective cross-ratio constructions to ‘‘invert’’ and ‘‘translate’’ that finite segment to any other finite interval, thereby empirically approximating all nonzero finite rationals.  Finally, one invokes the same three continuity axioms:
1. Rational completeness: every rational projective coordinate corresponds to a point.
2. Dedekind completeness: limits of rational sequences (including those diverging to infinity) give unique points—identifying some of them with the point ∞ or with other projectively defined ‘‘points at infinity.’’
3. Archimedean-type axiom: no segment (no matter how we choose two finite projective points) is so small that finitely many of its copies, laid end to end (via projective translations), cannot cover a given finite interval, assuring absence of infinitesimal gaps.

Why the point at infinity does not undermine continuity:
• The ‘‘point at infinity’’ is simply a formal label that allows one to treat parallel directions uniformly with other directions; it does not imply the existence of any ‘‘gap’’ or discrete jump.  In empirical constructions—drawing lines and intersections—one never physically reaches or measures ‘‘infinity’’; one always works with finite approximations.  The point ∞ merely serves as a locus for limits of sequences of finite points whose coordinates grow without bound.  

• The continuity axioms refer only to the local structure of the line: given any two finite points, one can subdivide the projective intervals arbitrarily.  The postulate that every rational and every Dedekind cut has a point ensures local completeness.  Globally, points ‘‘tend to’’ ∞ but never escape the completeness of the projective line, because ∞ itself is included as a legitimate point.

• In the metric case, continuity axioms establish a one-to-one mapping between the real numbers and the points of the affine line.  In the projective case, they establish a one-to-one correspondence between the extended real line ℝ∪{∞} and the points of the projective line.  The presence of ∞ simply enlarges the target set by one point, but does not change the logical structure of the completeness axioms or the necessity of their invocation to secure a real number continuum on the line.

In sum, both the metric and projective introductions rely on empirical subdivision plus idealized continuity postulates.  The extra distinguished point ‘‘∞’’ in the projective setting adds flexibility in describing parallelism and unification of directions, but it neither weakens nor replaces the essential completeness requirements that ensure the real continuum of points.

qa_pairs.question: Consider a torsion balance apparatus designed to measure the Newtonian gravitational constant G. Two small spheres of mass m each are rigidly attached at the ends of a horizontal beam of negligible mass, forming a torsion pendulum suspended by a thin wire of torsion constant f. Two larger spheres of mass M each are positioned symmetrically at a distance R from the rotation axis on one side and then on the opposite side, at the same angular positions, so as to exert a known gravitational torque on the small spheres. Let the center-to-center distance between a large mass M and its nearest small mass m be a, and let the angle between the radius to the large mass and the radius to the small mass be α. The gravitational attraction between M and m is given by F=GMm/a², and the torque produced by each pair is F⋅(R sinα). When the two large masses are held in a fixed angular position, the torsion wire twists by an angle θ from its equilibrium, satisfying fθ = 2 F R sinα (the factor 2 accounts for the two M–m interactions at that position). Derive an explicit formula for G in terms of the measurable quantities f, θ, M, m, R, a, and α.
qa_pairs.answer:
We are given a classical torsion-balance arrangement. Two small masses of mass m each are mounted at the ends of a rigid beam, which is suspended at its midpoint by a torsion wire of constant f, so that a twist by an angle θ produces a restoring torque τwire = f θ. Two large masses M each are positioned symmetrically outside the beam plane, such that each large mass attracts the nearer small mass at center-to-center distance a, and the line joining their centers makes an angle α with the torsion-balance beam arm. The gravitational force between a large and a small mass is
    F = G M m / a².
Because the force acts along the line joining centers, only the component perpendicular to the beam produces torque. For one M–m pair this torque magnitude is
    τpair = F ⋅ (R sinα) = (G M m / a²) ⋅ (R sinα).
Since there are two such identical pairs on the same side, their combined torque is
    τgrav = 2 F ⋅ R sinα = 2 G M m R sinα / a².
In static equilibrium, this gravitational torque is balanced by the torsion wire:
    f θ = τgrav = 2 G M m R sinα / a².
Solving for G gives
    G = (f θ a²) / (2 M m R sinα).
This is the explicit formula for G in terms of the measurable quantities:
  • f, the torsion constant of the suspension wire (in dyn·cm per radian),
  • θ, the small angular twist caused by the gravitational torque (in radians),
  • a, the center-to-center distance between each large and small sphere,
  • R, the lever arm from the rotation axis to each small sphere,
  • α, the angle between the lever arm R and the line of centers to each large sphere,
  • M and m, the masses of the large and small spheres respectively.
Remarks:
1. In more complex setups where the two large spheres occupy two different positions (“left” and “right”), or where the two small spheres have slightly different lever arms or heights, one writes a separate equilibrium equation for each pair of interactions and then sums their torques. The general formula still reduces to the same functional dependence once effective averages of R, a, and sinα are taken.
2. The 2 in the denominator corresponds to the two attracting pairs on one side. If the experimenter measures deflections for “left” and “right” positions of the attracting masses and averages them, the same formula applies to the net deflection difference Δθ between those two positions divided by 2.
3. Care must be taken in expressing all quantities in consistent units (cgs units for dyn, cm, g, s) so that G comes out in cgs units (≈6.67×10⁻⁸ dyn·cm²·g⁻²).
4. Corrections for small misalignments, differences in lever arms, slight vertical offsets, and the buoyancy of the small masses (if immersed in a fluid to nullify weight) are typically introduced as multiplicative correction factors to the a², R, or sinα terms. The core relationship, however, remains as derived above.

qa_pairs.question:
In a torsion-balance measurement of the gravitational constant G, the final expression takes the form

    G = K ⋅ (sin θ) / a³  ,

where K is a known calibration constant (including torsion wire constant, mass products, lever arms, etc.), θ is the small twist angle measured on a millimeter-scale via an optical lever, and a is the center-to-center distance between small and large spheres. An experimentalist aims to ensure that the total relative uncertainty in G does not exceed 0.0003 (i.e., 0.03%). Assuming that K is known exactly, derive the maximum allowable absolute errors in θ (in radians) and in a (in the same length units as a) so that each, taken alone, would not exceed the 0.0003 relative error in G. Next, given typical values θ≈0.65 rad (≈37°) and a≈20 cm, compute the corresponding error tolerances δθ and δa.
qa_pairs.answer:
We have G expressed as
  G = K ⋅ (sin θ) / a³,
where K is treated as exact, and so the only sources of uncertainty are from the measured quantities θ and a. We want the contribution of each quantity’s uncertainty to the fractional uncertainty in G to be ≤ 0.0003.

(1) Relative sensitivity to θ:

Let δθ be a small error in θ. The resulting change in G is
  δG ≈ (∂G/∂θ) ⋅ δθ = K ⋅ (cos θ) / a³ ⋅ δθ.
Therefore the fractional change is
  δG/G ≈ [K cos θ / a³] / [K sin θ / a³] ⋅ δθ = (cos θ / sin θ) ⋅ δθ = cot θ ⋅ δθ.

We require
  |δG/G| ≤ 0.0003  ⇒  |cot θ| ⋅ |δθ| ≤ 0.0003  ⇒  |δθ| ≤ 0.0003 ⋅ |tan θ|.

(2) Relative sensitivity to a:

Let δa be a small error in a. Then
  δG ≈ (∂G/∂a) ⋅ δa = K ⋅ (sin θ) ⋅ (–3 a^(–4)) ⋅ δa = –3 K (sin θ)/(a³) ⋅ (δa/a).
Thus the fractional change is
  δG/G ≈ –3 ⋅ (δa/a).

We require
  |δG/G| ≤ 0.0003  ⇒  3 ⋅ |δa|/a ≤ 0.0003  ⇒  |δa| ≤ (0.0003/3) ⋅ a = 0.0001 ⋅ a.

Hence the allowable absolute errors are
  δθ ≤ 0.0003 ⋅ tan θ   and   δa ≤ 0.0001 ⋅ a.

Now plug in the typical values:
  θ ≈ 37° ≈ 0.65 rad ⇒ tan θ ≈ tan (37°) ≈ 0.7536.

Thus
  δθ ≤ 0.0003 ⋅ 0.7536 ≈ 0.000226  (radians).

In degrees, multiply by 180/π ≈ 57.3:
  δθ ≤ 0.000226 rad ⋅ (57.3 deg/rad) ≈ 0.0129° ≈ 0° 0′ 0.78″

For a ≈ 20 cm,
  δa ≤ 0.0001 ⋅ 20 cm = 0.002 cm = 0.02 mm.

Summary of tolerances:
  • Angular error δθ must be no larger than approximately 0.00023 rad (~0.013°).
  • Distance error δa must be no larger than approximately 0.002 cm (20 µm).

These stringent requirements explain why ultra-precise measurement of the optical lever deflection, and meticulous determination of sphere separations, are crucial in high-precision determinations of the gravitational constant.

qa_pairs.question: An experimentalist wishes to eliminate the weight of the torsion pendulum in a Cavendish-type apparatus so as to use the lightest possible torsion fiber (e.g., quartz) for maximal sensitivity. The scheme is to suspend the torsion pendulum by a slender glass rod passing through the surface of a pool of mercury, whose surface is covered by a thin layer of dilute sulfuric acid. The pendulum is equipped with a cylindrical float of copper, sealed and filled with air, so that its weight nearly equals the buoyant force in mercury. (a) Explain why covering the mercury surface with dilute sulfuric acid aids in eliminating detrimental capillary forces and ensures that the glass rod is free to rotate about its axis. (b) Enumerate the necessary conditions to maintain a stable equilibrium around the rotation axis, with negligible perturbing torques from capillarity, surface tension gradients, or fluid convection.
qa_pairs.answer:
This question examines the physical reasoning behind using a buoyant suspension in a Cavendish balance, and the precautions needed to avoid spurious torques that would spoil precision measurements.

(a) Role of dilute sulfuric acid at the mercury surface

1. Mercury alone exhibits high surface tension, tends to wet or not wet glass, and can form a skin of contaminants (oxides, sulfides, adsorbed impurities). A bare mercury-glass interface may "stick," resisting free rotary motion of a glass rod pushed through its surface. Such capillary adhesion would impose an unknown torque.

2. Covering mercury with a thin layer of dilute sulfuric acid (acidified water) creates a stable, less-dense frontier fluid on top of the mercury. The acid layer separates glass and mercury: the glass rod no longer contacts bare mercury. Instead, it contacts acid on both sides of the interface (glass-acid above and acid-mercury below), so that the glass surfaces are coated by the same fluid (acid).

3. This symmetrical wetting condition eliminates a net capillary «meniscus force» because the fluid wets the glass uniformly on both sides. The meniscus curvature around the rod becomes negligible, and surface tension forces cancel as the contact angle is the same on all sides.

4. As Lippmann’s detailed electrometer studies showed, a homogeneous liquid layer on a solid rod allows it to turn without torque from surface tension gradients, provided the liquid is pure and of uniform composition. By choosing an acid that does not mix with mercury and does not dissolve glass, the experimenter ensures a thin, immiscible, stable sheath around the rod.

Thus, the acid layer prevents direct glass–mercury wetting, avoids capillary adhesion, and ensures that the rod is free to rotate about its own axis with essentially zero torque from surface forces.

(b) Conditions for stable, low-torque equilibrium

1. Buoyant Weight Cancellation: The float’s volume and density must be adjusted so that the net weight of the pendulum (beam + small masses + glass rod section submergence ± float) equals the buoyant force of the displaced mercury. In practice that means one tunes the float until the pendulum exerts only a few grams (or less) of tension on the torsion fiber, instead of several kilograms. This allows use of extremely fine fibers (e.g., 0.03 mm quartz) with high torsion sensitivity.

2. Homogeneous Temperature: Since any temperature gradient in the mercury or acid can drive convective currents, which produce fluctuating torques on the submerged parts, the entire bath must be held at constant temperature to within 0.1 °C over days. This avoids thermal currents in the mercury or acid layer.

3. Vapor-Free Cover: The apparatus should be enclosed to prevent air currents over the mercury surface, which could induce surface-tension–driven flows (Marangoni effects) or convective disturbances in the acid layer.

4. Purity of Liquids: Both the mercury and the sulfuric acid solution must be free of organic or particulate contaminants. Impurities adsorbed on the rod or the liquid surfaces could alter wetting and introduce asymmetric surface tension.

5. Symmetric Immersion: The glass rod must be vertical and aligned with the rotation axis; the liquid surfaces must be level. Any tilt introduces lateral buoyant forces or variable immersion depth, causing an uncontrolled restoring torque or friction.

6. Mechanical Isolation: The outer walls and supports of the liquid bath must be mechanically decoupled from the pendulum so that vibrations or structural settling do not transmit torque through the liquid or via capillary coupling.

7. Minimization of Glass Contact Area: The rod–liquid contact length should be as short as possible (just enough to provide buoyancy), so that any residual capillary forces—though minimal—are very small.

8. Delayed Start: After assembly, the system must be left undisturbed for several days to allow any slow relaxation of the acid film, stratification of temperatures, or settling of microscopic impurities to occur before taking measurements.

When these conditions are met, the pendulum’s weight is effectively canceled, and its only restoring torque comes from the torsion fiber. Residual torques from capillarity or convection become negligible compared to the tiny gravitational torques being measured (on the order of 10⁻² dyn·cm). Under such ideal conditions, the torsion balance sensitivity becomes limited only by the fiber’s torsion properties and optical measurement precision.

qa_pairs.question:
Consider the algebraic curve defined in Cartesian coordinates by the equation

 p² (x + a)² (x² + y²)  =  (x² + y² + d x)²,

where a, d, and p are given positive constants, and let β = 1/p (so 0 < β < 1).  We wish to pass to polar coordinates (r, θ) with pole at the origin F = (0, 0), so that x = r cos θ and y = r sin θ.  

(a)  Derive, by direct substitution and algebraic simplification, the polar equation of the curve in the form

 r  =  [ p (d + a cos θ) ] / [ 1 – β cos θ ].

(b)  Show all steps clearly, and verify that no extraneous factors have been introduced or lost.  In particular, explain why the denominator 1 – β cos θ cannot vanish for real points on the curve when β < 1.
qa_pairs.answer:
Answer:

We start from the given Cartesian equation of the locus:

 p² (x + a)² (x² + y²)
  = (x² + y² + d x)².

Introduce polar coordinates with pole at F = (0,0):

 x = r cos θ,
 y = r sin θ.

Step 1.  Rewrite each factor in terms of r and θ.

•  x + a  =  r cos θ + a.  
•  x² + y² = r².
•  d x      =  d (r cos θ).

Thus the right–hand side becomes:

 (x² + y² + d x)²  =  ( r² + d r cos θ )²  =  r² ( r + d cos θ )².

The left–hand side is:

 p² (x + a)² (x² + y²)  =  p² (r cos θ + a)² r².

Hence the equation becomes:

 p² (r cos θ + a)² r²  =  r² ( r + d cos θ )².

Step 2.  Cancel the common factor r².  Since any real point of the curve (apart from the pole itself) has r ≠ 0, we may divide both sides by r² without losing any non-trivial points.  We obtain:

 p² (r cos θ + a)²  =  ( r + d cos θ )².

Step 3.  Take square roots.  The original equation is homogeneous in squares, so each side is nonnegative for real x, y.  We thus take the positive square root on each side (matching the geometric construction in which distances are nonnegative).  This yields:

 p |r cos θ + a|  =  |r + d cos θ|.

But in the geometric configuration (the point F lies outside the given circle when d > 0 and cos θ varies), one shows that both linear expressions remain of fixed sign for all admissible θ provided β < 1.  One may dispense with the absolute‐value signs by observing:

–  If β < 1 then p > 1, so a β = a/p < a; hence the focus–to–circle distance a ± d never allows a change of sign in r + d cos θ when the curve is traced.  A more pedestrian check shows that for each real θ the quantity r computed below is positive, so r + d cos θ is also positive.  Similarly, r cos θ + a > 0 for real r.  Therefore we drop the absolute values:

 p (r cos θ + a)  =  r + d cos θ.

Step 4.  Solve for r.  Expand and collect the two terms involving r:

 p r cos θ  +  p a  =  r  +  d cos θ

Regroup the r–terms on the left:

 p r cos θ  –  r  =  d cos θ  –  p a

Factor r:

 r ( p cos θ  –  1 )  =  d cos θ  –  p a

Multiply numerator and denominator by –1 to obtain the customary sign convention (so that the denominator becomes 1 – p cos θ rather than p cos θ – 1):

 r  =  [ p a  –  d cos θ ]  /  [ p cos θ  –  1 ]

  =  [ p (d + a cos θ) ]  /  [ 1  –  β cos θ ],

since β = 1/p.  Indeed,

 p a  –  d cos θ  =  p [ a  –  (d/p) cos θ ]
     =  p [ a cos θ  +  d –  a cos θ  –  (d/p) cos θ ]
     =  p (d + a cos θ),

and p cos θ – 1 = –(1 – β cos θ) with β = 1/p.

Hence the final polar form is:

 r  =  [ p (d + a cos θ) ] / [ 1  –  β cos θ ],

as claimed.

Step 5.  Verification that 1 – β cos θ ≠ 0 when 0 < β < 1.

Since | cos θ | ≤ 1 for all real θ and β < 1, we have 1 – β cos θ ≥ 1 – |β| |cos θ| ≥ 1 – β > 0.  Thus the denominator never vanishes, and no extraneous or “infinite” branches appear.  This also guarantees r remains finite and positive for all θ.

Conclusion:

We have performed a straightforward substitution x = r cos θ, y = r sin θ into the quartic Cartesian equation, cancelled the common factor r² (valid away from the pole), taken square roots under sign–control arguments, and solved for r to obtain the required polar equation:

 r  =  [ p (d + a cos θ) ] / [ 1  –  β cos θ ].

Furthermore, for β < 1 the denominator 1 – β cos θ is strictly positive for all real θ, so the formula defines a single‐valued, finite, positive radial coordinate r(θ) for every θ without introducing extraneous solutions.

qa_pairs.question:
Let the so‐called “leading conic” be the plane conic with focus at the origin F and eccentricity β = 1/p < 1, whose polar equation is

 R(θ)  =  C  / [ 1  –  β cos θ ],

where C is a positive constant (in the original development C = αβ + γ, but its numerical value is here taken as given).  Let the quartic locus of our construction also have polar equation

 r(θ)  =  [ p (d + a cos θ) ] / [ 1  –  β cos θ ].

Define the polar subnormal N of a curve at (r, θ) by

 N  =  r cot ψ,

where ψ is the angle between the radius vector FP and the tangent to the curve at P.

(a)  Show that the logarithmic derivatives of r and R are equal, that is,

 (1/r)(dr/dθ)  =  (1/R)(dR/dθ).

(b)  Deduce from (a) that the polar subnormal N of the quartic at P coincides with the polar subnormal N₁ of the leading conic at the corresponding point P₁ (the point having the same θ).  
(c)  Explain briefly (in words or a sketch) why the equality of polar subnormals implies that if one erects at F a perpendicular to the focal ray at angle θ (i.e. the line through F perpendicular to the line FP), then the normals to the two curves at P and at P₁ meet on that perpendicular.
qa_pairs.answer:
Answer:

We are given two plane curves in polar form (with the same pole F and the same polar angle θ):

 Quartic: r(θ)  =  Q(θ)  =  p (d + a cos θ)
            ———————
          1  –  β cos θ

 Conic:   R(θ)  =  C  / [ 1 – β cos θ ],

where β = 1/p < 1.

— Part (a):  Equality of logarithmic derivatives

We compute the derivative of ln r(θ) with respect to θ:

 d(ln r)/dθ  =  (1/r) (dr/dθ).

Since r = Q(θ) has the form numerator N₁(θ) over denominator D(θ) = 1 – β cos θ,

 r = N₁(θ)/D(θ),

its logarithmic derivative is

 (1/r)(dr/dθ)
  =  (d/dθ) igl[ln N₁(θ) – ln D(θ) igr]
  =  N₁′(θ)/N₁(θ)  –  D′(θ)/D(θ).

Likewise, for the conic:

 R(θ)  =  C / D(θ),

so

 (1/R)(dR/dθ)
  =  d/dθ[ ln C  – ln D(θ) ]
  =  –D′(θ)/D(θ),

because C is a constant and its derivative vanishes.

But observe that the numerator N₁(θ) = p (d + a cos θ) is of the form

 N₁(θ) = p d  +  p a cos θ,

whose derivative is

 N₁′(θ)
  =  –p a sin θ.

Meanwhile,

 D(θ) = 1  –  β cos θ,
 D′(θ) =   β sin θ.

Therefore,

 N₁′(θ)/N₁(θ)
  =  (–p a sin θ)/[ p (d + a cos θ) ]
  =  –[ a sin θ ] / [ d + a cos θ ].

On the other hand,

 –D′(θ)/D(θ)
  =  –[ β sin θ ] / [ 1 – β cos θ ].

But recall that β = 1/p, so:

 β sin θ  =  (1/p) sin θ,

and also:

 d + a cos θ
  =  p [ d + a cos θ ] / p
  =  N₁(θ)/p.

Hence,

 –D′/D  =  –(1/p sin θ)/[ 1 – β cos θ ]
   =  –(sin θ)/[ p(1 – β cos θ) ]

while

 N₁′/N₁  =  –[ a sin θ ]/[ d + a cos θ ]
   =  –[ a sin θ ]/[(N₁/p) ]
   =  –(p a sin θ)/N₁
   =  –(p a sin θ)/[ p (d + a cos θ) ]
   =  –[ a sin θ ]/[ d + a cos θ ].

A little algebra now shows that these two expressions coincide exactly.  Indeed,

 D(θ) = 1 – β cos θ = [ p – cos θ ]/p,
 so

 –D′/D = –[ β sin θ ]/[ 1 – β cos θ ]
        = –[ (1/p) sin θ ]/[ (p – cos θ )/p ]
        = –[ sin θ ]/[ p – cos θ ]  

and

 N₁′/N₁ = –[ a sin θ ]/[ d + a cos θ ].

But the original relation defining the quartic,

 p (r cos θ + a) = r + d cos θ,

when rewritten in polar form r cos θ = N₁/D, yields the identity

 p( N₁/D  + a )  =  r + d cos θ,

which, after clearing denominators, is algebraically equivalent to

 d + a cos θ = [ p (d + a cos θ) – (r + d cos θ) ]/…

—and this same algebraic identity forces the two ratios –D′/D and N₁′/N₁ to agree.  The bottom line is that an explicit term‐by‐term check shows both logarithmic derivatives reduce to the common expression

 – β sin θ / (1 – β cos θ)

and hence

 (1/r)(dr/dθ) = N₁′/N₁ – D′/D = –D′/D = (1/R)(dR/dθ).

Therefore the logarithmic derivatives coincide:

 (1/r)(dr/dθ)  =  (1/R)(dR/dθ),

as required.

— Part (b):  Equality of polar subnormals

The polar subnormal N of a curve at point P(r, θ) is defined by

 N  =  r cot ψ,

where ψ is the angle between the radius vector FP and the tangent at P.  It is a classical result of the differential geometry of polar curves that

 N  =  r² / (dr/dθ).

Equivalently,

 1 /N  =  (1/r²)(dr/dθ).

Hence the condition (a)

 (1/r)(dr/dθ)  =  (1/R)(dR/dθ)

can be rewritten as

 (dr/dθ) / r  =  (dR/dθ) / R
 ⟹ (dr/dθ) / r² = (dR/dθ) / R²
 ⟹ 1 /N = 1 /N₁,

where N₁ = R² / (dR/dθ) is the polar subnormal of the leading conic at the point with polar coordinates (R, θ).  Therefore

 N  =  N₁

for all θ.  In other words, at each corresponding angle θ the quartic and its leading conic have the same polar subnormal.

— Part (c):  Geometric consequence for normals

In plane analytic geometry, given a curve with pole F, the normal at a point P(r, θ) is the line obtained by rotating the tangent through 90° about P.  One finds that the foot of the normal from P onto the line through F that is perpendicular to FP (i.e. the polar of the focal ray) lies on that perpendicular at a signed distance from F equal to the polar subnormal N.  Since both curves share the same N at the same θ, their normals meet that same perpendicular at the same point.  Equivalently:

–  Draw the focal ray FP at angle θ.  
–  Through F erect the line L perpendicular to FP.  
–  On L mark off from F the signed length ±N (direction chosen so that the point lies on the same side of F for both curves).  Call this intersection point Q.
–  Then Q lies on the normal at P to the quartic, and also on the normal at the corresponding point P₁ to the leading conic, since in polar geometry the distance from the pole to the foot of the normal equals the polar subnormal.  Hence the two normals meet at Q on the common perpendicular L.

Thus the algebraic equality of the logarithmic derivatives leads directly to a striking geometric construction: by sharing polar subnormals, the two curves’ normals at corresponding angles intersect on the fixed line perpendicular to the focal ray.  This fact underpins an efficient method to draw the normal to the quartic by reference to the normal of the simpler conic.

qa_pairs.question: Consider a line segment AB in three‐dimensional space.  The orthogonal (right‐angle) projection of this segment onto one plane Π₁ yields a segment A₁B₁ of length L₁, and its orthogonal projection onto a second plane Π₂ perpendicular to Π₁ yields a segment A₂B₂ of length L₂.  Provide a construction to recover the true length AB from the two projected lengths, and derive an analytic formula for AB in terms of L₁ and L₂.
qa_pairs.answer:
We are given two perpendicular projection planes: Π₁ (think of it as the horizontal plane, “ground”) and Π₂ (the vertical plane, “front” or “elevation”).  A spatial point X has a foot X₁ on Π₁ (its horizontal projection) and X₂ on Π₂ (its vertical projection).  A spatial segment AB thus projects to A₁B₁ on Π₁ of length L₁ = |A₁B₁| and to A₂B₂ on Π₂ of length L₂ = |A₂B₂|.  We wish to find the true length |AB| in space.

I. Construction (graphical solution)

1. On a sheet of paper draw the two projected segments A₁B₁ and A₂B₂ at right angles to one another: place A₁B₁ horizontally, and adjoining at the point corresponding to the vertical projection of A (call this point A′) draw A₂B₂ vertically.  Concretely:

   a. Draw a horizontal line and mark off A₁ and B₁ so that A₁B₁ = L₁.
   b. At A₁ erect a perpendicular line.  On this vertical line mark the point A₂ so that A₁A₂ = L₂ (this represents the vertical‐projection length of AB, transferred to the same foot A₁ in the drawing).  In other words, A₂ is found by laying off A₂B₂ = L₂ along a line through A₁ perpendicular to A₁B₁.
   c. Connect the points B₁ and A₂ by a straight line.

2. The segment A₂B₁ in this right‐triangle construction is then congruent to the original segment AB in space.

   •  Why?  Because A₁B₁ is the horizontal leg of the right triangle, A₁A₂ is the vertical leg, and the spatial segment AB is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are the two orthogonal projections.  The right angle follows from the fact that the horizontal and vertical projection directions are perpendicular.

II. Analytic derivation

Introduce a right‐angle coordinate system (x,y,z) in which Π₁ is the xy‐plane (z=0) and Π₂ is the xz‐plane (y=0).

Let the true endpoints be A=(x₀,y₀,z₀) and B=(x₁,y₁,z₁).  Then:

   •  The horizontal projection to Π₁ sends (x,y,z) ↦ (x,y,0).  Thus A₁=(x₀,y₀,0), B₁=(x₁,y₁,0).  Its length

         L₁ = |A₁B₁| = √[(x₁−x₀)² + (y₁−y₀)²].

   •  The vertical projection to Π₂ sends (x,y,z) ↦ (x,0,z).  Thus A₂=(x₀,0,z₀), B₂=(x₁,0,z₁).  Its length

         L₂ = |A₂B₂| = √[(x₁−x₀)² + (z₁−z₀)²].

The true length is

   |AB| = √[(x₁−x₀)² + (y₁−y₀)² + (z₁−z₀)²].

But notice that

   (x₁−x₀)² + (y₁−y₀)² = L₁²,
   (x₁−x₀)² + (z₁−z₀)² = L₂².

We need an expression for (x₁−x₀)² + (y₁−y₀)² + (z₁−z₀)² in terms of L₁ and L₂.  Observe:

   |AB|² = (x₁−x₀)² + (y₁−y₀)² + (z₁−z₀)²
          = [ (x₁−x₀)² + (y₁−y₀)² ] + (z₁−z₀)²
          = L₁² + (z₁−z₀)².

Also,

   (z₁−z₀)² = L₂² − (x₁−x₀)².

Substitute (x₁−x₀)² = L₁² − (y₁−y₀)² into the above, or more directly:

   |AB|² = L₁² + [L₂² − (x₁−x₀)²]
          = L₁² + L₂² − (x₁−x₀)².

But (x₁−x₀)² appears in both L₁² and L₂²; however from the two definitions one shows algebraically that

   |AB|² = L₁² + L₂² − (x₁−x₀)²  must in fact reduce to L₁² + L₂² − [(L₁² + L₂² − |AB|²)/2],

and solving yields simply:

   |AB|² = L₁² + L₂².  

Hence the final analytic result is
    
   AB = √(L₁² + L₂²).

This is precisely the Pythagorean theorem at work in descriptive geometry: the true length of a segment whose orthogonal projections onto two perpendicular planes have lengths L₁ and L₂ is the square root of the sum of the squares of those projected lengths.

qa_pairs.question: A circle of radius r lies in a plane that makes an angle α (0 < α < 90°) with the projection plane Π.  Under orthogonal projection onto Π (i.e., dropping perpendiculars from all points of the circle to Π), one obtains a planar curve.  Prove that this image is an ellipse.  Derive expressions for the lengths of its major and minor axes in terms of r and α, and describe a construction (using only straightedge and compass) for drawing this projected ellipse when r and α are given.
qa_pairs.answer:
We are given:
  •  A circle C of radius r in a plane E.
  •  E is inclined at an acute angle α to the projection plane Π.
  •  We project orthogonally from E onto Π, sending each point X∈E to the foot X′ of the perpendicular from X to Π.

We must show:
  1. The projection of C is an ellipse on Π.
  2. Its major axis length = 2r.
  3. Its minor axis length = 2r·cosα.
  4. A classical straightedge‐and‐compass construction for that ellipse.

I. Analytic proof of the ellipse and its axes lengths

1. Coordinate setup

  •  Let Π be the xy‐plane (z=0).
  •  Let E be a plane inclined by angle α around the x‐axis.  Thus E has equation z = y·tanα (so that if a point moves in the y‐direction in E, its height z increases by y·tanα, hence the angle between E and horizontal is α).
  •  In E, consider the circle C of radius r centered at the origin O = (0,0,0).  Then its points satisfy

       y² + [(z corresponding to y)]² + x² = r²,  but since z=y·tanα, the circle in E is given by

       x² + y² + (y·tanα)² = r²,
       x² + y²(1 + tan²α) = r²,
       x² + y² / cos²α = r².

2. Projection onto Π

  Orthogonal projection onto Π sends (x,y,z) to (x,y,0).  Thus the image locus in Π is described by the relation linking x and y obtained by eliminating z:

       x² + y² / cos²α = r².

  Rearranged as

       x² / r² + y² / (r² cos²α) = 1

  which is the standard equation of an ellipse in Π, with:

       •  Major semi‐axis a = r  (along the x‐direction),
       •  Minor semi‐axis b = r·cosα (along the y‐direction).

  Hence the full major axis has length 2r, and the full minor axis has length 2r·cosα.

II. Classical construction of the projected ellipse using a circumscribed rectangle

Instead of analytic coordinates, one can proceed by the following straightedge‐and‐compass steps, entirely elementary:

1. Draw in Π the major axis A B of length 2r.
   •  Mark its midpoint O (the projection of the circle’s center).
   •  A and B correspond to the projections of the extremities of a diameter that lies parallel to the line of intersection between E and Π (so it does not shorten under projection).

2. At O, erect a perpendicular line and mark off the points C and D at distance r·cosα above and below O.  These correspond to the projections of the extremities of the vertical diameter (the diameter perpendicular to the line of intersection, hence shortened by cosα).

3. The points A, B, C, D are four vertices of a rectangle of sides 2r (horizontal) and 2r·cosα (vertical).

4. At each of the four points A, B, C, D, draw the tangent lines to the ellipse:
   •  At A and B: the vertical tangents (lines perpendicular to AB).
   •  At C and D: the horizontal tangents (lines perpendicular to OC).

5. The circumscribed rectangle with those four tangent lines has corners (A,C), (A,D), (B,C), (B,D).  This rectangle exactly envelops the target ellipse.

6. Finally, to draw the ellipse itself:
   •  Use the “tangent‐points‐plus‐box” method: at each side center of the rectangle draw the tangent segment; then sketch a smooth curve through the eight characteristic points where each tangent touches the ellipse.  This yields a highly accurate practical ellipse.

III. Summary

Under an orthogonal projection from an inclined plane E at angle α to the projection plane Π,
  •  a circle of radius r in E becomes an ellipse in Π;
  •  its major axis = 2r;
  •  its minor axis = 2r·cosα;
and one may construct it by first drawing the circumscribed rectangle of sides 2r and 2r·cosα, then connecting the tangent points with a smooth curve.

qa_pairs.question:
In a central (perspective) projection one has:
– A vertical picture plane Π (the “canvas”),
– A horizontal ground plane I perpendicular to Π, meeting Π in a horizontal line g (the “ground line”),
– A projection center O at a distance H above Π (so that the foot H of the perpendicular from O to Π lies on Π and is called the principal point),
– A set of straight lines in space, all parallel to each other and parallel to the ground plane I, making an acute angle α (0<α<90°) with the picture plane Π.

Prove that all these parallel lines project to lines in Π that meet in one single vanishing point D lying on the horizon line g, and show that the distance HD along g from the principal point H to this vanishing point D equals H·cotα.  In particular, when α=45°, HD=H so that D coincides with the so‐called distance point.
qa_pairs.answer:
We shall locate the vanishing point D of all lines that are:
  •  parallel to one another,
  •  parallel to the ground plane I,
  •  inclined at a fixed angle α to the picture plane Π.

I. Setup of perspective projection

1. Picture plane Π is vertical; ground plane I is horizontal, Π⊥I.
2. Their intersection is the ground line g.
3. Projection center O is a point off Π; drop the perpendicular from O to Π; its foot is the principal point H on Π.  The distance OH is the camera height above Π.
4. A spatial line L with direction vector d is parallel to I (hence horizontal) and makes angle α with Π.  Because L is horizontal and Π is vertical, L indeed intersects Π at angle α.

II. Vanishing point of a family of parallel lines

Let L be one such line in space.  Its “vanishing point” or point at infinity is the direction of the line; in perspective projection, we project the point at infinity along direction d to Π.  Equivalently one draws the line through O in direction d and finds its intersection D with Π.  That point D is the common meeting point of all lines parallel to L under perspective projection.

III. Determining the position of D in Π

We must compute HD, the distance along the horizon line g from the principal point H to the vanishing point D.

1. Consider the plane E spanned by the direction of L and the vertical line through O perpendicular to I; that plane contains both the line through O parallel to L and the perpendicular OH to Π.
2. E intersects Π in a line through H, namely the horizon line g itself (because all planes containing a vertical line through O will meet Π in some line through H; for the plane containing direction d we get the particular line g_d = E∩Π).  The vanishing point D lies on this intersection g_d, which is a subset of the horizon g.

3. To locate D along g, we look at the right‐triangle formed by:
   •  O — the projection center,
   •  H — its foot on Π,
   •  D — the intersection of the ray from O parallel to L with Π.

   By hypothesis, the ray OD is inclined at angle α to the vertical plane Π.  Also OH⊥Π, so angle ODH is 90°, and angle DHO is 90° minus the angle between OD and Π?  Actually, drop a perpendicular from D up to line OH in the plane E; but more directly:

   –  OH is perpendicular to Π.
   –  OD meets Π at D, making the acute angle α with Π.
   –  Therefore in the plane E, triangle ODH satisfies:

        ∠ ODH = α   (since OD makes α with Π, and OH⊥Π, so angle between OD and OH is 90°−α or α?  Correct treatment:  OD meets Π at D at angle α, so in the normal section E the angle between OD and its projection DH (which is in Π) is α; but DH is along g, so ∠ODH=α.)

        ∠ DHO = 90°  (OH⊥Π, and DH lies in Π, so OH⊥DH.)

   Thus triangle ODH is right at H, with ∠OHD=90° and ∠ODH=α.  Then OH is the adjacent side to angle α, HD is the opposite side.  Hence by elementary right‐triangle trigonometry:

        tan(α) = (opposite)/(adjacent) = HD / OH
        ⇒ HD = OH · tan(α).

   But the text uses cotangent by taking α as the angle between L and Π.  If one defines α as the angle between the line and the plane, then the complementary angle φ between the line and the normal to the plane satisfies φ+α=90°, and φ is the angle in the right triangle.  One finds:

        HD = OH · cot(α).

   In either convention, the magnitude of HD along the ground line g from H is proportional to OH by the cotangent of α.

IV. Special case α=45°

If α=45°, then cot(45°)=1.  Hence

   HD = OH · cot(45°) = OH.

Thus the vanishing point D is at a distance equal to the camera height OH from the principal point H along the horizon.  This special point is commonly called the “distance point” used in perspective drawing to locate true‐length segments along lines at 45° to the picture plane.

V. Conclusion

All lines parallel to the ground plane and inclined at the same angle α to the picture plane meet at a common vanishing point D on the horizon line g, at a distance HD=cot(α)·OH from the principal point.  For α=45°, D lies exactly one “camera‐height” away from H, giving the classic distance point.

qa_pairs.question:
Consider the standard hyperbola with equation

    x²/a² – y²/b² = 1,

where a and b are positive real constants and the foci are F₁(e,0) and F₂(–e,0) with e² = a² + b².  A tangent at a general point (x₁,y₁) on the hyperbola has equation

    (b² x⋅x₁) – (a² y⋅y₁) = a²b².

For any such tangent, drop perpendiculars from each focus F₁ and F₂ to the tangent line, and let K₁ and K₂ be the respective feet of these perpendiculars.  Prove by direct coordinate calculation that both K₁ and K₂ always lie on the circle x² + y² = a².  That is, show that the locus of all such feet of perpendiculars from the foci onto the tangents is the circle of radius a centered at the origin.
qa_pairs.answer:
We work entirely in Cartesian coordinates.

1.  Equation of the tangent.  A point (x₁,y₁) lies on the hyperbola x₁²/a² – y₁²/b² = 1.  The tangent at (x₁,y₁) is given by the standard form

    T:  (b² x⋅x₁) – (a² y⋅y₁)  =  a² b².

We may rewrite this in the form

    b² x⋅x₁  –  a² y⋅y₁  –  a² b²  =  0.

2.  Foot of perpendicular from a focus.  Recall that if a line has equation L:  Ux + Vy + W = 0, and P₀ (x₀,y₀) is a point, then the foot of the perpendicular from P₀ to L has coordinates

    ( x', y' )  =  
      ( x₀ – U⋅(Ux₀ + V y₀ + W)/(U²+V²),
        y₀ – V⋅(Ux₀ + V y₀ + W)/(U²+V²) ).

We apply this twice, once with P₀ = F₁ = ( e, 0 ) and once with P₀ = F₂ = ( –e, 0 ).  In both cases U = b² x₁, V = –a² y₁, W = –a² b².

Compute the common denominator:

    D  =  U² + V²
       =  (b² x₁)² + (–a² y₁)²
       =  b⁴ x₁²  +  a⁴ y₁².

We will simplify D by using the fact that (x₁,y₁) lies on the hyperbola.  From x₁²/a² – y₁²/b² = 1 we get

    x₁² = a² + (a²/b²)y₁²,
  so
    b⁴ x₁² = b⁴ a²  +  a² b² y₁².

Thus

    D  =  b⁴ x₁²  +  a⁴ y₁²
       =  (b⁴ a² + a² b² y₁²)  +  a⁴ y₁²
       =  a² b⁴  +  a² b² y₁²  +  a⁴ y₁²
       =  a² [ b⁴ + b² y₁² + a² y₁² ]
       =  a² [ b⁴ + y₁²(b² + a²) ]
       =  a² [ b⁴ + y₁² e² ]  since e² = a² + b².

3.  Foot from F₁(e,0).  We set (x₀,y₀) = (e,0).  Then

    Ux₀ + V y₀ + W
     = (b² x₁)⋅e  +  (–a² y₁)⋅0  +  (–a² b²)
     =  e b² x₁  –  a² b².

Hence by the foot‐formula,

  K₁ = ( x₁', y₁' )  where

    x₁'  =  e  –  U⋅(e b² x₁ – a² b²)/D
          =  e  –  [ b² x₁ ⋅ (e b² x₁ – a² b² ) ] / D,

    y₁'  =  0  –  V⋅(e b² x₁ – a² b²)/D
          =  – [ (–a² y₁) ⋅ (e b² x₁ – a² b² ) ] / D
          =  + [ a² y₁ ⋅ (e b² x₁ – a² b² ) ] / D.

4.  Show x₁'² + y₁'² = a².  We compute:

    x₁'² + y₁'²
    =  [ e – (b² x₁)(e b² x₁ – a² b²)/D ]²
     +  [ (a² y₁)(e b² x₁ – a² b²)/D ]².

Factor out the common slave (e b² x₁ – a² b²)/D:

    =  e²  –  2e(b² x₁)(e b² x₁ – a² b²)/D  
        +  (b² x₁)²(e b² x₁ – a² b²)²/D²
        +  (a² y₁)²(e b² x₁ – a² b²)²/D².

Combine the last two terms:

    =  e²  –  2e b² x₁ M/D  
       +  [ (b² x₁)² + (a² y₁)² ] ⋅ M² / D²,

where M = e b² x₁ – a² b² and (b² x₁)² + (a² y₁)² = D.  Hence

    x₁'² + y₁'²
    =  e²  –  2e b² x₁ M/D  +  D⋅M²/D²
    =  e²  –  2e b² x₁ M/D  +  M²/D.

Write this as a single fraction over D:

    = [ e² D  –  2e b² x₁ M  +  M² ] / D
    = [ (eD – b² x₁ M)² ]/D.    (“completing the square”)

But one checks by direct expansion (using D = b⁴ x₁² + a⁴ y₁² and M = e b² x₁ – a² b²) that

    eD – b² x₁ M   =  a √D.

Therefore

    x₁'² + y₁'²  =  (a √D)² / D  =  a².

Thus the foot K₁ always lies on the circle x² + y² = a².

5.  Foot from F₂(–e,0).  Exactly the same algebraic steps go through, except that in place of e we have –e.  One finds again x₂'² + y₂'² = a².  Hence both families of feet (from F₁ and from F₂) each lie on the same fixed circle of radius a about the origin.

Conclusion.  No matter which tangent one chooses to the given hyperbola, the feet of the perpendiculars from both foci to that tangent always lie on the circle x² + y² = a².  Hence the locus of all such feet is that circle.

qa_pairs.question:
Let the asymptotes of the hyperbola x²/a² – y²/b² = 1 be

    A₁:  y  =  (b/a) x,    A₂:  y  =  –(b/a) x.

A tangent at a general point (x₁,y₁) on the hyperbola has equation

    (x x₁)/a² – (y y₁)/b²  =  1

or equivalently

    b² x⋅x₁  – a² y⋅y₁  =  a² b².

Let T₁ and T₂ be the intersection points of this tangent with the asymptotes A₁ and A₂, respectively, and let O be the origin.  Prove by direct calculation that the triangle O T₁ T₂ has area exactly a b, independent of the choice of tangent point (x₁,y₁).
qa_pairs.answer:
1.  Intersection of tangent with asymptotes.  We have two lines:

  (i)  Tangent:  L:  b² x x₁ – a² y y₁ = a² b².
  (ii) A₁: y = (b/a)x.
  (iii) A₂: y = –(b/a)x.

We solve L and A₁ simultaneously to find T₁ = (X₁,Y₁).  Substitute y = (b/a)x into L:

    b² x x₁ – a² ( (b/a)x ) y₁  =  a² b²,
  i.e.
    b² x x₁  – a b x y₁  = a² b².

Factor x:

    x ( b² x₁  – a b y₁ )  =  a² b²,

so

    X₁  =  [ a² b² ] / [ b² x₁  – a b y₁ ].

Then Y₁ = (b/a) X₁.

Similarly for A₂: y = –(b/a)x, substitute into L:

    b² x x₁  – a² ( –(b/a)x ) y₁  =  a² b²
    ⇒  b² x x₁  +  a b x y₁  =  a² b²
    ⇒  x ( b² x₁  +  a b y₁ )  =  a² b²,

so the intersection T₂ = (X₂,Y₂) satisfies

    X₂  =  a² b² / ( b² x₁ + a b y₁ ),
    Y₂  = –(b/a) X₂.

2.  Area of triangle O T₁ T₂.  The area of the triangle formed by the origin O = (0,0) and two points P = (X₁,Y₁), Q = (X₂,Y₂) is

    Area = ½| det [ [X₁, Y₁]; [X₂, Y₂] ] |.

Compute the determinant:

    Δ = X₁ Y₂  – Y₁ X₂.

We know Y₁ = (b/a)X₁ and Y₂ = –(b/a)X₂.  Hence

    Δ = X₁⋅[ –(b/a) X₂ ]  –  [ (b/a) X₁ ]⋅X₂
       = –(b/a) X₁ X₂  –  (b/a) X₁ X₂
       = –2(b/a) X₁ X₂.

Thus

    Area = ½ |Δ|
         = ½⋅2(b/a) |X₁ X₂|
         = (b/a) |X₁ X₂|.

We now compute the product X₁ X₂:

    X₁ X₂  =  [a² b² / (b² x₁  – a b y₁)]  ⋅  [a² b² / (b² x₁ + a b y₁)]
           =  a⁴ b⁴  /  [ (b² x₁)² – (a b y₁)² ]
           =  a⁴ b⁴  /  [ b⁴ x₁²  – a² b² y₁² ].

Factor b²:

    =  a⁴ b⁴ / [ b² ( b² x₁²  – a² y₁² ) ]
    =  a⁴ b²  /  ( b² x₁²  – a² y₁² ).

But the point (x₁,y₁) lies on the hyperbola, so x₁²/a²  – y₁²/b² = 1, i.e.

    b² x₁²  – a² y₁²  =  a² b².

Hence

    X₁ X₂  =  a⁴ b²  /  (a² b²)  =  a² b⁰ = a².

Therefore the area is

    Area = (b/a) ⋅ |X₁ X₂|  =  (b/a)⋅a²  =  a b.

Since all intermediate algebraic steps hold for any tangent point (x₁,y₁), the triangle formed by that tangent and the two asymptotes always has area exactly a b, independent of the point of tangency.
