qa_pairs.question: Some jurists have argued: "Whenever a person acquires someone else’s property under a valid contract, that contract alone confers a legal justification for retaining the sale-price—even if the contract ultimately fails to transfer ownership—because the contract grants the purchaser certain procedural safeguards (like Publiciana or usucapion) that validate his belief in ownership." Critically evaluate this argument in light of the distinction between enrichment ex re and enrichment ex negotiatione, explaining why the mere existence of a contractual title is insufficient to justify retention of the price in all cases.
qa_pairs.answer:
This argument collapses under a careful analysis of what constitutes unjust enrichment in Roman law. The essence of the problem is whether the seller’s retention of the price is legally justified by virtue of the contract or whether it is an unjust enrichment that springs from the thing’s wrongful depletion of the owner’s patrimony.

1. Contractual title versus justification of enrichment
   - A valid contract (titulus verus) indeed bestows upon the acquirer certain legal remedies against a dislodgment—the praescriptio longi temporis or the actio Publiciana. These rights protect the purchaser from simply having the thing reclaimed by the plaintiff (the real owner) out of hand. However, such procedural or possessory protections do not inherently transform every contractual acquisition into a pontifical grant of ownership. They are defenses to real actions, not sources of substantive property right. The contract presupposes the transfer of ownership, but if such transfer fails (due to lack of actual delivery or title defect), the contract remains an obligation, not a property right. 

2. Enrichment ex negotiatione versus ex re
   - The argument in question equates the contract’s procedural protections (Publiciana, usucapion) with "justification" of enrichment ex re. In fact, contract confers profit by ex negotiatione: it is the objectively agreed price for an intended transfer. Profit of this sort is legitimate and not actionable. But when retention of the price flows directly from the disappearance or wrongful acquisition by usucapion of the owner’s thing, it is an enrichment ex re and actionable unless the seller can recoup via an eviction-based regressus.
   - The mere existence of a contract does not eliminate an unjust enrichment ex re. If the contract fails to effect a true transfer yet the seller retains the price because the thing has perished or the purchaser has usucapited it, the price remains by virtue of the thing’s wrongful removal from the owner’s patrimony, not by virtue of the contract. The contract justified only ex negotiatione benefits, which alone are insufficient for restitution.

3. The decisive criterion: right of recourse (regressus)
   - A purchaser under a valid sale for consideration (titulus onerosus) does have a contractual remedy against his own seller if he is evicted. Thus, any price he retains after an eventual eviction will be recoverable, and so he suffers no net enrichment ex re. The contract secures him not just contractually but realiter: his regressus substitutes for the res he lost. In consequence, we treat his retained price as ex negotiatione and non-actionable.
   - In contrast, holders of the res by grant, inheritance, or putative title (titulus lucrativus or putativus) lack any regressus. When the owner’s real action is defeated by perishing or usucapion, these individuals simply retain the price, having no further remedy. That retention constitutes pure enrichment ex re, since it springs from the fact that the owner’s thing was lost and the acquirer permanently holds the price in its stead. Such enrichment is unjust and actionable.

4. Why procedural protections do not suffice
   - Defenses like Publiciana and usucapion regulate the relationship between possessor and litigant in an action; they do not confer ownership ex tunc. A possessor may fend off rei vindicatio, yet that does not justify keeping the sale-price if the possessor’s enrichment stems from the loss of the owner’s patrimony. The relevant test is recourseability, not defensibility in litigation. Even a putative purchaser might be shielded from real actions by Publiciana, but without regressus, any price he holds after the thing’s destruction will be unjustly held.

Conclusion: The mere validity of contract and the procedural shields it provides are not alone enough to justify retention of the price when ownership fails to vest. The true question is whether the seller can recourse for eviction. Contractual titles permit recourse for eviction only when the acquirer paid consideration (titulus onerosus); when they do not, retention of the price is enrichment ex re and must be restored.

qa_pairs.question:
In an ancient legal framework, two situations can deprive the original owner of a thing of the ability to vindicate it: 

A. The thing perishes while in the good-faith purchaser’s custody (casus fortuitus).
B. The good-faith purchaser acquires ownership by long possession (usucapion), after meeting statutory conditions.

A scholar contends that these two events should be treated differently when assessing whether a prior seller should be liable for unjust enrichment. He argues that usucapion represents a socially sanctioned limit on protection of ownership—purchasers are given a statutory window to reclaim possessory rights—whereas physical perishing is random harm requiring compensation. Critically evaluate whether, under principles of unjust enrichment tied to deprivation of the owner’s real action, these two events warrant distinct treatment or should be governed by the same rule. Discuss and justify your conclusion.
qa_pairs.answer:
An analytical assessment of the two scenarios under principles of unjust enrichment shows that they should be governed by the same rule:

1. Common criterion: loss of the owner’s real action
   - Both perishing of the thing (A) and usucapion by the purchaser (B) have the identical legal effect of extinguishing the owner’s rei vindicatio. The owner no longer can reclaim the res because the thing either no longer exists or has become legally vested in the possessor. From the standpoint of unjust enrichment, it is the deprivation of this real-action remedy that constitutes the owner’s patrimonial loss and gives rise to a matching gain in the hands of another party.

2. The locus of enrichment
   - In both cases the res is effectively converted into the sale-price held by the seller. The retention of that price stems directly from the owner’s loss. What matters is not the reason for loss (chance event versus statutory prescription) but that the causal nexus between owner’s loss and seller’s retention is the same: retention of the price in place of the thing.

3. Recourse right determines liability, not social policy about ownership limits
   - Some argue usucapion is a legislative compromise limiting rei vindicatio, implying that enrichment arising through usucapion should not trigger restitution. However, the basis of an unjust enrichment action is not the policy reasoning behind the owner’s loss but the fact of a non-compensated transfer of owner’s patrimony to another. In either scenario, the only difference that matters is the seller’s capacity to recoup the price by an eviction-based regressus.
   - A purchaser who acquired for value (titulus onerosus) can seek regressus after eviction whether the eviction arises from perishing or usucapion; hence, he never truly retains the price ex re. Those without regressus (titulus lucrativus or putativus) simply keep the price in both scenarios. The same logical mechanism of enrichment ex re applies to both.

4. Critique of the differentiation argument
   - The proposed differentiation treats the owner’s loss from perishing as a "damage requiring compensation" but treats usucapion as a voluntary renunciation or extinguishment of ownership by the legislature. Yet from the owner’s perspective, both outcomes are indistinguishable: she is deprived of her real right. The unjust enrichment paradigm focuses on patrimonial loss and gain, not on the normative policy of property acquisition. Distinguishing losses by causation (chance vs statutory) inserts an extraneous policy criterion into the enrichment analysis.

5. Conclusion: Uniform rule
   - Because perishing and usucapion both nullify the owner’s vindicatory right and result in the seller retaining the sale-price by virtue of the thing, they must be treated identically under unjust enrichment principles. The only relevant variable is the seller’s entitlement to regressus: if absent, the price is enriched ex re and restitution lies; if present, the enrichment is merely ex negotiatione and non-actionable. No separate rule for usucapion aligns with the foundational criterion of unjust enrichment.

qa_pairs.question:
A legal maxim from Roman jurisprudence states: “The price obtained from the sale of a thing does not proceed ex re but propter negotiationem.” 

Explain how this distinction supports limiting an owner’s restitution claim against a bona fide seller to cases where the seller cannot recoup the price through an eviction action. In your answer, illustrate:
- The conceptual difference between res-derived and negotiation-derived gains.
- Why gains propter negotiationem are not restitutionary.
- How a residue of res-derived gain appears only when the seller lacks an eviction recourse.
qa_pairs.answer:
The maxim underscores the fundamental analytic division in Roman doctrine between two sources of profit:

1. Negotiation-derived gain (lucrum propter negotiationem)
   - This gain arises from the contractual transaction itself. When a seller conveys a thing under contract, the price “proceeds from the negotiation”—it is the bargain’s quid pro quo. Because the contract establishes reciprocal obligations (deliver the thing vs pay the price), any profit the seller makes qua seller emerges from that negotiated exchange. Such gains are justified by the contract’s consensual origin and therefore cannot be reclaimed by the other party via unjust enrichment.

2. Res-derived gain (lucrum ex re)
   - A gain ex re arises when the seller benefits specifically by reason of the thing itself. The paradigmatic scenario is a bona fide sale of another’s property followed by the thing’s destruction or usucapion in the purchaser’s hands. Because the owner’s real action (rei vindicatio) is thereby defeated, the thing is effectively converted into price in the seller’s hands. That conversion is directly traceable to the thing’s loss—the "res" has yielded a price retained by the seller. Here the seller’s profit cannot be viewed merely as contractual; it is an unjust gain rooted in the disappearance of the res.

3. Why negotiation-derived gains are non-actionable
   - Roman law declined to treat ordinary contractual profits as unjust enrichment: a contract itself justifies retaining the price. One may not bypass the remedy of contractual action by recasting a simple bargain gain as a condictio sine causa. For this reason, prezzo ex negotiatione remains with the seller, even if subsequent events frustrate ownership transfer, unless an extra-contractual element of injustice intrudes.

4. The role of eviction recourse
   - When the purchaser can invoke an eviction action against the seller for reimbursement of price (regressus), any vestige of res-derived gain vanishes. The seller’s retention of the price is provisional: the owner, via purchaser, can recover it. Therefore, even if the owner ultimately fails in rei vindicatio, the seller does not "keep the res’s proceeds" unjustly; he is liable to return them to the purchaser upon eviction. That prevents any permanent enrichment ex re.
   - Conversely, if the seller lacks an eviction recourse—as when he acquired the thing gratuitously (inheritance, gift) or under a putative but invalid title—no mechanism exists to claw back the price. The owner’s lost res has been irreversibly turned into price held by the seller, and the seller lacks an eviction remedy. This absence of regressus transforms what was initially a negotiation-derived price into a res-derived gain: it persists only because of the thing’s wrongful depletion of the owner’s patrimony.

5. Conclusion: Limiting restitution claims
   - The maxim draws the line between legitimate contractual profit and unjust enrichment tied to the thing’s loss. A bona fide seller may hold prix ex negotiatione free of restitution claims, but if he ultimately retains that price in virtue of the res’s perishing or usucapion—without any eviction-based recourse—the price has become lucrum ex re. Only in that scenario does the owner have a restitutionary claim under the condictio sine causa. This conceptual distinction ensures that restitution claims are confined to truly unjust gains rooted in the owner’s patrimonial harm.

qa_pairs.question:
Within a broader discussion of unjust enrichment in cases involving alienation of another’s property, several jurists group together acquisitions by accession, mixture of money, specification, and sale as uniform grounds for condictio against the possessor. Yet it is argued that cases like accession deserve isolated treatment. 

Analyze why the case of accession—where one adds one’s own material (e.g., a piece of copper) to someone else’s material (e.g., a gold ingot) producing a new composite—may justify an enrichment claim on an independent basis, and why it cannot be subsumed under a single general rule with sale and other enrichments. In your answer, identify the specific features of accession that underpin its distinct treatment.
qa_pairs.answer:
The case of accession (accessio) exhibits several singular features that differentiate it from other forms of enrichment and justify discrete legal treatment:

1. Physical cohesion of disparate materials
   - Accession involves two separate corpus (bodies of matter) belonging to different owners. Upon uniting them, a new composite res emerges—yet the incorporated matter remains physically present at the site of the principal res. The material of the accessory does not vanish; it is literally part of the finished product. This corporeal continuance grants the accessory’s owner a tangible connection to the res long after accession.

2. Inviolability of owner’s material
   - Since the accessory matter subsists in the composite, the original owner of the accessory has a proprietary stake in the finished good. Even though nominal ownership transfers to the composite’s acquirer (by virtue of accession rules), the accessory-owner’s right against involuntary deaccession remains rooted in the physical continuity of his material.

3. Absence of pure price conversion
   - Unlike sale, where the thing becomes price and potentially disappears from the owner’s patrimony, in accession the owner’s accessorial matter continues as a part of a tangible asset. The enrichment to the acquirer is not solely a monetary profit; it is the enduring possession of another’s corporeal matter integrated into a new res. The acquirer’s gain thus cannot be conceptualized simply as negotiation-derived or price-based; it is a proprietary gain of a physical value.

4. Specific statutory remedies and texts
   - Ancient juristic texts grant the owner of the accessory a direct enrichment action against the possessor of the principal res who has added the accessory in good faith. These texts emphasize the location of the corpus near or within the principal res, calling upon the possessor to disgorge the accessory matter or its value. Such remedies differ from a condictio for a sale-price: they aim at restitution of the material or its equivalent.

5. Distinct justificatory principle
   - Accessio law is founded on the principle that one may not unjustly profit by physically appropriating another’s matter into a composite. The proportional value of the accessory, its inseparability, and its physical endurance distinguish it from contractual or tort-like enrichments. This justification rests on protecting proprietary integrity of one’s material, not on restoring a price wrongfully retained.

6. Why a unified rule fails
   - Attempting to subsume accession under a general unjust enrichment rule ignores the accessory’s continued corporeal presence and the proprietary nature of the enrichment. For sale or money mixture, the enrichment is abstracted as price or fungible matter; remedies focus on monetary recovery. For accession, the enrichment is concrete possession of a physical part, demanding an in-kind remedy or valuation based on the material’s continuance. No single formula (e.g., condictio sine causa) captures both.

Conclusion: The unique intersection of corporeal continuity, proprietary stakes in physical material, and specialized juristic enactments necessitate treating accession separately from sale, mixture, or specification. Only through isolating accession can the law adequately address the distinctive injustice of integrating another’s matter without proper entitlement.

qa_pairs.question:
Consider the following facts drawn from two Roman slave-sale contracts:  one dated 142 AD, the other 160 AD.  Each contains the phrase “apochatum pro uncis duabus,” literally “quittance for two ounces,” referring to the price which the vendor originally paid when acquiring the slave.  A nineteenth-century scholar (Mommsen) interpreted “two ounces” as two ounces of gold –– i.e. that the vendor’s original purchase price had been paid in gold weight.  A more recent critic (Appleton) points out the economic improbability of two distinct slaves (one Greek boy, one Cretan woman), sold eighteen years apart in a legionary camp in Dacia, having both been acquired by their immediate vendors for exactly two ounces of gold, and instead argues that “uncis duabus” is the legal formula fixing the fictitious price of mancipation, here expressed by weight of copper equal to the “as sextantali” (the half-ounce as), a standard dummy price—just as elsewhere one finds “sestercio nummo uno” or “assibus quattuor.”  Appleton further notes that two copper ounces (four half-ounce asses) correspond exactly to one sesterce at that period.  Under Dacia’s well-established Roman coin circulation (denarii, sesterces etc.), payment in gold weight is implausible; a fictitious copper price explains why identical “pro uncis duabus” clauses appear in two otherwise unrelated contracts.  

Critically evaluate these two interpretations:
  (a) “uncis duabus” = two ounces of gold weight, the vendor’s original real purchase price
  (b) “uncis duabus” = a fictitious price of two copper ounces (the as sextantali standard), equivalent to one sesterce, fixed by formula for mancipation

In your answer, set out clearly the legal and economic reasoning on each side, show how each accounts for the evidence of Roman coin shortages or sufficiency, the statistical improbability of identical gold-weight purchases, and the needs of mancipatory dummy prices, then conclude which interpretation is more convincing and why.
qa_pairs.answer:
To compare the two interpretations, we must weigh legal-procedural imperatives of Roman mancipation against the economic and statistical realities of Dacian legionary markets.  

1.  The gold-ounce hypothesis (Mommsen)

  Mommsen’s reading takes “uncis duabus” at face value – two ounces of gold – because he sees “apochatum” as the vendor’s delivery of the prior vendor’s receipt (“apoca”); the phrase simply records that the vendor had once paid two ounces of gold, and now hands that quittance to the buyer so that ownership transfer by mancipation (“per aes et libram”) is complete.  Roman tradition required that the seller not only perform the ceremony but also have paid (or secured) the purchase price; handing over the old receipt legitimated his title.  

  Objections:
  • Coinage abundance:  By 142–160 AD Dacia was thoroughly monetized in Roman silver (denarii) and bronze (sesterces, asses).  Occasional gold coins existed, but gold-weight transactions for slaves are nowhere attested.  Slaves sold for hundreds of denarii, not ounces of gold.  
  • Statistical absurdity:  Two very different slaves, in different years and likely at different local markets, would scarcely both have been acquired exactly for 2 oz of gold.  Appleton shows that, if we imagine millions of sales over centuries, the survivor set of four Dacian triptychs could not by chance include two with identical gold-weight origins.  
  • Local economics:  The presence of legionary pay and banking agents in Dacia makes coinage plentiful – there is no need to revert to gold bullion as money of account.  A bullion-only economy would have made payment by gold weight common, yet all other extant transactions in Dacia use denarii or asses.  

2.  The fictitious copper-weight price hypothesis (Appleton)

  Appleton observes that Roman mancipation required a nominal price fixed in a coin unit, but not necessarily paid in that coin.  Merchants wishing to conceal their own purchase cost would employ a dummy price – always the same token sum – then sell at a real market price without disclosing profit.  The canonical dummy prices were:
   – sestercio nummo uno (one sesterce)  
   – assibus quattuor (four asses)
   – uncis duabus (two ounces of copper)  
  In the first-century forms this “uncis duabus” was simply the as sextantali standard: each as weighed a half-ounce (sextantali), so two asses = one ounce and four asses = two ounces.  Four half-ounce asses therefore equaled one sesterce (i.e. two copper ounces = one sesterce).  Thus “uncis duabus” names the same dummy price as “sestercio nummo uno.”  

  Supporting points:
  • Uniformity in form:  Both triptychs use identically “apochatum pro uncis duabus” to denote the dummy price, showing the formula was copied from a standard legal template rather than reflecting the vendor’s real past outlay.  
  • Coherence with other clauses:  In non-mancipation slave sales and in sales of slaves acquired as booty or as accessory to a mother, the “apochatum” clause disappears or is replaced by equally formulaic terms — confirming it is not a recital of real payment but a legal fiction.  
  • Economic plausibility:  Merchants needed to preserve profit margins and avoid revealing their trade discounts; using a constant nominal token price allowed them to produce to buyers a title in which the only amount recited was the ficeious “two ounces.”  The real monetary exchange (e.g. 600 denarii, 420 denarii) was recorded elsewhere in the deed.  
  • Absence of bullion usage:  Nowhere does any other Dacian transaction record payment “pro uncis aurorum.”  Gold reserved for large state disbursements or imperial coin issues – not routine slave- sales.  

3.  Synthesis and conclusion

  (a)  Mommsen’s interpretation cannot surmount the economic implausibility or the statistical improbability of identical two-ounce gold payments; nowhere in the region’s rich corpus of sales documents does gold-weight appear as the contractual medium.  
  (b)  Appleton’s dummy-price interpretation explains the uniform formula, fits known mancipatory practices (“as nummo uno,” four asses, one sesterce), and aligns with the conceptual need of a merchant-seller to present a minimal token price while conducting a market transaction at a much higher real sum.  It also ties neatly to numismatic data showing that, in the early Empire, the half-ounce as was an official standard, and four such asses equaled precisely one sesterce.  

  Therefore, the fictitious copper-weight-price reading is far more convincing.  It respects the legal requirements of mancipation, the template-driven nature of Roman legal forms, the realities of Dacian coin circulation, and the commercial incentive to conceal purchase costs.  Mommsen’s gold-weight thesis fails under economic, statistical, and documentary scrutiny, while Appleton’s account renders every piece of evidence natural and coherent.

qa_pairs.question:
Roman authorities across several centuries adjusted the nominal weight of the copper coin known as the “as” to maintain a roughly simple ratio between silver and copper currency values.  Suppose we have the following data:

— Under the early Republic (the triental system), the as weighed one Roman pound (12 ounces) and was reckoned as 1/10 of a denarius, implying that a denarius’s silver was worth 240 times the copper of one as.  
— By a later measure called the sextantali (often attributed to mid-Republican war exigencies), the as weighed 2 ounces (1/6 of a pound), giving a silver-to-copper ratio of 140:1 (assuming 84 denarii per pound of silver).  
— Under Augustus’s reforms (oncal), the as weighed 1 ounce, shifting the ratio to 112:1.  
— Under a subsequent semi-oncal measure, the as weighed 1/2 ounce, ratio 84:1.  

Assuming that (i) coinage intrinsically derived its value from metal content, (ii) large inflows of silver (from war booty, trade with Greek cities, new mines) tended to depress silver’s relative value, and (iii) state officials sought to maintain simple, round ratios between silver and copper currency to avoid constant re-price‐setting in the marketplace, analyze how each successive reduction in as weight reflects responses to changes in silver abundance.  Then explain how this pattern illustrates the economic principle that “bad money drives out good” (Gresham’s Law) when precious metal is undervalued in coin, and why a government might deliberately debase copper coinage weight to stabilize bimetallic circulation.
qa_pairs.answer:
1.  Economic background: intrinsic-value coinage and bimetallism  

In a system where coins derive their purchasing power from metal content, the ratio of melt values between silver (denarii) and copper (asses) must correspond to market supply and demand of the two metals.  If the state strikes silver and copper coins at fixed metal weights, any divergence between intrinsic melt ratio and legal ratio spurs par of trade: undervalued metal is hoarded or exported, overvalued metal floods circulation.  Gresham’s Law—“bad money drives out good”—predicts that coins with melt values below face (bad) will circulate, while those with melt above face (good) will be withdrawn.  

2.  Republican triental as (12 oz, 1/10 denarius) → 240:1 ratio  

At inception of the denarius, legislated around 285 BC, the as weighed a full pound (12 oz), and 10 such asses equaled one silver denarius.  If 1 lb silver = 240 asses by weight (assuming 1 denarius = 1 oz of silver), then silver was 240 times more valuable than copper.  In an emerging silver coin age, silver was scarce — imported Greek coins prompted the first silver issue — and the high ratio reflected silver’s rarity.  Under this regime:  
  • Steady inflows of Greek and Carthaginian silver gradually depressed silver’s relative scarcity.  
  • By mid-Republic (Second Punic War), Rome faced ballooning debts and soldier pay.  

3.  Sextantali as (2 oz, 1/6 lb, still 1/10 denarius) → 140:1 ratio  

By reducing the as to 2 oz, yet keeping 10 asses per denarius, the state cut the copper content per as to 1/6  of earlier, halving the melt ratio to 140:1.  This adjustment served two ends:  
  (a)  It aligned the legal silver-to-copper ratio more closely with the market reality of abundant war-trophy silver.  
  (b)  It freed up more copper for minting coins to pay troops, while preserving bimetallic circulation.  

Because silver’s real market purchasing power had fallen (owing to large bullion inflows), copper coinage would otherwise have driven silver coins from circulation (Gresham’s Law) if the state had not debased the copper coin to maintain the ratio.  

4.  Oncal as (1 oz, 1/12 lb, 1/10 denarius) → 112:1 ratio  

Augustus’s monetary reforms standardized weights and measures across the Empire.  By cutting the as to 1 oz, the silver-to-copper ratio moved from 140:1 to 112:1.  Why 112?  Because silver’s continued influx from the East, plus growing state expenditures, further depressed silver.  To forestall Greshamian flight of silver coins, copper coin had to be lightened again.  

An 112:1 ratio remained a convenient round number under Augustus’s system of 84 denarii per pound (12 oz) of silver (84 / 12 = 7 denarii per ounce; each ounce of copper was thus 7 denarii / 1 oz = 112:1).  

5.  Semi-oncal as (1/2 oz, 1/24 lb, 1/10 denarius) → 84:1 ratio  

Subsequent fiscal strains (civil wars, imperial grants) further expanded silver supply in circulation.  By halving the as again to 1/2 oz, the ratio became 84:1, congruent with 84 denarii per pound of silver (a convention reported under Tiberius).  

6.  Gresham’s Law and deliberate debasement  

Each time silver became undervalued in coin relative to the market price, holders sold silver bullion or melted coins, hoarding copper.  To prevent silver’s disappearance and maintain a functioning bimetallic system, Rome systematically debased its copper coins — lowering weight so that their face value better matched their melt value relative to silver.  

By legislating successive as-weight reductions rather than allowing unregulated market arbitrage, the state:
  • Preserved circulation of both metals (no silver drain)
  • Supplied copper coinage to pay soldiers, officials, and public contractors
  • Retained a simple ratio easily understood by merchants and provincial treasuries

Each weight adjustment was thus a preventive strike against the “good money” (silver) fleeing circulation, and demonstrates an early instance of state-managed bimetallism.  By debasing copper coinage in measured steps, Rome balanced fiscal needs with the economic realities of metal markets, illustrating Gresham’s insight that only by aligning legal and intrinsic values could both metals stay in active use.

qa_pairs.question:
In Roman private law, transfer of certain property required a ceremonial sale known as mancipation (“per aes et libram”), always conducted at a nominal “dummy” price—one as—regardless of the item’s true value.  Later legal formulae standardized this fictitious price in three parallel expressions:  

  • “sestercio nummo uno” (one sesterce),  
  • “assibus quattuor” (four asses),  
  • “uncis duabus” (two ounces of copper).  

Two Dacian triptychs dated 142 AD and 160 AD each record a slave sale with the clause “apochatum pro uncis duabus,” meaning “quittance for two ounces.”  The repetition of this precise phrase in two independent contracts suggests it was inherited from an earlier Roman mancipation template.  

Explain why the mere fact that a late-Republic or early-Imperial legal formula uses “two ounces” rather than naming a coin (“as” or “sestercio”) implies three things:
  1) At the time the original template was composed, the standard copper as had a fixed legal weight of two ounces (the so-called “as sextantali”).  
  2) That weight standard was official and state-sanctioned, otherwise legal drafters would have used a named coin rather than an unstable bullion measure.  
  3) The persistence of “uncis duabus” in later formulas supplies independent confirmation of the as sextantali’s official status, even if direct state edicts survive in fragments or not at all.

In your answer, show how legal-formal templates preserve archaic technical standards, why a legalized weight unit must be stable, and why this weight-based clause serves as compelling evidence for the official origin of the as sextantali standard.
qa_pairs.answer:
Roman procedural law prized formulaic precision.  Legal acts were drafted from stock templates that contained fixed phrases copied verbatim, even long after the circumstances that originated those phrases had faded.  We can illustrate how “apochatum pro uncis duabus” preserves an archaic monetary standard as follows:

1.  Formulaic inheritance preserves archaic technical data  

  Roman lawyers compiled formularies – booklets of standard clauses – for every kind of legal transaction: sales, fiduciae, divorces, wills.  When a new deed was written, drafters inserted words from these formularies with minimal alteration.  Thus, phrases that once matched contemporary practice remained locked in their original form, becoming a living fossil of early law.  

  The clause “uncis duabus” appears identically in two slave-sale triptychs eighteen years apart, in distant copies, demonstrating it was part of an inherited template.  Since legal drafters in 160 AD had no reason to weigh copper bullion for mancipations, the clause is not a fresh technical instruction but a retained archaic formula.  

2.  Weight-based versus coin-named standards  

  A template specifying a monetary unit normally names the circulating coin: e.g. “sestercio nummo uno.”  But a weight measure – “two ounces” – only makes sense if that weight corresponds precisely to the legal standard.  If “two ounces” were a casual, approximate bullion weight, intermediate drafters would have replaced it with the name of the coin (as or sesterce) current in their day.  The fact that they did not implies the numerical weight was itself the canonical definition of the coin unit at template creation.  

  Thus, the clause must date from the period when an as formally was defined as two ounces (sextantali).  Only then was “uncis duabus” tantamount to “one as.”  A later editor, uncertain of its original meaning, might editorialize it into “as nummo uno,” but no such emendation occurred—testifying to confidence in two-ounce precision.  

3.  Official standardization underpins legal stability  

  Legal forms enshrined state-sanctioned standards.  If the as sextantali weight had not been fixed by some authoritative law or decree, variations in measurement practice would quickly have rendered “two ounces” meaningless or false.  Draftsmen encountering local deviation would have switched to naming the nearest equivalent coin, rather than perpetuating a non-official weight.  Since they did not, we infer that two ounces was a formally accepted standard for the as—a product of legislation or Senate decree—at the time the formula originated.  

  Moreover, Roman awareness of monetary upheavals (e.g. multiple as reductions) compelled jurists to maintain accurate forms; they would not perpetuate an inconsistent weight that no longer corresponded to legal reality.  The survival of “uncis duabus” thus certifies that, when the formula was first drafted, the as sextantali was official.  

4.  Independent confirmation of as sextantali’s official status  

  Direct evidence—such as a preserved Senate decree ordaining an as sextantali during the Punic Wars—is extremely fragmentary or lost.  Yet the legal-formular fossil provides independent corroboration: it shows that private law instruments recognized two ounces as the token mancipation price, itself anchored in the formally sanctioned definition of the as.  

  This legal-textual evidence complements numismatic and rhetorical sources (e.g. Pline’s statement that asses were “imposés” at sextantali weight during wartime scarcity) to demonstrate that the as sextantali was not a haphazard practice but an official monetary standard adopted by the Roman state.

Conclusion  

“Uncis duabus,” preserved verbatim in early-Empire sale contracts, is more than a curious archaic phrase: it is a strategic historical witness.  Its continued presence in legal templates signals that the as sextantali was a stable, state-sanctioned unit, defined as exactly two ounces of copper, and that this definition was sufficiently authoritative to be enshrined in private-law formularies for generations.

qa_pairs.question:
In the study of early Roman private law, the actio rei uxoriae is the praetorian remedy by which a wife could claim restitution of her dowry upon dissolution of marriage. Three main theories have been advanced to explain its original origin and form:

1) A stipulatory origin.  It is said that, before becoming a legal action, customary marriage contracts included a stipulatio—or even an informal pact—by which the husband promised, in the event of divorce, to leave the better part of the dowry with himself and to restore the remainder to his wife.  This is attested in a passage of Boethius (citing an earlier jurisconsult) which quotes a formula concerning "quod melius aequius erit apud virum remanere... quod non esset aequius aequum apud virum manere, id uxor post divortium reciperet."  Some scholars argue that the praetorian actio rei uxoriae simply formalized and replaced this stipulation, inheriting its formula and rules on the husband’s retentiones.

2) A domestic‐jurisdiction origin.  According to this view, in the old Roman familia the paterfamilias or husband was obliged by customary family law, whenever he repudiated his wife, to convene a domestic court (judicium domesticum) of relatives and friends, to pronounce divorce and to fix—with equity—the portion of her dowry the wife would retain or forfeit, depending on her marital misconduct.  When domestic procedure decayed, the praetor purportedly created the actio rei uxoriae as a public substitute for the old family arbitration, preserving its principles.

3) A penal origin.  Another scholar observes that the actio rei uxoriae shares its most distinctive traits with a group of "in bonum et aequum conceptae" actions—the actio injuriarum, the actio sepulchri violati and the actio de effusis et ejectis—which are all unquestionably penal, authorizing the judge to inflict an equity‐based amende arbitrarily fixed "quantum ob eam rem aequum videbitur."  He argues that the original actio rei uxoriae, likewise, was a private penal remedy against the husband’s unjust repudiation (injustum repudium), not a contract enforcement or family arbitration, and that its later development into a civil "restitutio" action obscured but did not erase its penal origin.

Summarize the principal arguments and textual evidence marshalled for and against each of these three hypotheses.  Then, critically assess which origin theory you find most persuasive, based solely on the strengths and weaknesses of these arguments and evidence.
qa_pairs.answer:
To approach the origin of the actio rei uxoriae one must weigh the three competing theories by examining their explanatory power and the force of the textual and logical objections against them.

1)  The stipulatory origin.  Proponents point to Boethius’ quotation (itself from some earlier jurisconsult) of a cautio formula: “quod melius aequius erit apud virum remanere... quod non esset aequius aequum apud virum manere, id uxor post divortium reciperet.”  They note that the formula of the actio rei uxoriae itself uses the words “quod aequius melius erit,” and that one of its central rules concerns the husband’s retentiones.  Thus, they infer that the praetorian actio rei uxoriae directly evolved from a stipulatio, transforming a private promise into a public right of action.  This hypothesis coheres nicely with the textual similarities and with the practice—attested by Servius Sulpicius via Aulu‐Gelle—that cautiones rei uxoriae existed before the action.

  Objections:  However, ancient law required that a stipulatio lay on a certum, a definite sum; an “incerta pecunia” or promissio in genere was void in the archaic period.  Hence the anecdote on Carvilius Ruga’s cautio, which deals in formulae of “what is better and fair,” must post‐date the actio (if built on its formula) rather than precede it.  Moreover, the cautio and action coexisted from Republic through Justinian, and courts made a sharp contrast between “actio ex stipulatu” and “actio rei uxoriae.”  It is implausible that the solemn cautio simply sprang from an unconscious transposition of a mature praetorian formula.

2)  The domestic‐jurisdiction origin.  Advocates draw on the Catonian anecdote (via Aulu‐Gelle): “Vir cum divortium facit, mulieri judex pro censore est: si quid perverse tetreque factum est a muliere, mulctatur; si vinum bibit... condemnatur.”  They argue that early Romans settled dowry disputes in a family judicium domesticum and that the actio rei uxoriae is exactly a praetorian substitute of that old domestic arbitrage.  This neatly explains why the actio rei uxoriae departs from typical contractual forms or legis actiones—its rules follow family‐court logic, awarding or reducing dowry shares based on the wife’s morality.

  Objections:  Firstly, domestically the decision‐maker was the pater himself or his concilium—the husband was judge in the first instance, yet the actio rei uxoriae is always directed against the husband, not against the wife as the domestic sanction would be.  Secondly, the necessity of a public action against one’s husband rings oddly if it merely formalized family arbitration.  Finally, contemporaries treated the actio rei uxoriae and the domestic actio de moribus as separate remedies with a point of contact but not as public and private variants of a single origin.

3)  The penal origin.  Here, the actio rei uxoriae is seen as a private penal sanction, like the actio injuriarum, the actio sepulchri violati, and the actio de effusis et ejectis: all are in bonum et aequum conceptae, permitting the judge to assess an amende arbitrarily (“quantum ob eam rem aequum videbitur”).  The actio rei uxoriae, originally, was not a contractual claim to recoup a promise but an offence remedy against unjust repudiation (injustum repudium).  This account explains several features:

  –  Its penal formula and lack of strict procedural form (in bonum et aequum concepta).  
  –  Its intransmissibility: upon the wife’s death, it died; upon the husband’s death before locus poenalis, it could not survive against his heirs.  This matches the intransmissible character of other penal actions (injuriarum, de moribus).
  –  Its co‐existence with the cautio: two parallel but independent penalties—one contractual caution, the other public sanction.
  –  Its reflection in declamatory rhetors, who speak of an "actio injusti repudii" or "malæ tractationis," clearly as a penal accusation.

  Objections:  One might argue that by classical times the actio rei uxoriae is decidedly civil, de bona fide, and that its link to other penal actions rests on analogy rather than explicit statements in the edict.  Yet, Roman law contains many examples of praetorian actions evolving from penal to civil as they become codified.  Further, an apparent late rule—in the Digest—allowing heirs of a husband who held dowry peculium to be sued under the actio rei uxoriae seems hard to square with a purely penal origin.  But this rule arises after successive reforms redefining the basis of the claim as the mere fact of having received dowry, rather than the delict of repudiation, and therefore post‐dates the ancient punitive scheme.

Critical Assessment:  The stipulation theory, though appealing for its textual resonance, founders on the archaic invalidity of incerta pecunia and the independent survival of cautio and actio for centuries.  The domestic‐jurisdiction theory illuminates the family context but misaligns the party roles (husband as judge vs. husband as defendant) and cannot account for the action’s later civil evolution.  By contrast, the penal‐origin hypothesis systematically explains the action’s formula, its procedural anomalies, its intransmissibility, and its rhetorical framing in declamation.  Moreover, the known Roman practice of converting family‐school penalties into public, then civil, remedies provides a plausible historical pathway: an originally punitive private remedy against unjust repudiation was, over generations, assimilated into the lex Aquilia‐like, bona fide restitution actions.  Therefore, on balance, the penal origin theory emerges as the most persuasive account of the actio rei uxoriae’s genesis.

qa_pairs.answer:
The classification of Roman remedies "in bonum et aequum conceptae" signifies a special procedural genus: the praetor grants a writ employing a formula that entrusts to the judge broad equity powers, notably the determination of a penalty or award in arbitrary measure—"quantum ob eam rem aequum videbitur."  This distinctive feature appears in three undisputedly penal actions:

  1)  Actio injuriarum:  classical formula “quanti ea condigna videbitur,” imposing an amende privata for personal insult.
  2)  Actio sepulchri violati: formula directs the judge to condemn for "dolus malus" in violation of a sepulchre to “quantum ob eam rem aequum videbitur.”
  3)  Actio de effusis et ejectis: for accidental spillage causing harm to a free person, the judge arbitrarily assesses “quantum ob eam rem aequum videbitur.”  

In each, the remedy’s core is punitive.  Its procedural form eschews the rigid intentio of contract or property suits; instead, it harnesses the magistrate’s discretionary justice.  When we turn to actio rei uxoriae, we encounter:  

  •  A formula containing "quod aequius melius erit," reflective of a norm of equity rather than fixed restitution;  
  •  The central concept of retentiones, allowing the accused husband to have a portion of the dowry withheld, akin to the adjustment of a penalty;  
  •  A writ framed to enable the judge to decide what sum the husband ought to return, without specifying a predetermined sum but instead invoking the judge’s conscience and sense of fairness.  

These formal affinities reinforce the notion that actio rei uxoriae belonged originally to the same category of punitive, equity‐based actions.  This alignment gains further weight from doctrinal parallels:

  –  Intransmissibility:  all these "in bonum" remedies died with the victim’s death or—where brought against the wrongdoer—could not be continued against heirs if the wrongdoer died before judgment on penalty (e.g., actio injuriarum, actio de moribus).  Actio rei uxoriae shows the same intransmissible pattern—extinguished by the wife’s death and, if the husband died prior to “mora” or mise en demeure, not surviving against his heirs.  This feature is wholly consistent with a punitive role and inconsistent with a purely contractual claim.
  –  Parallel evolution:  Just as injuria and fur­tum actions initially penal were later formalized into civil damage claims with bona fide language, so the actio rei uxoriae, once purely sanctional for unjust repudiation, became a praetorian civil remedy to secure dowry restitution.  The shift to bona fide formula and an emphasis on restitution rather than punishment corresponds exactly to analogous trajectories for other penal remedies that matured into civil suits.
  –  Rhetorical declamation:  declaimers of imperial schools of oratory speak of an actio "injusti repudii" or "malæ tractationis," clearly imagining a penal, accusatory remedy to avenge a wife’s moral and proprietary harm.  Quintilian equates this rhetorical creation explicitly with the legal actio rei uxoriae.  Such memory must derive from a genuinely punitive character long associated with the remedy.

Caveats:  Over time, actio rei uxoriae—and indeed the injuria‐based actions—acquired a predominantly restitutory, bona fide guise.  Their procedure was consolidated, civilianized, and they came to resemble contract or quasi‐contract remedies.  One might argue that convergence of form among disparate classes of action undermines the weight of analogy.  Yet the fundamental genesis—public sanction of moral delict—explains their shared model.  Moreover, textual evidence shows that these actions retained vestiges of their punitive roots even after centuries of civil reformation, notably in judicial discretion over “aequum.”  

Conclusion:  The formal concordance of the actio rei uxoriae with the quintessentially penal actions in bonum et aequum conceptae—through shared equitable formulas, intransmissible nature, and rhetorical tradition—constitutes a powerful composite argument.  Where three distinct remedial types exhibit identical procedural DNA to enforce a public penalty, it is most plausible that actio rei uxoriae, too, was born as a private penal sanction against unjust repudiation, subsequently retooled into a civil restitution action.

qa_pairs.question:
A hallmark of Roman private penal actions—such as the actio injuriarum and the actio de moribus directed against wrongdoing spouses—was their personal, non‐transmissible character: if the victim died, the action perished; if the wrongdoer died before condemnation, his heirs could not be sued on that claim.  In classical sources it is recorded that the actio rei uxoriae (the wife’s action for recovery of her dowry on divorce) likewise died with the wife and did not survive against the husband’s heir if the husband died prior to mise en demeure.  

Explain how this intransmissibility powerfully supports treating the primitive actio rei uxoriae as a penal remedy for "injustum repudium" rather than as a contractual or property action.  Compare how intransmissibility aligns with punitive actions and conflicts with what one would expect from a contract‐enforcement suit.  Base your analysis solely on the features and comparisons detailed above.
qa_pairs.answer:
The intransmissible character of a legal action—that neither the claimant’s nor the defendant’s heirs can continue it—signals a deeply personal remedy anchored in the moral reproach of a delict rather than in impersonal enforcement of contractual or proprietary rights.  In Roman private law, the following observations clarify why the actio rei uxoriae’s intransmissibility denotes a penal origin:

1)  Penal actions are personal and non‐fungible.  The actio injuriarum, founded on insult or assault to one’s person, extinguishes at the victim’s death: who else but the injured party could carry on the outrage’s private prosecution?  Likewise, succumbing to mortal wounds eliminates the interest of any heir in prosecuting the offender.  Conversely, contract claims (stipulatio, sale) are transferable: rights in rem or bona fide obligations in personam convey to heirs, because their object is a debt owed by the defendant to the deceased, now fallen to the heir by universal succession.

2)  The actio rei uxoriae, when triggered by divorce, derives from a husband’s "injustum repudium"—a wrongful repudiation understood as a quasi‐delict against the wife’s person and proprietary interest.  The wife alone suffers the moral and financial wrong; only she can assert the sanction.  If she dies, the cause vanishes: heirs cannot step in to vindicate her mistreatment, for the personal affront and breach of marital duty cannot readily be abstracted into a simple patrimonial claim.  Similarly, if the husband—or the wrongdoer—dies before the wife formally demands restitution or before judgment, the public‐law sanction loses its target; heirs cannot be compelled to pay a private penalty intended to chastise the wrongfinder himself.

3)  Textual confirmation appears in the Digest: a passage states that where dowry was given to a husband, and he died before mise en demeure, "if after his death no mora has intervened, the dowry remains with the husband’s heir."  This rule is identical to the treatment of penal actions of injuria and moribus, which die with the wrongdoer.  Were the actio rei uxoriae a contract‐based restitution action, the wife’s heirs would enforce it; were it a property claim, the obligation to return the dowry would bind the heir as universal successor or at least as a possessor of the husband’s estate.

4)  Contractual and property actions aim to restore the aggrieved party’s patrimony: their remedy is quantifiable and abstract.  They concern sums due or things owed and, as debts, survive against heirs.  The actio rei uxoriae, originally formulated in penal terms—allowing the judge to assess arbitrary punishment within the dowry’s capital—reflects private vengeance and personal retribution not easily commuted to a mere creditor‐debtor relation.  Only when, over centuries, the remedy was reframed as bona fide to secure restitution of specific things (res dotales) did it develop transmissibility features.

5)  The incompatibility of intransmissibility with contract law is underscored by contrast: stipulation and bona fide claims (negotiorum gestio, depositum) became transmissible once recognized by formulae vesting in heirs the status of litigants.  Yet even among these, actions having truly punitive underpinning (injuria) remained intransmissible.  The fact that actio rei uxoriae follows the punitive pattern and not the civil one strongly indicates that its origin was likewise punitive.

In sum, the personal, non‐transmissible nature of the actio rei uxoriae parallels unequivocally the core feature of Roman private penal actions.  It contradicts the expectations for a contractual or property‐based action, whose survival in the hands of heirs is a fundamental principle.  Thus, the remedy’s intransmissibility provides compelling evidence of its original design as a private sanction for unjust marital repudiation rather than as a mere means to enforce dowry promises.

qa_pairs.question:
In Roman legal scholarship, juristic fragments in compendia like the Digest were often subject to interpolation by later compilers. Consider a hypothetical fragment that states:

"If an heir is condemned to deliver a specific object but does not render it where it was, and thereafter, without the heir's fraud or negligence, it perishes, the legatee's condition becomes worse."

The clause "thereafter, without the heir's fraud or negligence" (postea sine dolo et culpa heredis) appears in some manuscripts but is disputed. Based on the principles of textual coherence and legal logic exemplified in a scholarly analysis of legatum per damnationem (the obligation to deliver a specific thing), outline a systematic method to determine whether this clause is likely an interpolation. Limit your method strictly to internal textual evidence and criteria demonstrated in the analysis.
qa_pairs.answer:
A systematic method to assess whether the clause “postea sine dolo et culpa heredis” is an interpolation must rest on internal evidence—syntactic coherence, thematic consistency, and alignment with the juristic context of legatum per damnationem—as follows:

1. Examine Semantic Necessity and Consistency with Obligation Type
   • The fundamental doctrine for both stipulatio ad rem dandi and legatum per damnationem teaches that the obligor is bound only ad dandum (to transfer ownership) and not ad facere (to preserve or guard). Liability for the perishing of the thing arises only when the obligor’s positive act contradicts the dandum, or when the obligor is in mora and the thing perishes post mora (per eum stetit, quominus daretur).
   • The introduction of “without the heir’s fraud or negligence” suggests liability only for fault—a departure from the classical rule that a positive act (factum imputabile) perpetuates the obligation irrespective of fault. In the established scheme, no mention of culpa or dolus is needed to exclude mere non‐performance; the mere fact that the thing perished post‐mora suffices to impose liability. This mismatch indicates thematic dissonance: culpa or dolus is not conceptually relevant to the argued regime.

2. Test Syntactic Cohesion and the Referent of Adverbs
   • The adverb “postea” (“thereafter”) demands a clear antecedent milestone within the text: either the moment of condemnation, the moment of non‐delivery, or the inception of mora. In the fragment as given, “postea” has no unambiguous anchor—does it refer to a chronological instant, a legal status change, or an event? Such ambiguity, unusual in lucid juristic formulations, signals that the clause may have been inserted without careful integration.

3. Scrutinize Grammatical Agreement and Pronoun Reference
   • The fragment’s subject is the heir (heres). Yet the interpolated clause speaks of “the heir’s fraud or negligence” (heredis), which presumes the heir as both subject and object of the same action. Classical compilers favored clarity: where the subject had just been stated as heres, we would expect a simple nominative or genitive in apposition to flow naturally. The doubling of reference is redundant and stylistically awkward.

4. Cross‐Compare Parallel Fragments for Uniformity of Doctrine
   • Other fragments dealing with perishing of the res certa (e.g., manumission of the slave, consecration of property as religious) repeat that only a positive act or post‐mora perishing gives rise to liability. They do not invoke culpa or dolus to qualify the perishing. The sudden introduction of fault‐based language in our fragment breaks the pattern uniform across all authentic fragments on legatum per damnationem.

5. Assess the Likelihood of Late Gloss versus Original Juristic Formulation
   • Later compilers sometimes introduced clarifying glosses to tie Roman fault‐based obligations to newer justinianic standards. The phrase “without the heir’s fraud or negligence” resembles such a gloss, seeking to harmonize neglect liability with post‐classical culpa concepts. Its presence in some manuscripts but absence in older recensions suggests it was not part of the original concise juristic decision but a later exegetical addition.

6. Evaluate Legal Logic for Redundancy or Conflict
   • If the clause were original, it would carve out an exception that liability does not arise when the thing perishes through no fault. Yet in classical legatum per damnationem, non‐liability requires only that the obligor did nothing to impede dandum; negligence in preservation—being no facere—was never deemed an impediment. The clause thus duplicates an already implicit exclusion, rendering it superfluous. Superfluous clauses are a hallmark of interpolations.

Conclusion
   By subjecting the fragment to these internal tests—semantic consistency with ad dandum vs ad facere obligations, syntactic clarity, cross‐fragment doctrinal harmony, avoidance of redundancy, and stylistic conformity—we deduce that the “postea sine dolo et culpa heredis” clause is most likely a later interpolation rather than part of the original juristic ruling.

qa_pairs.question:
Under Roman law, an obligatio rem dandi (an obligation to transfer ownership of a specific thing) is distinguished from an obligatio facere (an obligation to perform a service). A jurist argues that in a legatum per damnationem of a res certa (a specific thing), the promissor or heir is bound only ad dandum, not ad facere. Given these definitions, analyze two scenarios:

1) The promissor intentionally kills the specified slave before delivery.
2) The slave dies of natural causes during illness because the promissor failed to provide medical care.

Using the jurist's reasoning about ‘factum imputabile’ and ‘mora’, determine whether the promissor remains liable in each scenario and why.
qa_pairs.answer:
To resolve each scenario, we apply the jurist's strict distinction:

• Obligation Type: Obligatio rem dandi (ad dandum)
   - The debtor’s duty is solely to transfer full dominion of the res certa at the proper time. He is not bound to preserve, guard, or care for the thing (no obligatio facere). Liability attaches only if the debtor performs a positive act incompatible with delivery (factum imputabile), or if the debtor remains in mora and the thing perishes thereafter.

• Factum Imputabile vs. Mere Non‐Performance
   - Factum Imputabile: Any deliberate or involuntary act by the promissor that directly frustrates the dandum (e.g., destroying, alienating, consecrating the thing). This act perpetuates or even intensifies liability.
   - Mere Non‐Performance: Passive omissions, like failing to preserve, care, or protect the thing, do not themselves constitute a breach of an ad dandum obligation.

• Application of Mora (Delay)
   - If the debtor is in mora (i.e., fails to deliver when due), he stands for the risk of perishing thing (per eum stetit quominus daretur). Thus, if the thing perishes after due date, even without positive misconduct, liability continues.

Scenario 1: Promissor Intentionally Kills the Slave
   • This is an unequivocal factum imputabile: a positive act directly contradicting the duty to deliver. The jurist states: “If the slave owed is killed (without just cause) by the promissory party, the obligation perpetuates.”
   • Because the promissor committed an act that makes delivery impossible, he remains liable for the obligation’s value: he must pay pretium (the slave’s valuation), or suffer condictio rei certae if invoked. No defense of exceptio doli succeeds, since the act itself is the very wrongdoing the exceptio was designed to exclude.

Conclusion for Scenario 1: The promissor remains fully liable; killing the slave does not extinguish but rather reinforces the obligation.

Scenario 2: Slave Dies of Natural Causes Due to Neglected Care
   • Here, the death arose from a failure to provide medical assistance—an omission (non‐facere). The jurist emphatically denies an ad facere duty: “He is not bound to ‘facere,’ i.e., to guard, preserve, or safeguard the thing.”
   • Because the promissor’s omission does not conflict with the core duty to transfer dominion (he had no express duty to cure or nurse), it is not a factum imputabile. The mere fact of negligence does not trigger liability in this ad dandum obligation. Absent fraud or positive misconduct, the promissor is not held responsible for natural loss.
   • Moreover, there is no invocation of mora risk here if we assume death occurred before the due date. Even if it happened after, periculum rei post‐mora depends on the debtor’s failure to deliver on time, not on separate omissions. If the promissor had delivered on time, the risk would have transferred to the legatee.

Conclusion for Scenario 2: The promissor is not liable. The death by illness, resulting from mere neglect, does not breach an ad dandum obligation.

Summary
   • Killing the slave: positive interference = liability continues.  
   • Natural death from neglect: omission = no liability under ad dandum.  
   This analysis hinges on the jurist’s precise classification of duties and the principle that only facta imputabilia or post‐mora perishing of the thing trigger continued liability.

qa_pairs.question: In the context of Roman legacies, a legatum sinendi modo (a "legacy granting only the concession to allow the legatee to take the thing") entails that the heir must permit the legatee to acquire specified property. A scholar observes that the Latin verb "sinere" in legal usage can mean both "to allow" and "to actively facilitate" (i.e., to remove obstacles). Drawing on contractual analogies and servitude provisions discussed in the scholar's analysis, critically evaluate why the obligation under a legatum sinendi modo should be understood to include an active component of operam praestare (undertaking actions) rather than mere passive non-interference. Your answer should reconstruct the reasoning from first principles without assuming prior knowledge of external sources.
qa_pairs.answer:
The debate centers on whether "sinere" imposes only a negative duty (non-interference) or extends to a positive duty (facilitation). The scholar reconstructs the meaning by analogy to other legal constructs:

1. Comparison with the Contractual "Sinere" in the Lex Locationis
   • In the lex locationis (contract of hire for woodcutting), the stipulation "neve quem cingere caedere urere sinito" expressly prohibits interference. Yet a jurist clarifies that sinere here cannot mean mere refraining from cutting; it also obliges the owner to ensure the redemptor can cut the wood if he approaches the grove. That is, the hirer must not only abstain from hindrance but must actively prevent third parties from obstructing the hired woodcutting (operam dare). The jurist concludes: "sinere has two senses... it must be understood that the lessor... must also ensure by action that no one else cuts it."

2. Analogy to Fideicommissary and Usufruct Legacies
   • Certain fideicommissary legacies and usufruct legacies require the heir to provide access, keys, and documentation so that the beneficiary can exercise rights. These legacies are termed sinendi modo and find frequent use in property conveyances. Though framed as granting permission, they were treated by jurists as imposing an obligation akin to dandum plus facilitation—otherwise the legatee would be at the mercy of third-party obstacles.

3. Functional Necessity in the Obligation
   • The fundamental purpose of legatum sinendi modo is to confer on the legatee the practical ability to take possession. A purely passive non-interference would leave the legatee vulnerable if third parties interposed new claims or if the heir retained keys, title deeds, or entry codes. To achieve the testator’s intention—actual conveyance—the heir must undertake positive steps: produce instruments of transfer, grant physical access, remove locks, or even pay bribes to remove illicit blockages.

4. Juristic Resolution in Salvio Giuliano’s Writings
   • Salvio Giuliano equates interest on delayed legacies with fideicommissa only "in the legacy of leaving permission." He argues that the heir who allows but does not actively facilitate the legatee’s acquisition is effectively in mora. The remedy provided by iudex (award of interest and costs) presupposes that the heir failed to carry out an active duty, not merely omitted to object. This reflects the double sense of sinere: allowing and enabling.

5. Integration into the Schema of Ad Dandum vs Ad Facere
   • While a legatum per damnationem (ad dandum) binds the heir to grant ownership, a sinendi modo legacy overlays an additional ad facere obligation: the heir must perform whatever acts are necessary to remove obstacles to transfer. The scholar thus places legatum sinendi modo at an intermediate point between strict ad dandum and pure ad facere: it begins as permission but evolves into active cooperation to effectuate delivery.

Conclusion
   From multiple angles—contractual analogy, exigencies of testator intent, Salvio Giuliano’s views, and alignment with remedies awarded by judges—it becomes evident that "sinere" in the legacy context is not a mere negative duty. Instead, it carries a positive charge: the heir must undertake concrete steps (operam praestare) so the legatee may immediately and effectively claim the legacy. Without this active component, the testator’s will would be frustrated, and the legatee left with a hollow promise of permission.

qa_pairs.question: Imagine an heir subject to a legatum per damnationem for a particular slave. The slave is, through no fault of the heir, absent—having fled and currently untraceable. The legatee sues for delivery of the legacy. Using the reasoning found in juristic fragments on legatum per damnationem, delineate the logical structure of the heir’s defense based on an exceptio doli (a plea of no wrongdoing), including the proposal to offer a cautio (security) for restitution should the slave be apprehended. Explain under what conditions this defense succeeds, what obligations the heir must undertake, and its limitations.
qa_pairs.answer:
The heir’s defense unfolds through the following logical steps:

1. Identification of the Continuing Obligation
   • As heir condemned to deliver a specific slave, he remains under an ad dandum obligation. The legatee’s action is prima facie well founded: the heir owes the slave or its equivalent value.

2. Recognition of the Slave’s Absence Without Heir’s Fault
   • The heir asserts that the slave is absent—having fled—and that this absence is not imputable to his own fraud (dolus) or negligence (culpa). In legatum per damnationem, mere absence does not obliterate the heir’s duty if the absence resulted from a factum; yet if no impermissible factum occurred, the heir may challenge satisfaction of the demand.

3. Invocation of the Exceptio Doli
   • The heir raises an exceptio doli: “I have committed no wrongdoing; the thing is not mine to tender.” This exception allows him to resist immediate condemnation for payment of estimation (aestimatio), provided he offers an alternative security.

4. Offer of Cautio (Security for Restitution)
   • To prevent the legatee’s loss from processual delay, the heir offers a cautio—a guarantee that if the fugitive slave is later apprehended, he will hand him over. This aligns with the jurist’s prescription: “cavere debet heres de restitutione servi, non aestimationem praestare.” He must propose conditions under which, upon eventual recovery, the legatee can obtain the thing.

5. Conditions for Success of the Defense
   a. Absence of Heir’s Fault
      – If the flight or disappearance occurred without the heir’s positive act or negligent omission that would qualify as factum imputabile, the exceptio stands.
   b. Adequacy of the Cautio
      – The security must be sufficient to ensure prompt restitution upon discovery. It need not prepay the slave’s value but must guarantee delivery of either the actual slave or the equivalent valuation when the slave becomes available.

6. Limitations of the Defense
   • Fault by the Heir: If the slave fled due to the heir’s negligence in custody or was captured by enemies through the heir’s act (ab hostibus captus sit…ciuitate heredis), the exceptio fails; liability proceeds to aestimatio or condictio.
   • Multiple Legates: When the legacy names two alternative slaves, and one is present, the heir must tender the present one; the exceptio only excuses inability to produce the absent one.
   • Complete Absence of Any Slave: If both alternative slaves are missing and the heir cannot secure either, he may offer caution for both, but the legatee may still elect to demand immediate valuation rather than wait indefinitely.

7. Role of Judicial Discretion
   • The judge (iudex) supervises the adequacy of the cautio and may order interim protections for the legatee. The heir’s defense works only to defer final condemnation; it does not absolve him of eventual performance or valuation.

Conclusion
   The heir’s exceptio doli coupled with a proper cautio navigates between strict condemnation and outright defense. It succeeds only when absence is not imputable and the heir offers real security for restitution. Otherwise, the legatee may compel immediate valuation or seize any available slave as equivalent.

qa_pairs.question:
In an equitable legal system grounded on natural justice, any expenditure by one individual (the expenditor) for the benefit of another (the beneficiary) gives rise to a restitution claim if—and only if—certain conditions are met. Suppose we define "unjust enrichment" to occur when:

• The expenditor applies personal labor or pecuniary resources to the preservation or improvement of the beneficiary’s patrimony or personal condition; and
• The beneficiary’s estate or personal status is thereby made better or at least not worsened ("ut rem meliorem dominus habuerit aut non deteriorem"); and
• The expenditure was necessary or useful and proportionate to the beneficiary’s social standing; and
• The resources expended have not been lost, consumed without benefit, or voluntarily donated by the beneficiary; and
• The expenditure was not directed toward luxury or immoral purposes unless expressly authorized; and
• The expenditor maintained the serious will to benefit the beneficiary, so that if a fortuitous event frustrates the intended purpose, the expenditure is still recoverable.

Formulate precisely the necessary and jointly sufficient conditions (a condition set) under which the beneficiary is obliged to restitute the expenditor’s disbursements. Then, critically explain how each condition balances the universal principle of equity (“no one ought to be enriched at another’s expense and to another’s injury”) with the limits imposed by necessity, social status, and morality.
qa_pairs.answer:
A concise yet rigorous statement of the restitution conditions, distilled into logically distinct requirements, runs as follows:

1. Expenditure-Directed-to-Benefit (Intent): The expenditor must have applied labor or resources with a bona fide, serious will (serio volere) to confer a benefit upon the beneficiary. Mere involuntary or indifferent outlays do not found restitution.

2. Improvement-or-Conservation Criterion: The application must have resulted in an actual improvement of, or prevented deterioration in, the beneficiary’s patrimony or personal condition. In Latin: ut rem meliorem dominus habuerit aut non deteriorem.

3. Utility-and-Proportionality Constraint: The outlays must be necessary or useful (non superflua, non turpes) and proportionate to the beneficiary’s social status, intelligence, and condition (secundum consuetudinem domini). Ordinary sustenance, housing, or instruction up to the social norm qualifies; ostentatious luxuries exceed this boundary.

4. Preservation-of-Benefit Exclusion: If the expended thing was lost, consumed without any resulting benefit to the beneficiary, or voluntarily donated, no enrichment has in fact occurred and no restitution lies.

5. Morality-and-Authorization Boundary: Disbursements aimed at immoral or illicit ends—though spent for another’s welfare—are excluded unless there was explicit authorization by the beneficiary, which then converts the outlay into a binding mandate rather than a mere act of benevolence.

6. Continuity-of-Will under Fortuity (Sine Causa Principle): Should an unforeseen, extrinsic event frustrate the attainment of the intended benefit, restitution remains due so long as the expenditor’s benevolent intention persisted up to the moment of frustration (i.e., the failure is due to fortuitous causa). If, instead, the expenditor’s will changed or aborted the purpose, no claim arises.

Critical Explanation of the Balance:

• Universal Equity vs. Personal Sacrifice: The first two conditions enshrine the heard-of Latin maxim jure naturae aequum est neminem cum alterius detrimento et injuria fieri locupletiorem—no one should gain at another’s expense. They ensure that whenever one person enriches another by genuine improvement or conservation of the latter’s estate, equity demands restitution.

• Necessity and Social Norms: The third condition introduces a sociological calibration: "usefulness" must be gauged against prevailing social customs and the beneficiary’s status. Thus, an agrarian proprietor made no wealthier by marble statuary in his farmhouse, though such statuary might enrich an urban palazzo. This limit prevents trivial or counterproductive claims and aligns enrichment with reasonable human needs.

• Exclusion of Non-Beneficial Outlays: The fourth condition prevents a fiction of enrichment where no benefit actually accrued—outlay on things lost, consumed to no effect, or voluntarily transferred by the beneficiary leaves nothing against which to ground restitution.

• Morality Check: The fifth condition embodies the moral dimension; expenditures for depraved or illicit ends cannot be the bedrock of an equitable claim. By requiring explicit beneficiary authorization in those rare cases, the system disavows opportunistic restitution for disreputable purposes.

• Fortuity and Persistence of Intent: Finally, the sixth condition safeguards the expenditor from bearing losses due solely to chance, distinguishing those from losses occasioned by a change of mind. If the expenditor’s will remains earnest up to the frustrating event, equity steps in to restore fairness.

Collectively, these conditions crystallize the delicate equilibrium between the universal imperative that no one be unjustly enriched at another’s expense and the practical limits of necessity, social context, and moral propriety intrinsic to a nuanced doctrine of restitution.

qa_pairs.question:
Two creditors, Creditor A and Creditor B, hold successive pledges over the same immovable property as collateral for their respective loans. Creditor B advances additional funds after Creditor A’s pledge to mend the roof and prevent structural decay. The total proceeds from enforcing the pledgeized property prove insufficient to satisfy both loans. 

Drawing on a principle of unjust enrichment that gives preference to a creditor who has "laid money into the pledged property" (
pecunia in rem oppignoratam), analyze whether Creditor B is entitled to a preferred ranking over Creditor A. In your answer, explain the underlying rationale and the limits of this principle.
qa_pairs.answer:
Under the pertinent doctrine, any creditor who expends pecunia directly into the pledged property—either to restore dilapidation (restitutionem aedificii), to prevent decay (conservandam rem), or to improve it—acquires a preferred rank over earlier pledgees in the distribution of proceeds. The foundational criterion is that the creditor’s funds must have been used in such a manner that the property was made either better or at least not worse for the common pool (ut rem meliorem dominus habuerit aut non deteriorem). 

Application to Our Scenario:

1. Nature of B’s Expenditure
   • B’s advances for the roof repairs plainly qualify as an application in rem oppignoratam: they directly address the physical fabric of the pledged asset.
   • The expenditure is not superfluous; it prevents imminent harm. Consequently, it satisfies both the improvement-or-conservation test and the utility criterion.

2. Legal Effect: Preferential Ranking
   • Since B’s pecunia was applied to preserve the value of the collateral, Roman jurisprudence grants B a "potioritas in pignore," i.e., a superior claim in the distribution hierarchy, even though A’s pledge predates B’s.
   • This rule rests on natural equity: it would be unjust for A to benefit from the increased—or preserved—value that B’s funds secured without bearing any share of that expenditure.

3. Limits and Boundary Conditions
   • The funds must genuinely have preserved or improved the collateral. If B had applied them to mere cosmetic or luxury superstructures not reasonably necessary to prevent deterioration, the enrichment principle would not trigger.
   • B must prove that the moneys were actually laid out for the preservation or improvement. Post hoc or vague claims of expense are insufficient.
   • The rule does not extend to discretionary or unrelated enhancements (e.g., installing luxury amenities), unless the pledgee had explicit authority to undertake such outlays.

Rationale:

This preference rule crystallizes the broader maxim of unjust enrichment: one who enriches the common pool for the benefit of all creditors should not be left out of pocket simply because his pledge was subsequent in time. By securing B’s reimbursement first, the legal system aligns the economic incentives: creditors are encouraged to maintain the value of collateral, thereby protecting all parties’ interests and promoting market stability.

Conclusion:

Creditor B, having lawfully and usefully applied funds to preserve the pledged property’s integrity, acquires priority over Creditor A under the Roman principle of "pecunia in rem oppignoratam."
