qa_pairs.question:
An agent is entrusted by a principal to expend a sum of money for a specified benevolent purpose for a third party—for example, to purchase freedom for a slave within a stipulated time or to erect a modest dwelling for a destitute beneficiary. No formal mandate contract is concluded, thus the agent acts on the basis of the principal’s expressed benevolence. Before the agent completes the task, an unforeseen event occurs: in one case, the slave dies; in another, the materials for the house are destroyed by flood. 

Using the equitable principle that expenditures made bona fide to benefit another remain recoverable when thwarted by fortuitous causes—unless the agent’s will has changed—analyze under what circumstances the agent may recover his disbursements from the intended beneficiary. Specifically, distinguish:

(a) the effect of the event occurring before the lapse of any period during which performance was possible, and
(b) the effect of the event occurring after that period has run without performance.

Explain the reasoning by reference to the notions of a change of will (penitentia) versus an event beyond control (causa fortuita).
qa_pairs.answer:
We analyze under the rubric of the conditional gift or expenditure sine causa. The agent’s right to restitution turns on two factors: (1) whether the underlying purpose was rendered impossible by a fortuitous event or frustrated by the agent’s change of will, and (2) the temporal relation between the event and any period granted for performance. 

I. Event Before the Expiry of the Performance Period

  1. Preservation of Benevolent Will: If the event—such as the sudden death of the slave or a flash flood—occurs before the lapse of the time in which the agent could have executed the benevolent act, the agent’s intention to fulfill the grant remains unaltered at the moment of frustration.  

  2. Restitution Owed: Equity commands that the agent be reimbursed, since the failure of the benefit to vest in the third party stems exclusively from a causa fortuita outside the agent’s volition. Restitution is not "inhibenda nisi poeniteat" because no penitentia (change of mind) has intervened.

II. Event After the Expiry of the Performance Period

  1. Implicit or Explicit Lapse of Intent: Once the period capped for performance passes without execution, equity treats the agent’s inaction as, at best, negligence and at worst as a change of will. The agent had time and opportunity but failed to use it.

  2. No Restitution (Unless Express Repentance): The agent cannot claim reimbursement, because by letting the performance window close, he effectively renounced the benevolent purpose. Only if he demonstrates a concrete expression of repentance (poeniteat) within the period could restitution revive, but generally the right is extinguished.

III. Penitentia versus Causa Fortuita

  • Causa Fortuita: These are events—death, natural disasters—unforeseeable and extrinsic to will. When they alone prevent performance, the agent’s will remains intact, and equity compels restitution.  

  • Penitentia (Change of Will): If the agent, for any reason, retracts the benevolent intent before or within the performance period, no enrichment was aimed at the beneficiary; hence, no unjust enrichment claim exists.

Illustrative Example:

  • Agent given six months to purchase a modest plot and build a hut for the beneficiary. Month four: violent landslide destroys the site. The agent recovers all sums expended—materials bought, wages paid—since the failure is force majeure and his good will persisted.  

  • Conversely, if the agent simply never acted during the six months, excuses notwithstanding, he cannot demand restitution: by letting the period elapse, he manifested a de facto change of will.

Conclusion:

Roman equity thus finely discriminates between genuine misadventure and unexcused inaction. Only fortuitous frustration, coupled with an unbroken benevolent intention, warrants restoring the expenditor to his former state.

qa_pairs.question:
Legal tradition often equates two forms of sustenance as deserving restitution when provided by one party for the benefit of another: material sustenance (food, clothing, housing) and intellectual sustenance (education, tuition). Both are said to enrich the recipient’s person or patrimony rather than diminish them. 

Given the following guiding principles:

1. "Ut rem meliorem dominus habuerit aut non deteriorem" applies equally to corporeal goods and to the soul’s perfection (the mind’s cultivation).  
2. Material nourishment and tuition must each be "secundum consuetudinem domini," i.e., necessary or useful and proportionate to the beneficiary’s social status.  
3. Civil wisdom and eloquence, though invaluable, are not to be measured by monetary standards; however, instruction reasonably tailored to the student’s means is reimbursable if expressly demanded.  

Construct an analytical comparison of these two classes of outlays, explaining:

a) Why Roman jurists considered them analogous in principle;  
b) How they delineated limits on reimbursements to guard against abuse;  
c) What broader lessons about the nature of enrichment and equity this analogy reveals.
qa_pairs.answer:
a) Analogy in Principle:

• Common Functional Role: Just as food, clothing, and shelter are indispensable for maintaining and perfecting the human body, education and instruction are deemed necessary for preserving and cultivating the mind—"alimento spiritus." Both categories serve as "perfectibilia humana": one addresses corporeal needs, the other addresses intellectual and moral development.  

• Equity of Application: In both domains, an individual who, at another’s expense, supplies what is necessary or useful enriches the beneficiary either by conserving existing capacities or by conferring new ones. Thus, the same test "ut rem meliorem dominus habuerit aut non deteriorem" is invoked to determine whether an action de in rem verso lies for restitution.

b) Delineation of Limits:

• Proportionality to Social Status: For material sustenance, Ulpian required that the servant be fed or clothed "secundum consuetudinem domini," i.e., up to the customary standard of the master’s household—neither frugal nor extravagant. Analogously, for instruction, only such teaching as accords with the student’s condition and means is recoverable. Tuition in lofty arcana or esoteric arts beyond the student’s station falls outside the recoverable ambit.  

• Exclusion of Superfluity and Luxury: Any provision—be it sumptuous trappings in the meal or gilded rhetorical training—surpassing necessity or utility was held non "in rem versi." Luxurious or immoral outlays create no entitlement to restitution unless separately authorized by an explicit mandate.  

• Quantitative Restraint: Just as housing improvements must not impoverish the master by their excess, so too must the lender of education refrain from exorbitant fees. Roman jurists enforced a proportional cap, preventing a creditor from imposing pauperes servos in penuria under the weight of pedagogic sums.

c) Broader Lessons about Enrichment and Equity:

• Universality of the Improvement Principle: Whether corporeal or intellectual, any act that conserves or augments another’s estate or person falls within the ambit of reversible enrichment. This reflects a substantive conception of patrimony that transcends mere land and chattels, embracing human capital.  

• Integration of Moral and Social Values: By aligning legal remedies with community standards of necessity and decency, the doctrine safeguarded against both oppressive claims and moral sponsorship of vice. The proportionality requirement fuses legal formality with social norms.  

• Dynamic Conception of Patrimony: The analogy underscores that patrimonial value is not static or purely monetary but includes the ability to act virtuously and intelligently in civic life. Equity thus protects investments in personal development with the same vigor as those in tangible assets.  

In sum, the Roman framework’s parallel treatment of material and intellectual expenses illuminates a sophisticated theory of enrichment: one that captures the full spectrum of human capacities, anchors restitution in shared notions of necessity and moderation, and ultimately advances a holistic view of justice grounded in both economic and moral amelioration.

qa_pairs.question:
In Roman law, a pactum de non praestanda evictione generale is a side‐agreement in which the seller declares “nihil evictionis nomine praestitum iri,” seeking to exempt himself entirely from liability for eviction (i.e. from restituting any benefit to the buyer if the thing is lost through a third‐party claim). The dispute turns on the passage from Ulpian’s commentary (L. 11 § 18 D. de act. emt. et vend. 19. 1, taken from Ulpian in the Edict):

“Si aperte in venditione comprehendatur, nihil evictionis nomine praestitum iri. Nam si per se non videtur ex emto tenebitur; sed Julianus… neque ex stipulatu, neque ex emto.”

Here “stipulatio” denotes an express verbal promise by the seller, while “pactum” denotes a tacit or simple side‐agreement. Explain in detail:

1. How Ulpian structures his argument to distinguish between (a) an express stipulatio entered into for some eviction cases only, and (b) a general pactum de non praestanda evictione (whether expressly or tacitly concluded).
2. The philological and logical role of the particles “nam,” “nisi,” and “sed” in introducing, qualifying, and then rejecting Julian’s position.
3. Why, on Ulpian’s own principles of bonae fidei contractus, he concludes that a general pactum (whether express or tacit) frees the seller from any restitution—contrary to Julian’s view—and how the text’s structure and wording support this conclusion.
qa_pairs.answer:
Ulpian’s brief but densely structured passage performs three tasks in rapid succession:

I. Distinguishing Two Modes of Evictions‐Side Agreements
   1. Express “stipulatio” for specific eviction cases (“per se…”)
      • When the buyer and seller expressly stipulate—“per se”—that the seller will stand liable for eviction only in certain defined events, Ulpian says the seller neither answers “ex stipulatu” (by stipulation) nor “ex emto” (by virtue of the sale) for other eviction events. In other words, an express promise limited to enumerated cases cannot be extended by implication to all evictions.
   2. General pactum de non praestanda evictione (“Si aperte… nihil evictionis…”)  
      • When, however, the clause covers eviction liability in general—“Si aperte in venditione comprehendatur, nihil evictionis nomine praestitum iri”—Ulpian regards it as a full release of both obligations: neither the express stipulatio nor the underlying sale (actio emti) can be used to press any restitution.

By framing the opening sentence as a general condition—“If in the sale it is openly stated that nothing shall be rendered in the name of eviction”—he sets up the scope of a general pactum. He contrasts it with the limited stipulatio, thus showing that a single verbal formula (“nihil evictionis nomine praestitum iri”) suffices to extinguish both the incidental stipulation and the sale‐based warranty.

II. The Logic of “Nam,” “Nisi,” and “Sed”
   1. “Nam” (For) introduces Ulpian’s own clarification of the limited stipulatio case:
      • “Nam si per se non videtur ex emto tenebitur”—literally, “For if he has promised only for himself (per se), he does not seem to be held by the actio emti.”  
      • Here “nam” signals Ulpian’s own reasoning about why a limited stipulation cannot stretch to all evictions. It links back to the prior sentence by explaining the principle underlying express stipulations.
   2. “Nisi” (Unless/If not) marks a momentary doubt or counterfactual test:
      • Although in strict usage “nisi” often introduces an exception, its classical juristic role is to voice a possible objection or hesitation: “non videtur ex emto tenebitur, nisi …”—“he is not held by the actio emti, unless ….”  
      • Although the rest of the sentence does not complete the “unless,” the mere presence of “nisi” tells us that Ulpian is raising a hypothetical nuance or anticipating a challenge.
   3. “Sed” (But) signals outright dissent and introduces Julian’s contrary opinion:
      • “Sed Julianus… neque ex stipulatu, neque ex emto”—“But Julian says that in this case the seller is held neither on the stipulation nor on the sale.”  
      • By using the adversative “sed,” Ulpian intentionally sets Julian’s view in opposition to his own. Jurists typically employ “sed” to introduce a contrary position they do not accept.  

III. Ulpian’s Bonae Fidei Rationale and Final Conclusion

1. Bonae fidei Contractus requires full effect be given to the parties’ agreement (L. 11 § 1 D. de act. emt. et vend. 19. 1):  
   • “Nihil magis bonae fidei congruit quam id praestari quod inter contrahentes actum est”  
   • Whatever has been agreed between the parties must be performed in good faith: if nothing more is agreed, one resorts to the contract’s natural elements (“naturales”).

2. The natural incidence of a bonae fidei sale is that whatever is promised in the sale or side agreement is due; if nothing is stipulated for eviction, the natural warranty of “habere liceat” (the right to enjoy without disturbance) remains intact.

3. From this principle Ulpian derives:
   1. If the seller expressly limits his liability to particular eviction cases, he is exempt in all others. (Nam… si per se.)
   2. If the seller makes no reservation, the buyer may sue by actio emti for price and interest.
   3. If the seller explicitly reserves (pactum generale) that “nothing shall be rendered in name of eviction,” then neither the stipulation nor the sale warranty can be invoked. (Si aperte… nihil evictionis…)

4. By positioning Julian’s view—“neque ex stipulatu, neque ex emto”—after “sed,” Ulpian marks it as a dissenting minority opinion. He thus rejects Julian’s plea (grounded on the supposed unnaturalness of retaining the price while losing the thing) in favor of his own consistent application of good‐faith contract principles.

In sum, Ulpian’s structure:
• Opens with the broad conditional (“Si aperte…”) describing the general pactum.  
• Uses “nam” to explain the limited stipulation case.  
• Introduces a conceivable caveat with “nisi,” then discards it by invoking “sed.”  
• Cites Julian’s contrary stance as an object lesson in what Ulpian does not adopt.  
• Implicitly restates his rule of good faith: parties are bound by the literal agreement; a general renunciation frees the seller entirely.

Thus, through careful deployment of these particles and by contrasting express stipulation with a general pactum, Ulpian demonstrates that a pactum de non praestanda evictione generale—properly framed—absolves the seller from refunding both price and interest.

qa_pairs.question:
Some jurists tried to reconcile Ulpian and Julian on the effect of a pactum de non praestanda evictione generale by arguing that Julian’s rule—that the buyer may reclaim the entire purchase price despite such a pactum—only applies to the sale of uncertain things (emtio spei), whereas a sale of a specific thing (emtio rei certae) follows Ulpian’s view freeing the seller completely. Using only the definitions and reasoning given in the excerpt (including Paulus’s statement that “ex emto actio non ad pretium duntaxat sed ad id quod interest”), critically analyze why this dichotomy between emtio rei certae and emtio spei fails to establish a true agreement between Ulpian and Julian. In your answer, address:

1. How Julian himself defines emtio spei as a bonae fidei contractus, undercutting the claim that his rule applies only to uncertain‐object sales.
2. Why the fragment’s wording—particularly “ex emto non tenebitur”—lacks any linguistic support for restricting Julian’s rule to emtio spei alone.
3. How Jurists’ attempts to posit an emtio rei certae vs. spei distinction conflict with the text’s doctrine that the actio emti primarily seeks price restitution (“duntaxat ad pretium”) and then interest.
qa_pairs.answer:
The proposed emtio rei certae versus emtio spei distinction rests on three main contentions: that Julian limits his rule to uncertain‐object sales, that Ulpian’s language accommodates this carve‐out, and that the nature of the actio emti as a remedy for uncertain sales supports this. Each fails on textual and doctrinal grounds:

I. Julian’s Definition of Emtio Spei as Bonae Fidei Contractus
   1. Paulus declares explicitly in L. 8 D. de contrah. emt. 18 1 (ad fin.)  
      • “Emtio enim contrahitur, etiamsi nihil inciderit, quia spei emtio est.”  
      • Even a purchase of hope (anticipatory purchase of uncertain outcome) is fully a bonae fidei contract; Julian himself treats both emtio rei certae and emtio spei as falling under the same good‐faith regime.
   2. Therefore, Julian’s rationale—grounded in bona fides—cannot be limited to emtio spei, since he acknowledges both as bonae fidei sales. COVIDing one but not the other contradicts his premise about good faith.

II. The Lack of Linguistic Support in Ulpian’s Fragment
   1. Ulpian’s pronouncement “ex emto non tenebitur” appears without qualification or reference to the object’s certainty.  
      • No clause in the passage even gestures at reserving Julian’s exemption for uncertain objects only.  
   2. Attempts to reference “nisi… in spe” or to recast “nisi forte… rem alienam vendidit” as an ‘unless uncertain sale’ misread the “nisi” as signaling an exception for emtio spei. In fact, “nisi” here introduces a hypothetical objection, not a categorical carve‐out.
   3. If the text truly distinguished between sale types, Ulpian or Julian would have signaled terms like “spei,” “res incerta,” or “res certa.” No such markers appear in the passage.

III. The Role of the Actio Emti: Price First, Then Interest
   1. Paulus instructs in L. 70 D. de evict. 21 2:
      • “Evicta re ex emto actio non ad pretium duntaxat sed ad id quod interest competit.”  
      • The principal thrust of the actio emti is to recover the purchase price; only secondarily does it cover interest (“id quod interest”).
   2. If Julian’s rule were truly confined to emtio spei, one would expect a parallel rule limiting actio emti’s price component similarly. Yet Julian’s position, as Ulpian records, permits full price restitution in every eviction case, not just uncertain ones.  
   3. Reconcilers’ emtio rei certae carve‐out would leave the core purpose of actio emti— price restitution—untouched in ‘certain sales,’ undermining both the remedy’s doctrinal consistency and Julius’s own general statements about good‐faith contracts.

IV. Conclusion: The Dichotomy Fails

1. Julian makes no textual or conceptual distinction excluding emtio rei certae from his full‐restitution rule.  
2. Ulpian’s unconditional “ex emto non tenebitur” flatly rejects Julian’s remedy in all cases once a general pactum is made.  
3. The actio emti’s dependence on price recovery contradicts any theory that price restitution survives the pactum in one kind of sale but not another.

Thus, the attempt to harmonize Ulpian and Julian by invoking the uncertain‐object sale misses both the explicit good‐faith framework Julian applies to all sales and the clear, unqualified language Ulpian uses to enforce his own rule. The emtio rei certae vs. spei hypothesis is neither linguistically anchored in the fragment nor consistent with the broader doctrine of the actio emti.

qa_pairs.answer:
An analytical framework for distinguishing a “purely procedural” reform from one that also carries substantive effects must rest on clear, traceable criteria. Drawing solely on the Roman sources cited—Gaius’ fourth book of Institutes and Gellius’ anecdote about the disappearance of decemviral institutions—we may delineate three core criteria:

1.  **Scope of Changes**
   •  Procedural reforms alter only the manner in which litigants invoke and pursue rights (e.g., replacing one set of rituals with another) without affecting the content or scope of the rights themselves.  
   •  Material reforms either abolish, modify, or create new rights or obligations, or alter the very content of existing statutes.  

   Application to lex Aebutia  
   –  Gaius (§30–§56 of his fourth commentary) notes that under the legis actiones, litigants were “bound to recite exact words of statute and ritual.”  
   –  By contrast, the lex Aebutia authorized the praetor to use a formula that summarized “factual assertions” and framed two legal hypotheses (if P’s assertion is true, then condemn; if not, then absolve).  
   –  Gellius (Noctes Atticae XVI.10.8) states that entire decemviral institutions—talio (“eye for an eye”), the old usury limit of 25 asses, the adsertio of adsidui and subvades—vanished (“consopita sunt”) by virtue of the lex Aebutia.  
   –  Vanishing of these decemviral rights cannot be procedural only: it reflects the nullification of substantive rules.  

2.  **Presence of Explicit Ratification or Abrogation**
   •  A procedural statute normally makes no express reference to the abrogation or modification of existing substantive provisions; it merely says “procedure shall be X, not Y.”  
   •  A material statute typically contains clauses that refer directly or by necessary implication to “set aside,” “modify,” or “exclude” preexisting statutory commands.  

   Application to lex Aebutia  
   –  We have no surviving text of the lex Aebutia, but Gellius’ use of the perfect participle “lata” (the law having been passed) immediately followed by “consopita sit” (have been laid to rest) implies an intentional suppressive effect on the old rights.  
   –  Gaius’ repeated contrast between “articles which must be given by the lex (actiones)” and “those which the praetor grants from his potestas” strongly suggests that the lex Aebutia included an authorization for the praetor to withhold or deny the statutory remedy altogether when he deemed it obsolete or inequitable.  

3.  **Subsequent Legislative Silence and Systemic Impact**
   •  When a reform is purely procedural, later lawmakers often still find it necessary to revisit and amend substantive statutes as before.  
   •  When a reform in effect displaces the legislative role in a substantive area, the legislative assemblies cease producing new laws on the same subject, since the new machinery has supplanted them.  

   Application to lex Aebutia  
   –  Roman private-law legislation essentially halted after the mid-sixth century BC (i.e., the time assigned to lex Aebutia) until the Augustan leges Iuliae.  
   –  Meanwhile, the praetorian edict generated year after year a body of “honorary law” that filled all gaps, modified old statutes, and created new obligations—precisely the effect of a material reform.  
   –  If lex Aebutia had been merely procedural, we would expect the comitia centuriata or tributa to have continued to enact statutes regulating private-law topics; instead, they ceased to do so.  

Reasoned Conclusion  
Applying these three criteria to our sources yields a consistent verdict: the lex Aebutia did far more than swap out a ritualized formal action for a written formula.  Gellius’ explicit testimony that decemviral rights were “laid to rest” by lex Aebutia, combined with the extended description in Gaius of the praetor’s newly-granted power to withhold, adapt, or extend remedies in derogation of prior statutes, and the simultaneous cessation of comitial lawmaking in private law, all point to a substantive displacement of legislative authority.  In other words, lex Aebutia must be understood as a dual-aspect statute—procedural in form but equally material in effect—by which Rome vested the praetor with a de facto power to shape private substantive law on a case-by-case basis.  Thus the long-standing scholarly view of it as “purely procedural” cannot be sustained if we adhere strictly to the ancient evidence.

qa_pairs.answer:
The problem calls for an inductive reconstruction of lex Aebutia’s substantive provisions on the sole ground that it ‘‘laid to rest’’ a range of decemviral institutions en masse.  We proceed by enumerating the abolished rights, grouping them by their legal function, and inferring the clauses needed to extinguish them all at once.

I.  Abolished Institutions (Gellius Noctes Atticae XVI.10.8)
  1. Proletarii, adsidui, subvades – categories of ‘status’ (class distinctions) affecting succession and credits.  
  2. Lex talionis (retaliatory penalty ‘‘eye for an eye’’) – a punitive rule in the XII Tables governing certain delicts.  
  3. Viginti quinque asses – fixed monetary penalty for injuria in the Twelve Tables.  
  4. Futum cum lance et licio – harsh remedies (death by rope and spear) for certain thefts.  
  5. Centumviral actions – special suits before a hundred-judge panel under the Tables.

II.  Hypothetical Clauses of lex Aebutia

1. ‘‘Clause on Abolition of Outdated Statutory Remedies’’ (De Remediis Statutorum Veterum)
   •  Inference: Gellius says ‘‘lex Aebutia lata, consopita sunt . . . omnis illa duodecim tabularum antiquitas’’.  A single clause must have declared all remedies ‘‘vestigial’’ under the XII Tables to be ‘‘ineffective and abrogated’’ when a new praetorian formula existed.  
   •  Function: It sweepingly neutralized the application of decemviral penalties (talio, fixed 25-asse fine) by declaring them ‘‘not to be granted’’ in any praetorian proceeding.

2. ‘‘Clause on Authorization of Praetorian Equitable Remedies’’ (De Iure Honorario Formulis)
   •  Inference: Gaius describes that after lex Aebutia, ‘‘it was brought about that we litigate per concepta verba, id est per formulas’’, and the praetor ‘‘suppl[ied], correct[ed], or extended civil law’’.  A clause must have empowered the praetor to substitute new monetary or personal remedies (e.g., bonae fidei possessory actions, centumviral hereditatis actions) for all earlier savage or ritualistic sanctions.  
   •  Function: Rather than the Tables’ centumviral suit or the vestal rape formula, parties would ‘‘bring their claim in writing’’ and receive whatever ‘‘just and expedient’’ relief the praetor formulated.

3. ‘‘Clause on Status and Succession’’ (De Statibus et Hereditatibus)
   •  Inference: The disappearance of distinctions like proletarii, adsidui, subvades implies that lex Aebutia contained an article ‘‘concerning who may be suo jure heir or possessor’’, thereby overriding Table distinctions grounded in census classes.  
   •  Function: It would declare ‘‘all citizens having full rights of succession and possession, irrespective of previous status categories’’, thus unifying ‘‘heredis loco’’ and ‘‘bonae fidei possessor’’.

III.  Fitting Reconstruction to Overall Dual Nature

•  **Procedural Aspect**: The ‘‘De Iure Honorario Formulis’’ clause matches Gaius’ account of formula litigation, where the praetor ‘‘summarized contested facts’’ and ‘‘fixed the two suppositions (actor’s or defendant’s statement true or false).’’  This is the classic procedural innovation.  

•  **Material Aspect**: The ‘‘De Remediis Statutorum Veterum’’ and ‘‘De Statibus et Hereditatibus’’ clauses directly abolish half-remembered decemviral provisions and reshape core rights in succession and theft, demonstrating lex Aebutia’s power to effect substantive legal change.  Without such abrogatory articles, nothing in a mere procedure-only reform could erase the ‘‘25 asses’’ or ‘‘talio’’ from people’s minds or the courts.  

IV.  Conclusion on Reconstruction Methodology

By grouping the abolished institutions functionally, we see that lex Aebutia must have contained three building blocks:
  (1) A general abrogation of archaic statutory remedies,  
  (2) A broad empowerment of the praetor to craft new equitable remedies via formulae,  
  (3) A provision re-defining citizen status for succession and possession purposes.  

This exercise demonstrates how an effect (“consopita”) reported in Gellius, combined with Gaius’ procedural summary, force us to reconstruct substantive articles in lex Aebutia.  It also shows how providing the procedural ‘‘formula’’ alone would not have been enough to explain the wholesale disappearance of decemviral rights.  Such a law must, therefore, have been both procedural and material in design.

qa_pairs.answer:
To date individual clauses within the extensive Hadrianic edict into two broad periods—post-lex Aebutia (i.e., modifications of existing statutory law, 6th–8th centuries of Rome) versus pre-lex Aebutia (i.e., pre-existing practices absorbed into the edict)—we propose the following tripartite methodology:

1. Philological Criteria:  Terminology and Formulaic Language
   a) ‘‘Ex lege’’ versus ‘‘ex iurisdictio’’
      •  Post-lex Aebutia clauses often read ‘‘eo quod ex lege (or senatus consulta) [action] nascitur, perpetuo datur’’ vs. ‘‘quae ex mei iurisdictio [action] sunt, intra annum solum valent’’ (Gaius IV.32).  
      •  Pre-lex clauses typically frame actions as ‘‘[…] imitatur ius legitimum’’ or ‘‘praeter legem condītis’’ without invoking the procedural ‘‘formulae’’.  
   b) Recurring ritual terms (“sacramentum,” “vadimonium”) point to archaic provisions, while ‘‘concepta verba’’ or ‘‘formula’’ signal post-Aebutian innovations.  

2. Substantive Criteria: Modification or Abrogation of Decemviral Statutes
   a) Provisions ‘‘which imitate ius legitimum’’ (Gaius IV.110) but adapt it—for example, the bonae fidei possessory action (possessio ad usucapionem)—must postdate the abolition of decemviral theft rules and fixed-fine injuria.  
   b) Clauses creating entirely new delicts or remedies—such as those for peculatus (embezzlement by agents)—may derive from pre-Aebutian governor’s imperium (praetors peregrini) but have no counterpart in the Twelve Tables; they could be older than lex Aebutia or created soon after to fill gaps.  

3. Procedural Criteria: Validity Period and Scope
   a) ‘‘Perpetuae’’ (perpetual) versus ‘‘annuae’’ (annual) grants.  
      •  Actions grounded ‘‘ex lege’’ are valid ‘‘perpetuo’’; ‘‘ex iurisdictio’’ when ‘‘perorunt ab uno anno ad annum’’ (Gaius IV.31–32).  
      •  Thus, if a clause specifies ‘‘valet intra annum’’ it is almost certainly a post-Aebutian invention, since annual grants emerge from the new formula system.  
   b) Clauses addressing ‘‘quaestiones’’—the permanent criminal courts—are traceable to the political reforms of the 2nd–1st centuries BC, not to archaic civil enactments.  

Illustrative Examples

•  Example A (post-Aebutian): ‘‘Furti manifesti actio data est perpetuo tamen, quoniam ex iurisdictio procedit, intra annum valet’’ – although tied to a Table remedy (‘furtum manifestum’), its framing as ‘‘ex iurisdictio’’ with an annual validity dates it to after lex Aebutia.  
•  Example B (pre-Aebutian): ‘‘Cum verricidii delictum primum populus centuriis condemnasset, iterum actionem dare placuit praetoribus urbaniis’’ – invoking a centuriate vote and archaic delict suggests an origin before the new formula system.  

Sources of Error and Mitigation

1. **Terminological Drift**: Formulas and labels evolved; some post-lex Aebutia clauses might pretend archaic wording to lend solemnity.  
   –  Mitigation: Cross-reference with multiple manuscripts and juristic commentaries to detect inconsistent usage.  

2. **Retroactive Adaptation**: Hadrianic redactors sometimes retroject innovations onto earlier clauses.  
   –  Mitigation: Collate edict fragments preserved in earlier jurists (e.g., Paul, Ulpian) to gauge original wording.  

3. **Overlapping Scope**: Certain bonae fidei actions ‘‘imitate ius legitimum’’ yet newly articulate equitable principles.  
   –  Mitigation: Prioritize “annual/perpetual” criterion and explicit ‘‘ex lege/ex iurisdictio’’ tags over substantive affinity alone.  

By applying multiple, cross-validating criteria—philological labels, references to ‘‘legis actiones’’ versus ‘‘formulae,’’ express assignment of ‘‘perpetual’’ vs. ‘‘annual’’ validity, and mention of specific statutory origins—a historian can reasonably assign edictal clauses to pre- or post-lex Aebutian cohorts, while acknowledging and controlling for potential ambiguities.

qa_pairs.question:
Consider the following Latin juristic fragment, presented here with no external assumptions:  

“Dedi tibi pecuniam, ut mihi Stichum dares: utrum id contractus genus proportione emptionis et venditionis est, an nulla hic alia obligatio est quam ob rem dati re non secuta? in quod proclivior sum: et ideo, si mortuus est Stichus, repetere possum quod ideo tibi dedi, ut mihi Stichum dares. Finge alienum esse Stichum, sed te tamen eum tradidisse: repetere a te pecuniam potero, quia hominem accipientis non feceris…”  

Scholars have proposed several emendations of the word “pecuniam” (found three times) in this passage:  
• Replacing it with “Pamphilum,” on the theory that a Byzantine copyist misread an abbreviation “pam.”  
• Replacing it with “rem,” hypothesizing that a contract about a generic “thing” was original and later mis-abbreviated as “pec.”  
• Conjecturing “peregrinam pecuniam,” reading “pe. pec.” wrongly in a foreign coin context.  

Knowing that:  
– Standard medieval-Latin abbreviations for pecunia include “pec.”, “pec”, “pc”, “pca”, but never “pam.”  
– Abbreviation for “rem” is normally “R.”, and for “peregrinam” something like “pegr.” or “per.”  
– “Pamphilum” would itself be abbreviated “Pamph.” or “Pam,” but bears no resemblance to standard monetary terms.  

Which reading—“pecuniam,” “Pamphilum,” or “rem”—is most plausible on paleographic and contextual grounds? Provide a detailed argument using only the evidence given above.
qa_pairs.answer:
The reading “pecuniam” is overwhelmingly the most plausible. This conclusion rests on three lines of evidence: the established convention of medieval Latin abbreviations, the internal consistency of the fragment’s meaning, and the improbability of the alternatives.  

1. Abbreviation Practice.  
– Pecunia appears in manuscripts with abbreviations such as “pec.”, “pec”, “pc”, or “pca”. Nowhere in classical or medieval notation do we find “pam.” used for pecuniam.  
– “Re” for rem is normally “R.”; there is no historical instance of a scribe misreading “R.” as “P.” once, let alone three separate times. Similarly, “peregrinam” would be rendered as “pegr.” or “per.”, never as “pe. pec.”  
– “Pamphilum” itself is a proper name and would abbreviate as “Pamph.” or “Pam.”, not “pec.” or “pe.”. Thus no known paleographic pathway leads from a genuine “pam.” to “pecuniam” three times.  

2. Contextual Coherence.  
– The passage centers on the giving of money (“pecuniam”) to secure the transfer of the slave Stichus. Reading “pecuniam” seamlessly fits this logic: money was given in advance, and, if the slave dies or the transfer fails, the giver may recover that money.  
– If the text spoke of “Pamphilum” instead, the grammatical flow collapses: “Dedi tibi Pamphilum, ut mihi Stichum dares” forces the absurdity of swapping two slaves as the core example, though the fragment explicitly focuses on money.  
– If “rem” appeared, the phrase “Dedi tibi rem, ut mihi Stichum dares” would introduce confusion: it fails to specify whether the “res” is money, a slave, or another thing, and contradicts the conclusion that the money (the quid pro quo) must be recoverable. The fragment repeatedly returns to the idea of reclaiming money (“repetere a te pecuniam potero”), which only makes sense if money is the object.  

3. Frequency and Repetition.  
– The word in question occurs three times: “Dedi tibi pecuniam… repetere possum… repetere a te pecuniam potero.” To posit a uniform copyist error at every occurrence strains credulity. Errors in one line are common; the same misreading in three distinct instances strongly argues that the manuscript reading reflects the original.  

By contrast, the “Pamphilum” emendation relies on an unexampled and extravagant misinterpretation of “pam.” and lacks any external attestation. The “rem” hypothesis demands not just one but three identical scribal mistakes (reading “R.” as “P.” each time), defying the usual patterns of medieval paleography. Finally, the notion of “peregrinam pecuniam” imports an entirely new qualifier (foreign money) unsupported by the context or by abbreviation conventions.  

Hence, paleographic probability and internal coherence both compel us to retain the transmitted reading “pecuniam.”

qa_pairs.question:
A Latin juristic formula reads:  

“utrud id contractus genus proportione emptionis et venditionis est"  

Two interpretations have been proposed:  
1) Reading it as two words, “pro portione,” meaning “for a part [of the contract called sale],” thus suggesting the transaction shares only portions of sale’s equity.  
2) Reading it as one word, “proportione,” meaning “in analogy with” or “on the model of” sale, as used by Latin grammarians translating Greek ἀναλογία.  

Given that Roman grammarians (e.g., Varro, Aulus Gellius, Quintilian) define “proportio” as the translation of Greek ἀναλογία and use it for analogical reasoning; that the phrase here aims to ask whether the unknown contract aligns “on the model” of sale; and that no classical source uses “pro portione” in the technical sense “for a part of,” decide which reading is correct and justify how both linguistic usage and contextual purpose support your conclusion.
qa_pairs.answer:
The correct reading is the single word “proportione,” to be understood as “in analogy with” or “on the model of.” This interpretation aligns with classical grammatical usage, conceptual clarity, and context.  

1. Classical Usage of proportio.  
– Varro, in his De Lingua Latina, contrasts “ratio” (reason) and “proportio” (analogy), the latter translating the Greek term ἀναλογία.  
– Aulus Gellius explicitly states, “Aναλογία est similium similis declinatio, quam quidam latine proportionem vocant.”  
– Quintilian defines analogy (“proportio”) as that which relates an uncertain matter to something known, “ut id quod dubium est ad aliquid simile referat.”  
– Cicero, translating Plato and in other rhetorical passages, uses “proportio” in this technical sense. No comparable usage of two words “pro portione” meaning “for a part of” exists in classical jurisprudence or grammar.  

2. Contextual Necessity of Analogical Sense.  
– The jurist poses the question whether the novel contract “is a genus of contract in analogy with sale and purchase,” or merely “a gift for an unperformed exchange.”  
– If one read “pro portione” as “for a part [of sale and purchase],” the phrase becomes awkward: it would read “whether that contract is a genus for a part of sale and purchase,” which neither grammar nor legal reasoning supports.  
– The substantive issue is analogical comparison: “does this contract resemble sale, or is it nothing more than a unilateral gift?” The one-word “proportione” crisply captures this analogical inquiry.  

3. Manuscript and Scholarly Consensus.  
– Scribes and editors who preserve “proportione” recognize it as a single lexeme.  
– Even early glossators noted that the phrase must read “proportione” to be intelligible. Mirroring parallel passages in Justinian’s Pandects, the single-word form is consistent.  

Thus, both philological evidence and the juristic context compel us to interpret “proportione” as a single term meaning “by analogy with,” not the unlikely two-word “pro portione.”

qa_pairs.question:
In one fragment a jurist examines a transaction where A gives money to B so that B will transfer ownership of a slave Stichus to A:  

“Dedi tibi pecuniam, ut mihi Stichum dares… an id contractus genus proportione emptionis et venditionis est, an nulla hic alia obligatio est quam ob rem dati re non secuta?”  

He rejects calling it a regular sale (“emptio venditio”) and instead treats it as a mere “datio ob rem” (a giving for an unfulfilled exchange).  

We know that under Roman law by the classical period:  
– A consensual sale binds seller and buyer by agreement alone; the seller is not strictly obligated to perform traditional conveyance rituals (mancipatio) because the consensual contract makes the buyer owner by operation of law.  
– An obligation “to give” a thing (in legal stipulation) demands strict performance — the act of transfer (mancipatio or traditio) and guarantee against eviction.  

Analyze logically why this money–for–slave exchange could not be placed under the consensual sale framework, and why it instead must be viewed as a strict “obligation to give.” Focus only on the technical distinctions provided above, without introducing new legal doctrines.
qa_pairs.answer:
The transaction falls outside the consensual sale framework because its essential feature is the strict “obligation to give” (dare) rather than the mutual consent that creates ownership by operation of law. Two fundamental distinctions in the classical Roman regime explain why:  

1. Nature of Consensual Sale (“emptio venditio”).  
– In a consensual sale, the contract itself (agreement on thing and price) immediately confers ownership on the buyer.  
– The seller’s obligation is governed by bona fide standards; he need not perform formal conveyance ceremonies (e.g., mancipatio) to bind himself, because the buyer’s consent already effects the title.  
– If the seller fails to transfer possession or mancipate a res mancipi, the remedy is typically an actio ex vendita to enforce cleaning up defects, but not a direct compulsory performance of formal conveyance.  

2. Obligation to Give a Thing (Stipulatio “dare”).  
– A stipulation to give (dare) constitutes a precise obligation: the promisor must perform all acts necessary for the transfer (mancipare or tradere) and guarantee against eviction.  
– Failure to “give” the thing renders him liable for direct recovery of the very thing (or its price) by condictio or claim in factum.  

3. Application to the Money–for–Slave Exchange.  
– Here, A conveys money in advance, conditioning performance on B’s actual transfer of Stichus via ritual conveyance plus eviction guarantee. These features signal a strict “dare Stichum” obligation: A could reclaim the money (condictio ob rem dati) immediately if B neither completed the mancipation nor provided eviction warranty.  
– If the transaction were a consensual sale, B’s bare agreement to transfer would suffice to confer title, and A would become owner once price and consent occurred—even without formal mancipatio. Yet the fragment insists that only physical mancipatio/traditio plus eviction guarantee suffice, displacing the consensual model.  
– Moreover, in a sale the buyer need not obtain an eviction promise at the moment of contract; the seller’s good-faith duty and subsequent remedies suffice. Here the jurist demands a specific eviction promise, characteristic of stipulatory “dare” obligations, not sales.  

Hence, because the transaction imposes the ritual transfer and eviction guarantee as conditions of performance—elements central to the stipulation “dare,” but alien to the consensual sale—the jurist correctly excludes it from the sale contract and treats it as a strict obligation to give.

qa_pairs.question: In early Roman law, “militia” could be alienated by private contract; it denoted a civil public office carrying, beyond regular stipends, an occasional bonus or premium called a “salarium.” Suppose a seller of such an office agrees in writing that the purchaser shall receive not only the office itself but also any “salarium” due, and further undertakes to transfer to the purchaser whatever legal remedies he possesses to recover that salarium. Once the salarium becomes payable by the treasury or official fund, what precise performance must the seller render to satisfy this clause? In particular, must he simply pay any sums he has already collected, or is there a different obligation concerning the seller’s own causes of action? Explain fully the rationale behind your answer.
qa_pairs.answer:
In Roman legal practice the “salarium” of a public office (militia) is understood not as part of the ordinary salary for work performed, but as a personal premium or bonus arising by imperial grace or custom. When seller and purchaser agree that the salarium shall go to the purchaser, they are not merely swapping a fixed debt already owing; they are transferring the entire right to recover whatever future or contingent bonuses accrue by virtue of the office. Consequently, as Ulpian interprets Scaevola’s text, the seller’s obligation is not simply to pay over any sums he has already received, but to hand over to the purchaser all of his extraordinary legal remedies—actiones extraordinariae—by which those bonuses can be claimed from the public treasury or responsible party. 

In practical terms, that means the seller must execute a formal cession of his personal causes of action: he must deliver to the purchaser the writs, procedural steps, and judicial rights under which he could have sued for the salarium. Only by transferring those actiones extraordinariae does the purchaser acquire the full capacity to demand and enforce the bonus when it falls due. If the seller merely paid the purchaser what he had already received, any uncollected or prospective salarium going forward would remain beyond the purchaser’s reach; the purchaser could not step into the seller’s shoes in court. By contrast, assignment of the extraordinary remedies places the purchaser in the identical position the seller once occupied, so that all future judgments or settlements for the salarium will enure to the purchaser’s benefit. 

This solution accords with the contractual principle that parties may transplant not only a thing but also the right of its full recovery, provided the seller cedes whatever legal powers he holds over it. It preserves the fairness of the bargain by ensuring the purchaser captures the entire economic value of the office, ordinary salary and extraordinary premium alike, whereas a simple cash payment of past receipts would shortchange him when new salaria accrue.

qa_pairs.question: A Roman testator writes in his will: “I bequeath to my freedman Sticho the public office (militia) I hold, on the condition that, so long as he lives with my young client Seius and provides him board and clothing, he shall enjoy that office when Seius reaches his twenty-fifth year.” In fact, Sticho cohabits faithfully with Seius until Seius’ untimely death at age twenty, before the twenty-fifth year. Explain whether Sticho can compel the testator’s heirs to provide him with that office, and if so, at what point in time he is entitled to take possession. Justify your answer by reference to Roman principles governing conditions in legacies of public offices.
qa_pairs.answer:
Under classical Roman law a conditional legacy imposes on the legatee the duty to fulfill the stipulation before acquiring the bequest; here Sticho must cohabit with and maintain Seius until Seius turns twenty-five. When an external event—Seius’s death at age twenty—renders performance of the condition (continued cohabitation until twenty-five) objectively impossible, the condition is nevertheless deemed fulfilled by reason of the legatee’s diligent performance up to the point of impossibility. This principle arises from the equity that, once the legatee has done everything in his power and the sole barrier to completion is an event no one could prevent, the condition is “satisfied” by the exhaustion of the legatee’s obligation. 

Scaevola, in his responsum, applies this rule to public office legacies. He holds that since the testator’s aim was to secure Seius’s welfare—and Sticho faithfully discharged that task until death—the heirs cannot evade their duty by pointing to the premature end of cohabitation. Consequently, Sticho acquires the right to the office. However, practical delivery of the office still awaits the date set by the testator: Sticho may not assume the office immediately upon Seius’s death, but only upon the completion of the twenty-fifth year that would have been Seius’s age. The reason is that the testator linked the office’s grant to the future date; even though the condition is treated as “met,” the temporal term for possession remains unchanged. 

Thus, Sticho can enforce the bequest against the heirs, but his entitlement materializes only when the original anniversary of the twenty-fifth year arrives. This balances the legatee’s forfeiture-freedom—he will not lose the office for reasons beyond his control—with deference to the testator’s timetable.

qa_pairs.question: Under Roman law, a public office (militia) was generally considered alienable and bequeathable, yet slaves had no capacity to acquire legal rights. A master, in his will, orders that his own slave is to receive his office “militia” by means of a fideicommissum (a confidential legacy). How should the court determine whether the slave himself—or instead the master’s heir—may claim that office? Identify the criterion governing this choice and explain the reasoning.
qa_pairs.answer:
Roman jurists recognized that nominally giving legal rights to a slave cannot directly transfer those rights, since slaves are incapable of acquiring either ownership or public office. When a will purports to leave an office by fideicommissum to a slave, the courts thus ask: Did the testator appreciate that his beneficiary was a slave? Two situations arise:

1. Testator knew the beneficiary was a slave.  In that event, the testator must have understood that the legacy of an office would fail if literally bestowed on a slave, and so must have intended instead that the heir receive the monetary equivalent—the office’s market value. The heir is accordingly entitled to the “aestimatio,” i.e. the assessed price of the office. The slave himself cannot claim so personal a bequest, because capacity to hold office was confined to free persons and the testator’s conscious choice was to confer value on the estate rather than to frustrate his own will.

2. Testator did not know the beneficiary was a slave.  If the testator was unaware of the slave’s condition, it would undermine his fundamental intention to ascribe an operative legacy; he would not knowingly have created a wholly null disposition. Equity therefore compels a more liberal construction: the fideicommissum should fail at the slave’s expense—he cannot be the claimant—but the heir cannot invoke the slave’s incapacity against the testator’s hidden design. The heir is thus prevented (“persecutio fideicommissi denegatur”) from enforcing mere invalidity to defeat the legacy. Instead, the heir must in good conscience honor the legacy for the benefit of the slave, procuring the office for him once he is free or otherwise meeting the testator’s underlying charitable purpose.

Accordingly, the knowledge of the testator regarding the slave’s status is the touchstone. If aware, the legacy converts to a pecuniary claim (aestimatio) by the heir; if unaware, the heir cannot reject the legacy outright, and equity requires that the slave eventually obtain his office when able.

qa_pairs.question: Within the mid-2nd century compilation of Roman juristic sources known as the Digest (I,2,2), we read of early jurists Publius Mucius Scaevola, Marcus Junius Brutus, and Marcus Manilius. The passage states: “ex his Publius Mucius etiam decem libellos reliquit, Brutus septem, Manilius tres: et extant volumina scripta Manilii monumenta.” However, the final words “scripta Manilii monumenta” have been judged corrupt, and successive editors have proposed various emendations. Summarize in detail each of the following scholars’ emendations: 1) Theodor Mommsen; 2) Francesco Ferrini (as adopted by Lenel and Bremer); 3) Franz von Pernice; and 4) the rearrangement proposed by Zimmern. Then explain Otto Hirschfeld’s critique of each proposal and reconstruct his own favored reading and reasoning. In your analysis, emphasize the internal textual plausibility arguments Hirschfeld uses—such as interpolation likelihood, expected specificity of titles, and manuscript evidence—to defend retaining “monumenta” and emending “scripta” to “inscripta.”
qa_pairs.answer:
Context and textual problem: In Digest I,2,2 (an abridged juristic history under Hadrian) Pomponius names three early Roman jurists as founders of civil law. He records that P. Mucius left ten booklets, Brutus seven, and M. Manilius three, concluding “et extant volumina scripta Manilii monumenta.” The phrase is clearly corrupt: it purports to say “and the volumes written by Manilius, monumenta, are extant.” But “monumenta” as title and “scripta” as verb both seem problematic. Editors have attempted to emend both words or the arrangement. Otto Hirschfeld carefully surveys these proposals and offers his own reconstruction.

1) Theodor Mommsen: In his edition of the Digest, Mommsen found “monumenta” incongruous and conjectured that the word was an interpolation. He proposed deleting “monumenta” entirely—restoring the text simply to “et extant volumina scripta Manilii,” “and the volumes written by Manilius still survive.” Mommsen’s objections: “monumenta” may have been later inserted by glossators or scribes; no further designation of Manilius’ works is supplied, so the title is suspect.

2) Francesco Ferrini (adopted by Lenel and Bremer): Ferrini argued that the verb “scripta” was itself wrong and should read “inscripta,” “inscribed.” Thus the phrase would be “et extant volumina inscripta Manilii monumenta,” “and the volumes inscribed ‘Manilii monumenta’ survive.” Lenel and Bremer accepted the shift from “scripta” to “inscripta” but did not accept further changes.

3) Franz von Pernice: In his Zeitschrift für Rechtsgeschichte article, Pernice proposed emending “monumenta” to “monimenta,” on the basis that “monimenta” (from monere) would be a more fitting term to denote legal reminders or cautions—i.e. summaries of procedural actions rather than generic “works.” Pernice thus read “volumina inscripta Manilii monimenta.”

4) Rearrangement by Zimmern: Otto Zimmern did not so much emend individual words as transpose them, proposing: “et extant volumina Manilii inscripta monumenta,” shifting the emphasis so “the volumes of Manilius titled ‘monumenta’ are extant.” Zimmern thus agreed “inscripta” was correct but inserted “monumenta” as a title in apposition to “volumina Manilii.”

Hirschfeld’s critiques and favored reading:

A) Against Mommsen’s deletion of “monumenta”: Hirschfeld points out that it is hard to see how exactly “monumenta” could have been interpolated. A scribe would have needed to introduce an entirely new substantive, and yet it fit grammatically without dislocation. Moreover, if one were to strip away the only title given to Manilius’ works, one would expect another, more specific designation to have existed in surviving manuscripts. The total absence of any other title suggests that “monumenta” is genuine.

B) Against Ferrini’s “inscripta” for “scripta,” Hirschfeld actually agrees—but only partly. He concedes that “inscripta” makes sense: authors often marked their works with inscriptions of titles. The sole attestation of “scripta” may be a copying error for “inscripta.” Thus he adopts Ferrini’s emendation of the verb but rejects Ferrini’s conjecture of merging the words into “inscripta Manilii monumenta” without clarifying the apposition relationship.

C) Against Pernice’s “monimenta”: Hirschfeld finds the argument linguistically weak. The derivation of “monimenta” from monere (to warn) is attractive in isolation, but it imposes a specialized legal meaning that the manuscripts give no hint of. Moreover, the orthographic shift from ‘u’ to ‘i’ in manuscript tradition would be unusual. Pernice’s conjecture had already been refuted by its own advocates (e.g. Bremer) for lack of any external support. Hirschfeld therefore rejects “monimenta.”

D) Against Zimmern’s word order: Hirschfeld acknowledges that Zimmern’s reordering is plausible. Yet he argues that the simpler conjecture is to preserve the word order orthographically attested, altering only the suspect verb. A more radical reshuffling is unnecessary and invites the same skepticism as wholesale deletion.

Hirschfeld’s preferred reading: “et extant volumina inscripta Manilii monumenta.” In his view the evidence supports emending only “scripta” to “inscripta,” as manuscript tradition commonly confuses the two, while retaining “monumenta” as the genuine title of Manilius’ three volumes. His key tests are:
• Interpolation implausibility: dropping “monumenta” leaves no alternative title. Introducing “monumenta” is unlikely as a gloss. 
• Expectation of detail: if “monumenta” were wrong, the text would specify the nature of Manilius’ writings more precisely.
• Manuscript consistency: no variant spells “monumenta” differently; the only variant verb is “scripta.”

By minimal emendation—only one letter change—Hirschfeld achieves a coherent sense: “the volumes inscribed ‘Monumenta’ by Manilius still survive.”

qa_pairs.question: In a passage of Cicero’s De re publica (Book II, chapters 14–15), Scipio recounts how King Numa Pompilius mitigated martial impulses “animis propositis legibus his, quas in monumentis habemus.” Lists of possible referents for “monumenta” have included annales maximi, pontifical registers, temple pontifical books, and collections known as the Ius Papirianum. Summarize the main alternative identifications of Cicero’s “monumenta” that Hirschfeld critiques (including proposals by Mai, Dirksen/Creuzer, Osann, Villemain, Schubert, Voigt, Zumpt, and Probus). Then analyze Hirschfeld’s argument that the “monumenta” here must be the still-famous Monumenta of M. Manilius. Explain how Hirschfeld uses Cicero’s own deployment of Manilius within the dialogue—his direct quotations and Scipio’s immediate next question on Pythagoras—to support this identification, as well as why he dismisses a link to pontifical or augural books. Assess the cogency of Hirschfeld’s linking of external textual context, authorial presence, and terminological uniqueness in this interpretation.
qa_pairs.answer:
Context: Cicero’s De re publica II 14–15 reports how Numa Pompilius tamed Roman warlike tendencies with religious rites founded on “the laws which we possess in our monumenta.” The term “monumenta” here is not self-explanatory. Different scholars have offered varied interpretations over the past two centuries.

Alternative identifications: 
• Karl Ludwig von Mai (no commentary) simply remained silent on what these “monumenta” were. He offered no interpretation, leaving Cicero’s referent undetermined.
• August Dirksen (cited by Creuzer) thought Cicero deliberately employed an indefinite term for an unspecified written source: “monumenta” just means “records,” without naming the exact collection. According to this view, Cicero obscures his source.
• Friedrich Osann believed Cicero referred vaguely to “written sources” without specifying which ones; the term is generic for documentary texts.
• Abel-François Villemain translated freely as “archives” (“par des lois que nous conservons dans nos archives”), ignoring precise denotation to render modern French.
• Johann Christian Schubert argued that “monumenta” must be the Annales Maximi—the year-by-year priestly records kept by pontiffs—because they were the primary ancient records of religious and legal acts. But he acknowledged he could not explain how “monumenta” came to denote these.
• Hermann Voigt, in his study of the Leges Regiae, cited the passage but did not offer an explanation of the term’s import.
• Carl Friedrich Zumpt connected “monumenta” to the pontifical books of rites (Pontificalbücher) or the Ius Papirianum, the early law code attributed to a Papirius. He suggested that Numa’s laws were preserved in collections of sacred law but offered no explicit textual rationale for “monumenta.”
• Probus, in a scholion on the Digest (De notis § 1), once referred to pontificum monumenta, but this was in a generic gloss on pontiffs’ records, not in Cicero’s text.

Hirschfeld’s objections to these proposals:
• Generic readings (Dirksen, Osann, Voigt) ignore the fact that Cicero elsewhere specifies exact sources when known. Here he names “monumenta” deliberately.
• Villemain’s free translation betrays a modernizing impulse, not a philological answer.
• Schubert fails to show how “monumenta” came to mean the Annales Maximi, nor does he connect Cicero’s context—speaking of archaic Numaic laws—to yearly chronicles of magistrates.
• Zumpt’s pontifical-books identification requires star inference—that Cicero would name temple registers without indicating their priestly nature. But Scipio is not introduced as a pontiff, and elsewhere Cicero distinguishes pontifical from augural books.
• The Ius Papirianum is a later juristic compilation of royal laws. Zumpt’s and others’ linking to it is premature: Cicero mentions the “monumenta” before any discussion of Papirian law, and Scipio distinguishes “pontificii libri” (pontifical books) from “augurales” (augural) separately (Rep. II,31). Cicero’s interlocutor Scipio was an augur, not a pontifex, so he would not refer to pontifical archives as “monumenta.”

Hirschfeld’s positive identification with Manilius’ Monumenta:
• Manilius in De re publica: Cicero explicitly introduces M. Manilius as a major participant in the dialogue (Rep. I,12; I,13; III,10; V,2). He calls him “vir prudens” (I,12,18) and “iuris noster interpres” (III,10,17). His presence is assured.
• Immediate textual link: In Book II, chapter 15 (immediately after Scipio’s mention of “monumenta” in 14,12–13), Manilius himself speaks to ask a legal-religious question concerning Numa’s relationship to Pythagoras. This sudden turn to a jurist who had published “Monumenta” underscores that Cicero’s prior reference to “monumenta” means Manilius’ work. Cicero thus signals to the informed reader: “These laws ‘in our monumenta’ are in that very book we are about to hear from its author.”
• Cicero’s further allusion: In Book V, chapter 2, Scipio praises Numa as “qui legum etiam scriptor fuisset,” “who had been a writer of laws,” adding “quas scitis exstare” (“which, as you know, survive”). This compliment addresses the author Manilius in the dialogue.
• Unique term: No other jurist’s writings are ever called “Monumenta.” We know from Pomponius (Digest I,2,2) and subsequent citation (Festus; Arnobius) that Manilius wrote a work entitled Monumenta, likely a collection of ancient Rome’s sacred and civil foundations (especially Numa’s laws).

Hirschfeld’s argument disarms pontifical or augural identifications: Cicero always indicates priestly registers explicitly as “pontifical books” or “augural books” when he means them (Rep. I,40; II,31). Here he uses a standalone term “monumenta,” paralleling Pomponius’ use of “Monumenta” as Manilius’ title. Moreover, Scipio’s role as an augur is never conflated with pontifical duties, so “monumenta pontificum” is excluded.

Assessment of Hirschfeld’s cogency:
• Internal consistency: He leverages Cicero’s narrative strategy—authorial shifts in dialogue—to tie an otherwise unexplained term to Manilius’ forthcoming speech.
• Terminological uniqueness: “Monumenta” never appears as a generic label elsewhere for religious records; its sole technical occurrence is as the title of Manilius’ work, cited by Pomponius.
• Circumstantial evidence: Later brief citations from Festus and Arnobius attribute ritual-historical notes (on human sacrifice; Novensiles) to Manilius’ Monumenta, reinforcing that his work contained corpus of archaic rites and laws that Cicero could summarize.

In sum, Hirschfeld’s argument robustly integrates textual context, dialogue structure, and philological uniqueness to demonstrate that Cicero’s “monumenta” must be Manilius’ Monumenta, not any generic or pontifical records.

qa_pairs.question:
Scholars have debated the relationship and relative chronology between two ancient collections of early Roman law: the Monumenta of M. Manilius and the so-called Ius Papirianum, as reported by Pomponius in the Digest (I,2,2).  

Summarize Otto Hirschfeld’s case for (a) the independence of the two collections—i.e., that Manilius’ Monumenta is not merely another name for the Ius Papirianum nor dependent on it—and (b) the priority of the Monumenta in collecting Numa’s laws.  In your summary, include his critique of the traditional account of the Papirian law collection (drawing on Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Pomponius, Asconius, Livius, Cicero’s silence in ad Familiares IX,21, and genealogical distortions by Valerius Antias or Licinius Macer), his analysis of how later jurists like Paulus and the anecdotal citations in Festus and Arnobius point to distinct content and dating, and how this leads to Hirschfeld’s conclusion that the Monumenta pre-date and then feed into the Ius Papirianum.  Critically evaluate the strength of Hirschfeld’s reconstruction of the two works’ interrelationship.
qa_pairs.answer:
Overview of the two collections:  
• Manilius’ Monumenta: a three-volume work by M. Manilius (consul 149 BC), cited by Pomponius as surviving in substantial form, likely a compilation of archaic or Numaic laws, rites, and historical documents, with a strong religious-historical emphasis.  
• Ius Papirianum: a juristic title for a compilation of the ‘royal laws’ (leges regiae), traditionally ascribed to an early Pontifex (Manius or Publius Papirius), reported in Dionysius, Pomponius (§ 2 and § 36), and later juristic commentaries.  

(a) Independence of the collections: 
1. Separate attribution in Pomponius (Digest I,2,2): Pomponius lists Manilius’ three volumes and, separately, Papirius’ compilation of leges regiae. He does not equate them; he treats them as distinct juristic authorities.  
2. Flawed Papirian tradition: 
– Dionysius of Halicarnassus (III 36) relates that Ancus Marcius’s wooden tablets wore away, and ‘after the exile of the kings’ they were recopied by a priest Gaius Papirius, “hierophant,” which scholars equated with Pontifex Maximus, thus inventing an ancient Papirius collector.  
– In another passage (V 1), Dionysius mentions a Manius Papirius as Rex Sacrorum, without connecting him to leges regiae.
– Pomponius (§ 2) calls the compiler Sextus Papirius, and (§ 36) Publius Papirius—varying praenomina within a few lines, corruptions that many have tried to correct. 
– Attempts by Zumpt and Voigt to standardize the praenomen (e.g., correcting Sextus to Secundus or Publius to Sextus) rest on conjecture, yet Pomponius elsewhere regularly preserves praenomina or cognomina when he knows them.  
3. Cicero’s silence: 
– In ad Familiares IX, 21 (around 46 BC), Cicero refutes Paetus’s mistaken genealogy of the Papirii, noting that in early Republic times they were patricians—yet he mentions no ancient priest or law-collector among them. If Papirius the compiler of royal laws had been known, Cicero (ever sensitive to antiquarian lore) would have cited him when correcting Papirii genealogy. His silence suggests no such tradition yet existed.  
4. Genealogical distortions: 
– Licinius Macer and Valerius Antias are likely culprits in fabricating Papirius ancestors and priestly offices to embellish a patrician gens, not genuine record-keeping. 

(b) Priority and transmission: 
1. Monumenta as first compilation of Numaic laws: 
– Cicero (Rep. II,14) refers to “leges…quas in monumentis habemus,” which Hirschfeld identifies with Manilius’ Monumenta by internal dialogue cues (as shown in the previous question).  
– Festus (p. 334) and Arnobius (Nat. 3,38) cite ritual-law items (e.g., suppression of human sacrifice; Novensiles) from Manilius, indicating content rooted in archaic law. 
2. Ius Papirianum emerges later and subsumes Monumenta content:  
– Pomponius still records Monumenta as extant alongside Papirian law, but later jurists increasingly cite Papirian laws under topics of ritual (Servius on Aeneid 12.836: lex Papiria de ritu sacrorum). 
– Paulus, in his commentaries, mentions a separate commentator Granius Flaccus on the Ius Papirianum, showing a juristic tradition distinct from Manilius.  
3. Chronological plausibility: 
– Papirian compilation, as described by Dionysius, is placed “after the exile of the kings,” broadly the early Republican period, perhaps in the Decemviral era adjacent to the Twelve Tables, centuries after Manilius.  
– Manilius, consul in 149 BC, wrote a retrospective antiquarian work, but his Monumenta survive as a distinct, earlier published corpus of Numaic materials referenced by Cicero at mid-Republican date.  

Conclusion and evaluation:  
Hirschfeld’s reconstruction rests on careful separation of later legendary tradition (Papirii genealogies, Dionysius’ garbled account) from documented juristic practice (Pomponius, Cicero, Festus, Arnobius). His strengths:  
• He marshals Cicero’s silence in ad Fam. IX 21 as strong evidence that no well-known Papirian law collector existed in the era just before Caesar.  
• He treats Pomponius’ variants on Papirius’s praenomen as corrupt rather than evidence of multiple compilations.  
• He integrates fragmentary citations of content (human-sacrifice laws) to show Monumenta’s distinct scope.  
• He plausibly dates Papirian law to early Republican rituals, which could only have absorbed Monumenta’s materials secondarily.  

Possible weaknesses:  
• The absolute chronology remains partly hypothetical: precise dates for the original Papirian compilation and its reception by jurists like Paulus are unclear.  
• Cicero’s silence can prove only absence of evidence, not necessarily evidence of absence—but Hirschfeld argues that Cicero would have eagerly cited a Papirian antiquarian.  
• Linking Festus and Arnobius citations to Monumenta depends on textual inference; without an explicit name in those fragments, attribution is probable but not certain.  

Overall, Hirschfeld constructs a coherent case for seeing Manilius’ Monumenta as the earliest organized exposition of Numa’s laws, later subsumed into an expanding corpus of regiae leges under the Papirian name. His judicious use of both internal evidence (dialogue context, manuscript variants) and external silence (genealogical tracts, juristic commentaries) offers a compelling model for disentangling two overlaid traditions of archaic Roman legal lore.

qa_pairs.question:
In the reconstruction of the Julianic Edict concerning the actio publiciana, Professor Perozzi argues that the absence of any mention of the traditio (delivery) in the edict’s clause can be inferred from the commentary fragment quoted in Digesta 16.1.7 §11, which runs in translation roughly as follows:

“‘Ut igitur publiciana competat, haec debent concurrere: ut et bona fide quis emerit, et ei res empta cum nomine sit tradita; ceterum ante traditionem, quamvis bonae fidei quis emptor sit, experiri publiciana non poterit.’”

Perozzi contends that this fragment reveals an absurdity if the original clause had mentioned traditio — namely, that it would have been superfluous for the commentator to add “ceterum ante traditionem…experiri publiciana non poterit.” He therefore concludes that the edict’s clause must have omitted any reference to delivery, and that the commentator is here supplying the missing condition. 

Professor Pacchioni disputes this reasoning. Drawing upon Pacchioni’s critique as presented in the excerpt, analyze in detail the logical flaw that Pacchioni identifies in Perozzi’s use of this commentary fragment to argue for the absence of traditio in the edict. Your answer should stand alone and fully explain the relevant reasoning.
qa_pairs.answer:
Professor Pacchioni’s critique focuses on the validity of inferring the omission of any mention of traditio (delivery) in the Julianic edict’s clause from the appearance of a commentator’s remark in Digesta 16.1.7 §11. The fragment in question declares that for the actio publiciana (the praetorian remedy) to be available, two conditions must concur: 1) the buyer must have purchased in bona fide, and 2) the res empta (purchased thing) must have been tradita (delivered) to him; furthermore, “ceterum ante traditionem…experiri publiciana non poterit” — “but before delivery, although one be a bona fide purchaser, he cannot use the publiciana.” From this, Perozzi reasons that if the edict’s original clause had itself mentioned delivery, it would have been quite pointless for the commentator to repeat that no action is possible before delivery. Hence he infers that the edict must have omitted any reference to traditio, and that the commentator is here introducing it.

Pacchioni exposes a multilayered flaw in this argument, which can be synthesized into three main points:

1. Misidentification of the Scope of the Commentary Fragment:
   • Pacchioni insists on distinguishing carefully between a commentary on the edict itself (commentarius ad edictum) and a commentary on the formula used in court pleading (commentarius ad formulam). The fragment at Digesta 16.1.7 §11 commentators on the words “et ei traditus est” (and it is delivered to him) in the *formula* as transmitted by Gaius IV.36 (providing for the upcoming nisi-case). In other words, this remark resolves an issue in the formula — which already mentions delivery outright — rather than explaining or supplementing the praetorian edict’s clause. Since the formula does mention delivery explicitly, there could be no surprise that the commentator needed to restate that delivery is a prerequisite. The real import of the fragment, Pacchioni argues, is to interpret those words of the formula under which it appears.
   • Consequently, the commentator’s “ante traditionem…experiri publiciana non poterit” does not seek to add an unexpressed requirement into the edict (as Perozzi would have it), but rather to elucidate how the formula’s wording “and it is delivered” should be understood in connection with the requirement “nondum usucaptum” (not yet usucapted). It clarifies that delivering the thing is what initiates possession and thus enables the possibility of usucapio — a detail about the *formula’s* mechanics rather than the edict’s terms.

2. Unwarranted Use of “Argumentum ad Absurdum”:  
   • Perozzi relies on an *argumentum ad absurdum*: if the edict itself had already demanded traditio, it would be absurd for the commentator to restate that no remedy attaches before delivery.  
   • Pacchioni counters that the “absurdity” disappears once one recognizes that the commentator is not paraphrasing the edict (where delivery might already be presupposed) but explicating the procedural significance of the formulaic words. A commentary can repeat an express term of the *formula* to show what consequences flow from it. It is by no means pointless to say “before delivery you may not invoke the action” if one is guiding a judge in applying the formula’s phrasing to the facts.

3. Failure to Recognize the Functional Interplay of Edict, Formula, and Commentary:  
   • Pacchioni emphasizes that Roman procedural texts are structured in three layers: the praetor’s edict (announcing the remedy in general terms), the formula (the precise linguistic vehicle by which the remedy is claimed in a trial), and later juristic commentaries (resolving interpretive or technical queries about how to use the remedy).  
   • In the formula reported by Gaius, “traditus est” is already present — so a commentary explaining how delivery matters to usucapio naturally focuses on the formula, clarifying that possession must actually commence via delivery before time can run. It does not follow that the edict originally omitted any mention of delivery.
   • Thus, Pacchioni shows that Perozzi’s method confuses layers and commits a category error: seeing a commentator explain the formula’s words “it is delivered,” he treats it as if the commentator were glossing the edict’s clause. But since the formula *already* mentions delivery, the commentator’s explanation is perfectly coherent and expected — and conveys no reliable information about what the edict said.

In sum, Pacchioni demonstrates that the commentary fragment is directed at the formula of procedure rather than at the edict clause, that repeating a requirement in commentary is no absurdity when the requirement forms part of the formula being interpreted, and that therefore no sound inference can be drawn from this fragment about whether the original edict clause mentioned traditio. The logical flaw is the mistaken conflation of commentary on the formula with commentary on the edict, leading to an unfounded negative inference about the edict’s text.
